A.q: A 59-year-old man has been intubated and mechanically ventilated for 3 days after a motor vehicle crash. He develops a new fever, purulent endotracheal secretions and a new infiltrate. How should this pneumonia be classified?
opts: The health care-associated category is retired and is no longer used to classify pneumonia or choose therapy. Tell: the current labels are community acquired, hospital acquired and ventilator associated, decided by setting and timing.

Correct. Ventilator-associated pneumonia develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation, and he has been ventilated for 3 days. Colonized secretions inhaled through the tube cause it, and it carries higher mortality and a longer intensive care stay.

Community-acquired pneumonia is acquired outside the hospital or present early in admission. His began after 3 days on the ventilator. Tell: an infection that starts after more than 48 hours of intubation is not community acquired.
ruled out by a stated finding

Hospital-acquired pneumonia is pneumonia 48 hours or more after admission; when it follows more than 48 hours of endotracheal intubation, the specific label is ventilator associated. Tell: the breathing tube decides the name.

A.q: A 52-year-old man has 12 mm of induration on a tuberculin skin test. His chest radiograph shows a fibrotic upper-lobe lesion, he does not recall ever being treated for tuberculosis, and he has no symptoms. Which step must come before latent-infection treatment?
opts: Correct. Fibrotic lesions warrant review of prior treatment and exclusion of active disease, and tuberculosis disease must be excluded before latent-infection treatment begins. Imaging cannot reliably determine activity, so microbiologic testing answers that question.
A repeat skin test in 8 to 10 weeks

Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after exposure is for an early negative result after a recent exposure. Tell: his test is already positive, and his lesion raises the question of active disease, which must be excluded.
A second chest radiograph in 1 year

Waiting a year leaves possible active disease unaddressed; fibrotic lesions warrant exclusion of active disease now. Tell: imaging cannot reliably determine activity, so microbiology is needed before treatment.
The blood test shows infection, which his skin test already shows, and neither test distinguishes latent infection from disease. Tell: the missing step is excluding active disease.

A.q: A 33-year-old woman with asthma wakes with cough and mild wheeze. Her peak flow is 70% of her personal best, placing her in the yellow zone of her written action plan. What does the plan direct her to do first?
opts: Going to the hospital belongs to the red zone and the danger signs, such as trouble walking or talking from breathlessness or blue lips. At 70% with mild symptoms she is in yellow. Tell: yellow means add quick relief and keep the controller.
Stop her controller until she feels better

The yellow zone keeps the green-zone controller going while adding quick relief; stopping it removes her anti-inflammatory treatment as she worsens. Tell: the plan adds medicine in the yellow zone, it never subtracts.
Add quick-relief medicine and keep her controller

Correct. In the yellow zone, 50% to 79% of personal best, asthma is getting worse: she adds quick-relief medicine (a short-acting beta-2 agonist) and keeps taking her green-zone controller. An oral steroid is added only if she does not return to green after an hour.
Start an oral steroid right away

The oral steroid enters the yellow-zone plan second, if her symptoms and peak flow do not return to green within an hour of quick-relief treatment. Tell: the first yellow-zone step is quick-relief medicine plus her usual controller.

A.q: A 44-year-old man who drank methanol has a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L) and a carbon dioxide of 29 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). By the Winter formula, what does his carbon dioxide show?
opts: A respiratory alkalosis is a primary fall in carbon dioxide, and his fall is fully accounted for by the compensation the Winter formula predicts, 27 to 31. No second disorder is needed to explain a 29. Tell: inside the range means compensation alone explains it.
ruled out by a stated finding

Impending respiratory failure is signaled when the carbon dioxide is higher than the Winter prediction, with an added respiratory acidosis. His 29 is within the expected 27 to 31. Tell: the warning is a carbon dioxide above the range.

An added respiratory acidosis is shown by a carbon dioxide higher than the Winter prediction, above 31 here. His 29 is inside the range of 27 to 31. Tell: compute 1.5 x 14 + 8 before calling it a second disorder.

Correct. Winter formula: 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, plus or minus 2, so 27 to 31. His 29 sits inside that range, so the fall in carbon dioxide is the expected respiratory compensation for his elevated-gap metabolic acidosis from methanol, with no second disorder.

A.q: A 66-year-old man with asthma had facial flushing, red eyes and wheezing several hours after taking aspirin last month. He now has low back pain from lifting. Which medication should he avoid?
opts: Meloxicam is a selective anti-inflammatory drug, and selective agents may be used in aspirin-sensitive asthma. It is a safe pain option for this man. Tell: the agents he must avoid are the non-selective ones, such as ibuprofen and naproxen.

Albuterol is his short-acting rescue bronchodilator, which every patient with asthma needs; it relaxes airway smooth muscle and is not a trigger. Tell: the medications that worsen aspirin-sensitive asthma are aspirin and its non-selective relatives.

Correct. Flushing, conjunctival irritation and wheeze after aspirin, even when delayed up to 12 hours, mark aspirin-sensitive asthma. Ibuprofen is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug that cross-reacts and must be avoided; selective agents may be used.

Celecoxib is a selective anti-inflammatory drug, which aspirin-sensitive patients may take, so it is not one he must avoid. Tell: his aspirin reaction rules out the non-selective group, of which ibuprofen is the common example.

A.q: A 55-year-old woman with known hypercalcemia has a metabolic alkalosis, a high urine chloride and a normal blood pressure. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 45 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). In which group of metabolic alkalosis does she belong?
opts: Post-hypercapnic alkalosis is saline responsive and follows rapid correction of chronic hypercapnia; she has neither a low urine chloride nor that history. Tell: it sits on the saline-responsive list.
Saline-responsive alkalosis has a low urine chloride (below 25 mEq/L) and volume contraction. Hers is high. Tell: high urine chloride rules out the responsive type.
ruled out by a stated finding

The hypertensive group (primary aldosteronism, mineralocorticoids, licorice) needs a raised blood pressure. Hers is normal, and hypercalcemia sits in the normotensive group. Tell: blood pressure splits the unresponsive causes.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A high urine chloride (above 40 mEq/L) marks saline-unresponsive alkalosis; with a normal blood pressure it is the normotensive group, which lists hypoparathyroidism and hypercalcemia and severe potassium depletion.

A.q: Which psychiatric conditions appear in the differential diagnosis of asthma?
opts: Correct. Psychiatric causes in the differential are conversion disorders, emotional laryngeal wheezing and, rarely, malingering or factitious disorder. They can mimic asthma, which is one reason an objective lung function test is part of the diagnosis.
Neither is listed as an asthma mimic. Tell: the psychiatric differential is conversion disorder, emotional laryngeal wheezing and, rarely, malingering or factitious disorder.

These are not the conditions listed. The psychiatric differential is conversion disorder, emotional laryngeal wheezing and, rarely, malingering or factitious disorder. Tell: the listed mimics produce a wheeze-like noise, not just a feeling of breathlessness.

Neither is listed as an asthma mimic. Conversion disorder and emotional laryngeal wheezing are, with malingering rarely. Tell: the mimics are conditions that can produce laryngeal noise, not primary mood or psychotic disorders.

A.q: A 60-year-old man with type 2 diabetes treated with metformin received several liters of normal saline during abdominal surgery. He has had no diarrhea. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.33 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 33 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 17 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 141 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 114 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which explains this blood gas?
opts: Diabetic ketoacidosis raises the gap with ketones; his gap of 10 is normal and his chloride high. Tell: ketoacidosis belongs to the elevated-gap mnemonic.

Correct. Low pH with a low bicarbonate is metabolic acidosis; the gap is 141 - (114 + 17) = 10, within 9 to 15, with a high chloride: a normal-gap, hyperchloremic acidosis. Saline infusion is a listed normal-gap cause (chloride retention).
Metformin causes an elevated-gap acidosis, above 15. His gap is 141 - (114 + 17) = 10, and his chloride is high. Tell: a normal gap with a high chloride points to the normal-gap list.
Hypoventilation raises carbon dioxide above 44; his is 33, lowered as compensation (Winter: 1.5 x 17 + 8 = 33.5). Tell: the low bicarbonate, not the carbon dioxide, matches his pH.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.q: A 75-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is reviewed for comorbidities that become more important with age. Which condition should be added to his screening at this age?
opts: Nasal polyps are common in intrinsic asthma, not an age-related comorbidity of this disease. Tell: screening at his age adds bone health and falls. They are not part of this disease's screening list.
Exercise-induced bronchospasm is common in children and adolescents with asthma. Tell: older adults with this disease are screened for osteoporosis, frailty, falls and cognitive decline.

Correct. Comorbidities in older adults add osteoporosis, frailty, falls and cognitive decline to cardiovascular disease, metabolic disease and depression. Inhaled corticosteroid-related fracture risk adds to the concern about bone health.
Allergic rhinitis belongs to the atopic triad of asthma and is not on this disease's comorbidity list. Tell: the age-related additions are osteoporosis, frailty, falls and cognitive decline.

A.q: A 44-year-old woman has a positive interferon-gamma release assay. She also reports 5 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss. Which action should be avoided at this point?
opts: A positive result requires clinical evaluation and chest imaging, so a radiograph is exactly what she needs. Tell: the action to avoid is treating latent infection before disease is excluded.
Symptoms require microbiologic testing, with 3 sputum specimens 8 to 24 hours apart. Tell: testing is required; preventive treatment before excluding disease is what to avoid.

Correct. Tuberculosis disease must be excluded before latent-infection treatment, and a positive result requires evaluation for disease before preventive treatment. Her cough, night sweats and weight loss make disease possible, so she needs chest imaging and sputum testing first.
Risk history guides evaluation alongside symptoms, imaging and microbiology. Tell: taking her exposure history is good practice; starting preventive treatment now is the mistake.

A.q: A 64-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 17 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 2. She has had no exacerbations in the past year. Which initial maintenance regimen is most appropriate?
opts: An inhaled corticosteroid adds pneumonia risk and is considered in group E with eosinophils of 300 or more. She is group B, low risk. Tell: group B's start is the 2 long-acting bronchodilators, without a steroid.

Correct. A score of 17 and a dyspnea grade of 2 mean more symptoms, and no exacerbations means low risk, which is group B. Group B starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic, ideally in a single inhaler for convenience.
Long-term azithromycin is used rarely and increases resistance and side effects. Tell: a symptomatic, low-risk patient starts on dual long-acting bronchodilators.
One bronchodilator is the start for group A, with fewer symptoms. Her score of 17 and dyspnea grade of 2 put her in group B. Tell: more symptoms call for both long-acting bronchodilators.

A.q: A 27-year-old man has just finished a 5-day course of oral corticosteroids for an asthma exacerbation and feels well. He asks whether he must slowly taper the medicine. Which reply is correct?
opts: He should continue it long term

Long-term systemic corticosteroids are reserved for refractory or poorly controlled cases because of side effects such as osteoporosis and hypertension. Tell: after an exacerbation course he returns to his inhaled controller, not to oral steroids.
He must taper over the next 2 weeks

A taper is not required after a short exacerbation course of systemic corticosteroids. Tell: short courses for exacerbations stop without a taper, while long-term systemic use is the setting where dose minimizing matters.
He should switch to an inhaled form for 5 days

Inhaled corticosteroids are long-term controllers whose maximum response may take months, not a 5-day bridge. Tell: the exacerbation course simply ends without a taper, and his regular inhaled controller continues.
No taper is needed after a short course

Correct. Systemic corticosteroids are used for control during exacerbations as a short course, and no taper is required. Long-term systemic therapy is different; it is reserved for severe or refractory cases at the minimum dose needed.

A.q: In acute bronchitis, what does green or yellow sputum indicate?
opts: No clue to a viral or bacterial cause

Correct. Colored mucus can occur in acute bronchitis but does not differentiate viral from bacterial infection. Purulent or colored sputum does not establish bacterial infection and does not justify antibiotics.

This is a common mistaken belief: purulent or colored sputum does not establish bacterial infection and does not justify antibiotics. Tell: routine antibiotics are not given regardless of sputum color.
Pertussis is suspected from a paroxysmal cough, post-tussive vomiting, a whoop or a relevant exposure. Tell: sputum color is not one of its clues.
Pneumonia is suggested by fever, abnormal vital signs, hypoxemia or focal consolidation, not by sputum color. Tell: colored sputum does not separate viral from bacterial illness.

A.q: A 38-year-old woman develops an acute respiratory acidosis after aspiration pneumonitis two hours ago. When will her kidneys begin to compensate?
opts: Renal compensation begins within 6 to 12 hours and may be complete in days, not weeks. Tell: hours to start, days to finish.
In 6 to 12 hours, completing over days

Correct. In respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride and retain bicarbonate; this begins 6 to 12 hours after onset, and complete compensation may take days. At two hours her bicarbonate is near normal.
They do not; the lungs compensate instead
When the cause is respiratory, the compensation is renal: the kidneys retain or excrete bicarbonate. The lungs compensate for metabolic disorders. Tell: respiratory problem, renal fix.
Within minutes, completing in an hour
Breathing changes carbon dioxide quickly, but renal bicarbonate control works over hours to days. Tell: the kidneys are the slow system.

A.q: Spirometry shows obstruction and the forced vital capacity is also low, raising the possibility of a mixed disorder. Which measurement confirms it?
opts: Diffusing capacity is reduced in emphysema and separates it from chronic bronchitis and asthma. Tell: it does not measure lung size, so it cannot confirm restriction.
An arterial blood gas measures oxygen and carbon dioxide and is usually kept for deteriorating or severe exacerbations. Tell: restriction is a volume question, answered by total lung capacity.

Correct. When an obstructed study also has a low forced vital capacity, a mixed obstructive and restrictive disorder is possible and is confirmed with total lung capacity. Lung volumes identify hyperinflation or coexisting restriction.
The bronchodilator response tells reversible from irreversible obstruction. Tell: the question of added restriction is answered by total lung capacity.

A.q: An 81-year-old woman with community-acquired pneumonia is alert and oriented. Her blood urea nitrogen is 17 mg/dL, respiratory rate 34/min and blood pressure 132/56 mm Hg. What is her CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) score?
opts: A total of 1 counts age alone. She also has a respiratory rate of 34, which is 30 or more, and a diastolic pressure of 56, which is 60 or lower. Tell: tachypnea of 30 or more and either low pressure reading each add a point.

A total of 2 misses the blood pressure point. Low blood pressure scores for a systolic below 90 or a diastolic of 60 or lower, and her diastolic is 56. Tell: a normal systolic pressure does not cancel a low diastolic one.

Correct. Confusion 0 + urea 0 (17 is not above 20) + respiratory rate 1 (34 is 30 or more) + blood pressure 1 (a diastolic of 56 is 60 or lower, even with a normal systolic) + age 1 (81) = 3. That is high severity, with a risk of death of 15 to 40%: hospital and urgent senior review.
A total of 4 would add urea, but her blood urea nitrogen of 17 mg/dL is not above 20. Tell: the urea point needs more than 20 mg/dL, so she has three points, not four.

A.q: Which cause of acute respiratory acidosis is a central nervous system depressant?
opts: Correct. Central nervous system depression from recreational drugs, an intracranial catastrophe or intravenous sedation causes acute respiratory acidosis by suppressing breathing, so carbon dioxide is retained.
Caffeine is a listed toxic cause of respiratory alkalosis. A depressant such as intravenous sedation causes acute respiratory acidosis. Tell: stimulants lower carbon dioxide, depressants raise it.

Thyroxine appears among the causes of respiratory alkalosis. A central nervous system depressant like intravenous sedation causes respiratory acidosis. Tell: the stem asks for a depressant, and thyroxine is not one.

Salicylates are a toxic cause of respiratory alkalosis, not a depressant of breathing here. Intravenous sedation depresses breathing and causes acute respiratory acidosis. Tell: salicylates, caffeine and nicotine drive ventilation up, sedation drives it down.

A.q: A 26-year-old woman who is 14 weeks pregnant comes in during October and asks about vaccines. Which vaccine should be avoided during her pregnancy?
opts: An age-appropriate recombinant vaccine may be used in any trimester of pregnancy. Tell: inactivated and recombinant vaccines are both acceptable; the live attenuated vaccine is the one avoided.
An age-appropriate inactivated vaccine is recommended in any trimester of pregnancy. Tell: the restriction in pregnancy is on the live attenuated product, not on inactivated vaccine.
Tdap is given during every pregnancy to protect against pertussis. Tell: Tdap is one of the vaccines recommended in pregnancy, so it is not the one to avoid.

Correct. In pregnancy, influenza vaccination uses an age-appropriate inactivated or recombinant vaccine in any trimester, and the live attenuated vaccine is avoided. Live attenuated vaccine has pregnancy and immunocompromise restrictions, so her pregnancy rules it out.

A.q: A 29-year-old woman who is 24 weeks pregnant has had 3 days of fever, myalgias and cough, and she is not short of breath. Influenza is strongly suspected, and a molecular test has been sent. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Correct. Pregnancy in any trimester is a high-risk group, and oseltamivir is preferred for high-risk patients, including in pregnancy. It is started promptly, even after 48 hours of symptoms, without waiting for confirmation in a high-risk patient.

Baloxavir is not recommended in pregnancy, and its single-dose use is limited to uncomplicated influenza within 48 hours. She is pregnant and at day 3. Tell: both the pregnancy and the timing rule baloxavir out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Clinical suspicion can justify treatment, and confirmation is not awaited in hospitalized, high-risk or progressively ill patients. Indicated antivirals are not withheld while results are pending. Tell: her pregnancy makes her high risk.

Risk status supports prompt antiviral treatment even when symptoms began more than 48 hours ago, and pregnancy is a high-risk group. Tell: the 48-hour limit applies to baloxavir in uncomplicated cases, not to oseltamivir in a pregnant patient.

A.q: A 66-year-old thin man with a long smoking history breathes through pursed lips. He has a barrel chest, distant breath sounds and hyperresonance to percussion. His diffusing capacity is reduced, and he produces little sputum. Which subtype best describes his disease?
opts: The chronic bronchitis subtype brings cough with sputum, rhonchi, possible cyanosis and edema, and a normal or near-normal diffusing capacity. He has little sputum and a reduced diffusing capacity. Tell: the reduced diffusing capacity singles out emphysema.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A thin patient with pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, distant breath sounds and hyperresonance, little sputum, and a reduced diffusing capacity is the classic emphysema picture (the pink puffer), from alveolar destruction and loss of elastic recoil.
Fibrosis is restrictive and shrinks the lungs, so hyperresonance and a barrel chest from hyperinflation do not fit. Tell: his findings show too much air in the chest, not too little.

Asthma's exam is often normal between exacerbations, and it does not destroy alveoli or lower diffusing capacity. Tell: a barrel chest with a reduced diffusing capacity in a long-time smoker is emphysema.

A.q: Which compensates more for the same change in carbon dioxide: acute or chronic respiratory acidosis?
opts: A respiratory disorder is compensated by the kidneys, not the lungs, and the renal response is larger when chronic. Tell: the compensating system for a respiratory problem is renal.

Correct. Bicarbonate rises about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide in acute respiratory acidosis, but about 3.5 mEq/L per 10 in chronic. Renal compensation takes days to complete, so chronic compensates more.
Acute compensation is smaller, about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg, because the kidneys have not caught up. Chronic is larger, about 3.5 per 10. Tell: more time means more renal compensation.
The table gives different magnitudes: about 1 per 10 acutely and 3.5 per 10 chronically. Chronic compensates more. Tell: the two rows have different numbers.

A.q: After a positive tuberculin skin test, what separates latent infection from tuberculosis disease?
opts: Correct. Neither the skin test nor the interferon-gamma release assay distinguishes latent infection from disease, so a positive result requires clinical evaluation and chest imaging; symptoms or suspicious imaging then require microbiologic testing.

The interferon-gamma release assay also detects an immune response to infection, so it cannot separate latent infection from disease either. Tell: neither the skin test nor the blood test sorts latent from active.

Induration is read against risk-based cut-offs to decide whether the test is positive; it shows infection, not whether disease is present. Tell: size decides positive or negative, not latent or active.
A repeat skin test in 8 weeks

Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for an early negative result in a recent contact, not for sorting a positive one. Tell: a positive result goes to clinical evaluation and imaging.

A.q: A 55-year-old man has asthma symptoms throughout every day, uses his rescue inhaler several times a day, wakes with symptoms nearly every night, and is extremely limited in daily activities. His forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 52% predicted. Which severity classification fits?
opts: Intermittent asthma allows symptoms on 2 or fewer days a week and normal function between exacerbations. He is symptomatic all day with 52% function. Tell: no feature here is near the intermittent column.

Mild persistent asthma means symptoms on more than 2 days a week but not daily, with a 1-second volume above 80%. Every feature he has is far worse. Tell: extreme limitation and 52% function are severe-column findings.

Moderate persistent asthma has daily but not continuous symptoms, waking more than once a week but not nightly, some limitation, and a 1-second volume of 60% to 80%. His 52% and nightly waking exceed that. Tell: under 60% is severe.

Correct. Symptoms throughout the day, rescue use several times a day, night awakenings often 7 times a week, extreme limitation and a 1-second volume below 60% predicted define severe persistent asthma.

A.q: A 41-year-old man with minimal smoking history has emphysema with a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.61. His chest x-ray shows the changes mainly in the lower lobes. Which test is most appropriate to find the cause?
opts: Correct. Patients under 45, or without significant exposure, should be evaluated for alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, and basilar emphysema adds to the suspicion. A level below 11 micromol/L with a severely deficient genotype is diagnostic.
Chest computed tomography can categorize emphysema but is generally not needed and does not identify the cause. Tell: the deficiency is diagnosed by the enzyme level and genotype.
An arterial blood gas is usually done only in a deteriorating or severe exacerbation. Tell: it describes gas exchange, not why a 41-year-old with little exposure has basal emphysema.
B-type natriuretic peptide is checked when associated heart failure is suspected. Tell: his age, minimal smoking and lower-lobe emphysema call for an alpha-1 antitrypsin level.

A.q: A 68-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted to the intensive care unit with severe community-acquired pneumonia. Pseudomonas grew from his sputum during an admission last year. Which agent provides reliable antipseudomonal coverage?
opts: Vancomycin is the methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus agent, added only when that organism's risk or local prevalence supports it. It does not cover Pseudomonas, a gram-negative rod. Tell: match the drug to the organism in the history, and his is Pseudomonas.

Moxifloxacin does not provide reliable Pseudomonas coverage, even though it is a respiratory fluoroquinolone used for community-acquired pneumonia. Tell: his Pseudomonas history needs cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam.

Correct. Prior respiratory isolation of Pseudomonas is assessed as a resistant-pathogen risk, so an active antipseudomonal agent is added. An antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam is used; moxifloxacin and ertapenem are not reliable options for Pseudomonas.

Ertapenem is named, with moxifloxacin, as not a reliable antipseudomonal option. Tell: being a broad agent does not make it antipseudomonal; cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam is the reliable choice.

A.q: A 58-year-old man with ventilator-associated pneumonia has had an adequate response to culture-directed antibiotics. What is the usual total duration of therapy?
opts: Three days is the floor for a clinically stable, nonsevere community-acquired pneumonia, not for ventilator-associated pneumonia. Tell: the hospital and ventilator pathway uses about 7 days when the response is adequate.

At least 5 days is the minimum for severe community-acquired pneumonia. His pneumonia is ventilator associated, where 7 days is usual. Tell: 5 belongs to severe community-acquired disease, 7 to the hospital pathway.

Correct. For hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia, a 7-day course is usual when the response is adequate, adjusted to clinical response, with prompt de-escalation as cultures clarify the diagnosis.

Fourteen days is longer than needed when the response is adequate; the usual course is 7 days, adjusted to clinical response. Tell: longer courses are for complications or specific pathogens, not an adequately responding ventilator pneumonia.

A.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: A 63-year-old woman with septic shock has a lactate elevation. Sodium 132 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), potassium 4.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L), chloride 96 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L), bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is her anion gap?
opts: Correct. Anion gap = 132 - (96 + 12) = 132 - 108 = 24, above 9 to 15: elevated. Lactic acidosis, the L of the mnemonic, raises the gap through unmeasured anions.
28 adds the potassium of 4.0 to the sodium. This formula uses sodium minus (chloride plus bicarbonate) only: 132 - 108 = 24. Tell: leave potassium out.
36 is 132 - 96, leaving out the bicarbonate. Both chloride and bicarbonate are subtracted: 132 - 108 = 24. Tell: two anions go inside the parentheses.
48 adds the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it (132 - 96 + 12). The correct result is 132 - (96 + 12) = 24. Tell: the parentheses make the bicarbonate a subtraction.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
A.q: A 74-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation takes a long-acting beta agonist, a long-acting antimuscarinic and an inhaled corticosteroid; he rarely uses albuterol. His atrial fibrillation episodes and palpitations have become more frequent since his regimen was started. Which component is most likely contributing?
opts: The inhaled corticosteroid's listed risks in older adults are pneumonia and fractures, not arrhythmias. Tell: palpitations and more atrial fibrillation point to the beta agonist.

Correct. Long-acting beta agonists produce sympathetic stimulation that can cause tachycardia and arrhythmias and can make atrial fibrillation worse; their cardiac effects are a listed concern in older adults. With rare albuterol use, the daily beta agonist is the likely driver.
Long-acting antimuscarinics are poorly absorbed, and their adverse effects are limited mainly to dry mouth. Tell: worsening atrial fibrillation fits the sympathetic stimulation of the beta agonist.
Excessive albuterol carries cardiac risk, but he rarely uses it. Tell: the daily long-acting beta agonist delivers continuous sympathetic stimulation, the likelier cause.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
A.q: A 78-year-old woman received a respiratory syncytial virus vaccine last year and asks whether she needs another dose this fall. Which counseling statement is accurate?
opts: Repeat dosing is not currently recommended after the single adult dose of respiratory syncytial virus vaccine. Tell: the adult recommendation is one dose for those 75 or older and those 50 to 74 at increased risk.
Every 10 years is the interval for Td or Tdap boosters, not for respiratory syncytial virus vaccine, which is a single adult dose. Tell: she already had her one dose and needs no more.

Correct. Respiratory syncytial virus vaccination is one dose for all adults aged 75 or older and for adults 50 to 74 at increased risk, and repeat annual dosing is not currently recommended. She already had her one dose.
Respiratory syncytial virus vaccine is not currently an annual adult vaccine, unlike influenza, which is given every year. Tell: one dose covers her; the yearly schedule belongs to influenza.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
A.q: A 36-year-old pet-shop employee has had a week of fever, severe headache, photophobia and a nonproductive cough. His pulse is 72/min with a temperature of 103°F, his spleen is palpable, and macular rashes on his face resemble the rose spots of typhoid fever. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mycoplasma causes gradual fever, persistent cough and headache, often in school-age children and young adults in group outbreaks. It has no bird exposure link and no Horder spots. Tell: sick birds plus facial rose-spot rashes point to Chlamydia psittaci.

Influenza symptoms can appear suddenly, over as little as a day, but his pulse is slow for his fever and his spleen is enlarged. Tell: relative bradycardia, splenomegaly and Horder spots point away from influenza.

Correct. Psittacosis is an occupational infection of pet-shop and zoo employees and poultry workers, caught from birds such as parakeets. Severe headache, photophobia, a dry cough, relative bradycardia, splenomegaly and Horder spots (facial macular rashes like typhoid rose spots) complete the picture.

Histoplasmosis follows inhaled soil or bird or bat droppings and causes fever, chills, myalgias, dry cough and headache. It is not described with relative bradycardia, splenomegaly or Horder spots. Tell: the facial rash and slow pulse belong to psittacosis.

A.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: A 41-year-old woman with Crohn disease has had profuse watery diarrhea for five days. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.31 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 31 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 137 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 112 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Respiratory acidosis needs a high carbon dioxide, and hers is 31, which is low. The low bicarbonate of 15 is what matches the acidemia. Tell: her low carbon dioxide is respiratory compensation.
ruled out by a stated finding
Metabolic alkalosis is a high pH with a high bicarbonate. Hers is 7.31 with a bicarbonate of 15, the reverse on both. Tell: diarrhea loses bicarbonate, which lowers it.

The gap is 137 - (112 + 15) = 10, inside 9 to 15, so it is normal, not elevated. Her high chloride of 112 is the hyperchloremic pattern of the normal-gap type. Tell: elevated-gap acidosis is normochloremic, and her chloride is high.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. The pH of 7.31 is acidemia, and the bicarbonate of 15 is low and matches it: metabolic. Gap = 137 - (112 + 15) = 10, within 9 to 15, with a high chloride, so it is a normal-gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis. Bicarbonate loss in diarrhea fits.

A.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
A.q: Which hazard of oxygen therapy is a risk for anyone near the patient, not only the patient?
opts: Correct. Fire is the hazard that threatens anyone near the patient, not only the patient, because oxygen is highly flammable. The others (hypercapnia, mucosal irritation, vasoconstriction) injure only the person receiving the oxygen.

Mucosal irritation affects the airway lining of the patient receiving oxygen and does not endanger bystanders. Fire is the hazard that reaches anyone near the oxygen. Tell: the key is the only hazard here that can harm other people.

Hypercapnia, carbon dioxide retention, is a hazard only to the patient breathing the oxygen, not to bystanders. The hazard that reaches others is fire. Tell: ask who is harmed; carbon dioxide retention affects the patient alone, fire affects everyone nearby.

Vasoconstriction is a physiologic effect in the patient's own vessels, not a danger to those nearby. Fire is the listed hazard that endangers everyone near the oxygen. Tell: the key spreads beyond the patient; vasoconstriction stays inside the patient.

A.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
A.q: A 44-year-old man who ingested ethylene glycol has an arterial pH of 6.62 (normal 7.35 to 7.45). Which complications does this pH threaten?
opts: Correct. A pH below 6.7 is unsustainable and may cause cardiac hypocontractility and irritability, seizures, cerebral edema and metabolic disturbances; it may warrant therapy to normalize the pH along with treating the cause.
Reduced release is an alkalosis effect (left shift). Acidosis lowers hemoglobin's affinity and increases release. Tell: the extreme-pH list is seizures, cerebral edema and cardiac effects.
Tetany from increased calcium binding with albumin occurs at a high pH, in severe respiratory alkalosis. His pH is 6.62. Tell: tetany belongs to alkalemia.
Potassium entering cells is the shift of alkalosis. In acidosis potassium leaves cells, so hyperkalemia may be present. Tell: acidosis raises potassium.

A.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
A.q: A 68-year-old woman going home on oxygen asks what signs to post. Which signage is taught?
opts: A sign with her pharmacy's number
The pharmacy's number is not part of the signage taught. The signs are No Smoking and, potentially, Oxygen in Use. Tell: signage addresses the fire hazard, not contact information.
No Smoking and Oxygen in Use signs

Correct. Home oxygen teaching is to post No Smoking signage, and potentially Oxygen in Use signs, within the home. Oxygen is highly flammable, and the signs warn everyone who enters, including visitors and firefighters.
A sign with her oxygen flow rate

A sign with her oxygen flow rate is not part of the signage taught. The taught signs warn about smoking and oxygen use because of the fire hazard. Tell: signs are for warning others, not for recording her prescription.
A sign with her recertification date

Her recertification date is not a posted sign. Recertification is about keeping home oxygen qualified at 12 or 3 months, whereas signs are about safety in the home. Tell: dates belong in her chart; warnings belong on the wall.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
A.q: A 68-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a resting oxygen saturation of 93%, but during a walking test she drops to 85%. She is mobile and reports exertional breathlessness. Which oxygen plan is indicated?
opts: Oxygen for more than 15 hours a day requires severe resting desaturation, 88% or less at rest. She is 93% at rest. Tell: her drop happens with exertion, so oxygen is given during exertion.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Severe exertional desaturation, 88% or less with exertion, qualifies for long-term oxygen during exertion. Her resting saturation of 93% is moderate desaturation, without a resting indication, so oxygen is used with activity.
Her drop to 85% while walking is severe exertional desaturation, which qualifies for oxygen during exertion. Tell: a normal-looking resting value does not rule out an exertional indication.
Night-only desaturation leads to an evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea, and her drop happens while walking. Tell: oxygen should match the setting where she desaturates, exertion.

A.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
A.q: A 64-year-old woman completes the 8-item symptom assessment test, each item scored 0 to 5: cough 2, phlegm 1, chest tightness 1, breathlessness on a hill or flight of stairs 3, limitation of home activities 2, confidence leaving home 1, sleep 1, and energy 2. What is her total score?
opts: Eleven drops 2 points, as if the energy item (2) were left out. Tell: all 8 items count, so add energy back: 11 + 2 = 13. Either way, her total of 13 is above the line of 10.
Twelve misses 1 point, as if one of the 1-point items (phlegm, chest tightness, confidence or sleep) were skipped. Tell: there are four 1-point items, and all of them count.

Correct. Cough 2 + phlegm 1 + chest tightness 1 + breathlessness on stairs 3 + home activities 2 + confidence leaving home 1 + sleep 1 + energy 2 = 13. A total of 10 or more counts as more symptoms when assigning her group.

Fourteen adds a point that is not there, as if breathlessness on stairs were scored 4 instead of 3. Tell: recheck each item; the correct sum is 13. An extra point would not change her group, but it is not the sum.

A.q: A 59-year-old man with alcoholism and chronic liver disease has community-acquired pneumonia and is stable for outpatient treatment. He had anaphylaxis to amoxicillin in the past. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Doxycycline by itself is for outpatients without comorbidities. His alcoholism and chronic liver disease call for a combination or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: with comorbidities, doxycycline only partners a beta-lactam.
Amoxicillin by itself is for outpatients with no comorbidities, and he has alcoholism and liver disease as well as an amoxicillin allergy. Tell: two separate clues rule this option out.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Alcoholism and chronic liver disease are listed comorbidities, so he needs a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin). His amoxicillin anaphylaxis removes the amoxicillin-based combination, leaving the fluoroquinolone, with a review of QT, interactions and fluoroquinolone risks.

This is a comorbidity regimen, but amoxicillin-clavulanate contains the amoxicillin that caused his anaphylaxis. Tell: allergy history is reviewed first, and it removes this combination, so the respiratory fluoroquinolone is the remaining listed option.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
A.q: A 27-year-old man describes cough and chest tightness with cold air and smoke over several months. His spirometry is normal, with no meaningful change after albuterol. Asthma is still suspected. Which test is most appropriate next?
opts: Correct. Bronchial provocation testing with methacholine or histamine is useful when spirometry is not diagnostic, as here, where a typical history meets normal spirometry. His normal lung function also clears the rule that provocation is not done below 65% predicted.

An exercise challenge is the provocation test used when exercise-induced bronchospasm is suspected. His triggers are cold air and smoke, not exercise. Tell: for a nondiagnostic spirometry with general triggers, methacholine or histamine challenge is the test.
ruled out by a stated finding

Annual spirometry is for monitoring the progression of known disease, not for settling a suspected diagnosis today. Tell: when spirometry is not diagnostic, bronchial provocation testing is the next test.

The chest x-ray in asthma is usually normal or shows hyperinflation, so it adds little after normal spirometry. Tell: when spirometry fails to show asthma, the next step is to provoke airway hyper-responsiveness with methacholine.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: Which three components establish the diagnosis of asthma?
opts: History, chest radiograph, and allergy testing

A chest radiograph is usually normal or shows hyperinflation, and allergy testing identifies triggers; neither measures airflow. The diagnosis needs an objective lung function test such as spirometry. Tell: only an airflow measurement can show the reversible obstruction that defines asthma.
History, physical exam, and objective lung function

Correct. Asthma is diagnosed from the history, the physical examination and an objective measurement of lung function. The objective measure matters because the exam can be normal between attacks, and it feeds both the diagnostic criteria and the severity classification.
Physical exam, serum immunoglobulin E, and sputum culture

Immunoglobulin E separates extrinsic from intrinsic asthma and sputum culture looks for infection; neither establishes asthma. The diagnosis rests on history, physical exam and objective lung function. Tell: a normal immunoglobulin E does not exclude asthma, since intrinsic asthma occurs with a normal immunoglobulin E level.
Symptom response to an oral corticosteroid trial

A steroid trial is not how asthma is diagnosed; systemic steroids are reserved for exacerbations and severe disease. The diagnosis needs history, physical examination and objective lung function. Tell: the objective test is spirometry before and after a bronchodilator, not a drug trial.

A.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
A.q: A 24-year-old man with a panic attack is breathing fast, with perioral numbness and tingling hands. His roommate hands him a paper bag to breathe into. What is accurate education about the bag?
opts: It safely corrects his carbon dioxide
The bag fails to correct carbon dioxide, and it may lower oxygen. Its effect is placebo. Tell: the paper bag fails on both counts, carbon dioxide and safety.
It is unnecessary and may lower his oxygen

Correct. Breathing into a paper bag is not necessary for hyperventilation: it fails to correct the carbon dioxide and may decrease oxygen, and any benefit is placebo. Hyperventilation is usually self-limited, and the cause is treated.
It is needed to prevent tetany

Tetany can occur in severe respiratory alkalosis from low ionized calcium, but the bag does not prevent it; hyperventilation is usually self-limited. Tell: treat the cause, not the carbon dioxide with a bag.
It works by raising his bicarbonate
Rebreathing does not act on bicarbonate; bicarbonate changes come from the kidneys over hours to days. The bag's benefit is placebo. Tell: bicarbonate is renal and slow; no bag reaches it.

A.q: An 80-year-old woman with dysphagia after a stroke lives at home. She has 3 days of fever, a productive cough and a new right lower lobe infiltrate, and imaging shows no abscess or empyema. She is admitted to a general ward with nonsevere pneumonia. She has never had methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas isolated and has had no recent intravenous antibiotics. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Support without antibiotics is the plan for chemical aspiration pneumonitis, a sterile injury after a witnessed aspiration. She has 3 days of an infectious syndrome with a compatible infiltrate, which is aspiration pneumonia and needs antibiotics. Tell: established infection needs antibiotics.

Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas coverage is added only for validated risks, such as prior respiratory isolation or recent hospitalization with intravenous antibiotics, and she has none. Tell: without those risks, nonsevere ward pneumonia takes a beta-lactam plus a macrolide.
ruled out by a stated finding

Weeks of a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor is the lung abscess plan, and anaerobic coverage is added only when abscess or empyema is suspected. Tell: her imaging shows neither, so she takes the ordinary nonsevere ward regimen.

Correct. Fever, productive cough and an infiltrate in a patient at risk of aspiration is aspiration pneumonia, an infection treated with the regimen for its setting and severity: here nonsevere pneumonia from home on a ward, a beta-lactam plus a macrolide. With no abscess or empyema, anaerobic coverage is not added.

A.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
A.q: A 66-year-old woman with confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 8 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 1. She was admitted to the hospital once in the past year for an exacerbation. Using the 2020 four-group scheme, which group is she in?
opts: Correct. A symptom score of 8 and a dyspnea grade of 1 mean fewer symptoms, and 1 exacerbation leading to hospitalization means high risk. In the 2020 scheme, few symptoms with high risk is group C (in the current scheme she would be E).
Group B is more symptoms with low risk; she has few symptoms and high risk. Tell: she sits in the opposite corner of the grid from B. Her symptom score of 8 is under 10 and her dyspnea grade is 1.
Group D needs more symptoms (score 10 or more, or dyspnea grade 2 or more) as well as high risk. Her score is 8 with grade 1. Tell: few symptoms plus high risk is C.

Group A is few symptoms with low risk, but her hospitalization makes her high risk. Tell: 1 admission alone moves her to the high-risk row. Her symptom score of 8 alone would fit A, but risk decides the row.

A.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
A.q: A 67-year-old man has a myocardial infarction and is placed on oxygen in the ambulance although his saturation was 98%. Which effect of oxygen makes this a problem?
opts: Correct. His saturation was 98%, so he was not hypoxic. Oxygen is not given in a myocardial infarction unless the saturation is below 91%, because oxygen causes vasoconstriction. Giving it to a man with a normal saturation exposes him to that effect without benefit.

Carbon dioxide retention is a listed hazard of oxygen, but it is not the reason oxygen is withheld in a myocardial infarction; that reason is vasoconstriction. Tell: the myocardial infarction rule points to vasoconstriction.

Fire risk is real around any oxygen, but it does not explain why oxygen is withheld at a saturation of 98% in a myocardial infarction. Tell: the myocardial infarction caution is about vasoconstriction, not ignition.

Mucosal irritation is the dryness and soreness of the nose from oxygen, especially without humidity at higher flows. It does not explain why oxygen is avoided in a myocardial infarction. Tell: irritation is local; vasoconstriction is the cardiac concern.

A.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
A.q: An 80-year-old man on home oxygen at 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier complains of a sore, dry nose and occasional bleeding. Which change addresses the cause?
opts: Apply a petroleum lip and nose balm

A petroleum-based balm is on the list of products to avoid with home oxygen, because oxygen is highly flammable. It would not be an appropriate treatment for his nose. Tell: petroleum products stay away from oxygen.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. He is on 5 L/min by nasal cannula with no humidifier, and has a sore, dry nose with bleeding. That is mucosal irritation. Humidity is used with cannula flow rates greater than 4 L/min, so adding humidity to the oxygen treats the cause.

A non-rebreather mask is a high-fraction device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well. He has a sore nose, not worsening hypoxia, and the mask would not solve it. Tell: his problem is dryness at a flow above 4 L/min.
Raising the flow to 6 L/min keeps him above 4 L/min, where humidity is already needed and he has none. A higher flow leaves the missing humidity in place. Tell: fix the humidity, not the flow.

A.q: A 28-year-old woman shared an office with a coworker diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis 2 weeks ago, and her exposure has now ended. She has no symptoms and no immune problem, and her interferon-gamma release assay today is negative. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: A negative test 2 weeks after exposure may simply be too early, because early infection can produce a negative result. Tell: the repeat test 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is what clears her.
Repeat the test in 8 to 10 weeks

Correct. Early infection can produce a negative skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, so testing is repeated 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure when indicated. She is symptom-free and immunocompetent, so no immediate disease evaluation is triggered.
Latent-infection treatment is for documented infection after disease is excluded, and her test is negative. Tell: the next step is to repeat the test 8 to 10 weeks after her last exposure.
Sputum testing is for symptoms or suspicious imaging suggesting pulmonary disease. Tell: she is symptom-free; her question is infection, answered by repeating the immune-response test later.

A.q: A 60-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 70% predicted, a 6-minute walk distance of 420 meters, a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 2, and a body mass index of 25. Based on her BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index, what is her estimated 4-year survival?
opts: About 18% belongs to scores of 7 to 10. Her total is only 1. Tell: only the dyspnea grade of 2 earns a point. Her walk distance of 420 meters and 1-second volume of 70% both score 0.
About 57% belongs to scores of 5 to 6. Her total is 1. Tell: a 1-second volume of 70% and a walk of 420 meters each score 0. Her body mass index of 25 scores 0 as well.
About 67% belongs to scores of 3 to 4. Her total is 1, from the dyspnea grade alone. Tell: 0 to 2 points predicts about 80%. She would need 2 more points to reach 3.

Correct. 1-second volume 70% (65 or more) = 0 + walk 420 meters (350 or more) = 0 + dyspnea grade 2 = 1 + body mass index 25 (over 21) = 0, for a total of 1. Scores of 0 to 2 predict about 80% 4-year survival.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
A.q: How is emphysema defined?
opts: Narrowing of the bronchioles is small airway disease, a third component under the umbrella term. Tell: emphysema involves the alveoli themselves, which are destroyed and permanently enlarged.
Reversible bronchospasm is the hallmark of asthma, whose obstruction improves after a bronchodilator. Tell: emphysema's alveolar destruction is permanent, so its obstruction does not reverse.

Chronic cough and sputum for at least 3 months a year over 2 years is the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis. Tell: emphysema is the one defined by pathology, the destroyed and enlarged alveoli, not by symptoms.
Destruction and enlargement of the alveoli

Correct. Emphysema is an anatomic, pathologic definition describing destruction and permanent enlargement of the alveoli, with air trapping. That separates it from chronic bronchitis, which is defined clinically by chronic cough and sputum.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
A.q: After a recent tuberculosis exposure, a first tuberculin skin test is negative. When is the test repeated?
opts: Two to 4 weeks may still be too early: early infection can produce a negative result, and the repeat is set at 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Tell: the repeat window is 8 to 10 weeks.
Four to 6 weeks falls short of the repeat window of 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Tell: the immune response needs time; wait 8 to 10 weeks.

Correct. Early infection can produce a negative skin test or blood assay, so testing is repeated 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure when indicated. Symptoms or high clinical suspicion still require disease evaluation now.
Sixteen to 20 weeks is later than needed; the repeat is 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure. Tell: the window is 8 to 10 weeks, not months later.

A.q: A 30-year-old man with no medical conditions has community-acquired pneumonia confirmed on chest radiograph and is stable for outpatient care. Molecular testing is positive for a respiratory virus, and he can be seen again in 2 days. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Atypical coverage is added when indicated in bacterial community-acquired pneumonia, but a viral-positive healthy outpatient with close follow-up may avoid antibacterial therapy entirely. Tell: adding drugs is the opposite of what his result allows.

Amoxicillin is the outpatient choice when bacterial community-acquired pneumonia is treated in a patient without comorbidities. Here the viral result, absent comorbidities and close follow-up allow the antibiotic to be skipped. Tell: this exception needs all three conditions, and he has them.

Ceftriaxone with a macrolide is an inpatient regimen for nonsevere pneumonia that needs a ward bed. He is stable for outpatient care. Tell: place of care comes from oxygenation, vital signs and severity scoring, and his are reassuring.

Correct. A viral-positive outpatient without comorbidities may avoid empiric antibiotics when close follow-up is reliable. His positive molecular test, absent comorbidities and arranged review in 2 days meet those conditions; antibiotics treat a bacterial syndrome, not a positive viral test.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: A 46-year-old woman has new-onset persistent wheezing and cough that began last year. She has nasal polyps. Allergy skin tests are negative and her serum immunoglobulin E is normal. She had a wheezing episode after taking aspirin for a headache. Which type of asthma is most likely?
opts: Catamenial asthma is timed to predictable points of the menstrual cycle, and her history gives no cyclic pattern. Tell: her clues are polyps, adult onset and an aspirin reaction, the intrinsic profile, not a monthly rhythm.

Occupational asthma follows workplace sensitization and improves on weekends and vacations; nothing in her history points to work. Tell: polyps, aspirin sensitivity and negative allergy tests describe intrinsic asthma, while occupational asthma is defined by its work pattern.

Extrinsic asthma is allergen-triggered and atopic, so skin tests would be positive and immunoglobulin E raised. Her tests are negative and immunoglobulin E normal. Tell: negative allergy testing rules out the allergic, extrinsic form.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Adult onset, persistent symptoms, nasal polyps, negative skin tests with a normal immunoglobulin E, and aspirin sensitivity all fit intrinsic asthma, the non-atopic form seen in about 10% of patients, which is usually more severe and persistent.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
A.q: A 71-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has had a chronic productive cough and weight loss. Her sputum acid-fast smear is positive. Which testing will identify the mycobacterial species?
opts: A smear identifies a group of organisms, the acid-fast bacilli, however often it is repeated; it does not distinguish tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria. Tell: species identification needs molecular testing and culture.

Correct. A positive acid-fast smear supports mycobacteria but cannot distinguish tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria. The species is confirmed with molecular testing and culture, and it matters because transmission and treatment differ.

Computed tomography can show patterns such as nodular bronchiectasis or fibrocavitary disease, but imaging supports suspicion and cannot confirm the organism. Tell: only microbiology, molecular testing and culture, names the species.

An interferon-gamma release assay is a blood test of the immune response to tuberculosis infection; it does not identify the organism growing in her sputum. Tell: the isolate's species comes from molecular testing and culture of the specimen.

A.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
A.q: A 40-year-old woman has persistent asthma symptoms and frequent rescue inhaler use despite a prescribed inhaled corticosteroid plus long-acting beta-2 agonist. She has not been seen since the prescription 6 months ago. Which step should come first?
opts: Monoclonal antibodies are specialist therapy for severe disease that persists despite proper treatment. Her adherence and technique have not yet been checked. Tell: non-compliance, the most common cause of poor control, is ruled out before escalating.

Correct. Non-compliance is the most common reason for poor symptom control, and follow-up visits review medications, compliance and correct use before adjusting therapy. Her increased rescue use signals poor control, so adherence and technique are checked first.

Long-term systemic steroids are kept for refractory cases because of osteoporosis, hypertension and ulcer risk. Tell: refractory means poor control despite correct use, which has not been established in this patient.
Steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon, while non-compliance is the most common reason for poor control. Tell: check the common cause, adherence and technique, before chasing a rare one.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
A.q: What is the main limitation of a positive Pneumocystis polymerase chain reaction result?
opts: Correct. Polymerase chain reaction for Pneumocystis on induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage is highly sensitive but can detect colonization, so a positive result is interpreted with the symptoms, the imaging and the organism burden rather than read as proof of pneumonia.
It needs a lung biopsy specimen

Lung biopsy is rarely needed and is kept for when less invasive studies are nondiagnostic; the test is run on induced sputum or lavage fluid. Tell: the limitation of the result is colonization, not the specimen it needs.

This reverses the real problem: the polymerase chain reaction is highly sensitive. Its weakness is the opposite problem, a positive result from colonization. Tell: a sensitive test's risk is a positive that does not mean disease, so weigh symptoms, imaging and organism burden.
It cannot be run on induced sputum

Induced sputum is one of the two recommended specimens: induced sputum or bronchoalveolar lavage is sent for microscopy and/or polymerase chain reaction. Tell: the specimen to avoid relying on is spontaneously expectorated sputum, which has poor sensitivity.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
A.q: For at least how long is chronic cavitary histoplasmosis treated?
opts: A month echoes the old 4-week symptom rule, which the current guidance replaces. Tell: chronic cavitary disease needs azole therapy for at least 12 months.
Three months is far short of the course for chronic cavitary disease. Tell: the azole is given for at least 12 months.
Six months is half the needed course. Tell: chronic cavitary histoplasmosis needs at least 12 months of azole therapy.
Correct. Chronic cavitary disease requires prolonged azole therapy, usually at least 12 months. The current updates replace a simple 4-week symptom rule for deciding treatment.

A.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
A.q: A 52-year-old woman with a body mass index of 58 has loud snoring, witnessed pauses in breathing at night and daytime sleepiness. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 55 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 30 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Her bicarbonate is high, but her pH is not high; the raised carbon dioxide of 55 explains the low pH, so the bicarbonate is compensation. Tell: with a high carbon dioxide and a low pH, the bicarbonate is responding, not driving.
Respiratory alkalosis needs a low carbon dioxide, and hers is 55. She is retaining carbon dioxide, the opposite. Tell: hypoventilation raises carbon dioxide, hyperventilation lowers it.

Correct. The pH of 7.34 is just below normal, with a carbon dioxide of 55 that is high and matches it. Bicarbonate is 30, a rise of about 5 (1.5 x 3.5), the size of chronic compensation. Obesity, sleep disordered breathing and chronic hypercapnia form the obesity hypoventilation triad.

Acute compensation would leave bicarbonate near 25 to 26 (55 is 15 above 40). Her 30 is the fuller chronic renal response, matching a long-standing condition. Tell: obesity hypoventilation is chronic, so expect the larger bicarbonate rise.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
A.q: A 27-year-old woman with asthma notices that her wheezing and chest tightness flare at the same predictable point in every menstrual cycle and are mild the rest of the month. Which type of asthma describes this pattern?
opts: Correct. Catamenial asthma is asthma whose symptoms occur at predictable times during the menstrual cycle, as with this woman's monthly flares. It is one of the other types of asthma alongside occupational, cardiac, exercise-induced and aspirin-sensitive patterns.
Aspirin-sensitive asthma flares after taking aspirin, and the stem mentions no drug. Tell: her flares are tied to the menstrual cycle, not to a medication.
ruled out by a stated finding
Occupational asthma follows the work week, improving on weekends and vacations. Her flares follow her menstrual cycle. Tell: a monthly rhythm points to hormones, a weekly rhythm to the workplace.

Intrinsic asthma is defined by negative allergy testing, adult onset and often nasal polyps, not by cyclic timing. Tell: the decisive clue here is the predictable menstrual timing, the definition of catamenial asthma.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
A.q: A 35-year-old man with asthma and a body mass index of 36 asks how his weight relates to his asthma. Which statement is accurate?
opts: Obesity matters just for exercise-induced symptoms
The link between obesity and asthma is not limited to exercise; asthma is more frequent and harder to control overall above a body mass index of 30. Tell: the effect covers his asthma as a whole.
Obesity has no link to asthma
Obesity is a listed endogenous factor: asthma is more frequent in people with a body mass index above 30. Tell: weight is linked to both how often asthma occurs and how hard it is to control.
Obesity makes asthma symptoms more difficult to control, not milder. Tell: a body mass index above 30 is linked to more frequent asthma and harder control.
Obesity makes asthma harder to control

Correct. Asthma is more frequent in people with a body mass index above 30, and their symptoms are more difficult to control, although the mechanism is unknown. His body mass index of 36 places him in that group.

A.q: A 70-year-old unvaccinated man with diabetes and heart failure has mild coronavirus disease 2019 that began 6 days ago. His oxygen saturation is 96% on room air. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Systemic corticosteroids are not used for coronavirus disease 2019 without hypoxemia unless another indication exists. His saturation is 96% on room air. Tell: dexamethasone belongs to the hospital pathway for hypoxemia.

Molnupiravir is an adult alternative only when the preferred options are unsuitable, and remdesivir is still available within its 7-day window. Tell: the preferred option comes first when it is still possible.

Correct. A high-risk outpatient with mild or moderate disease and no hypoxemia is offered nirmatrelvir/ritonavir within 5 days or a three-day intravenous remdesivir course within 7 days of symptom onset. At day 6 only the remdesivir window is still open, and his age, comorbidities and lack of vaccination make him high risk.
Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir must start within 5 days of symptom onset, and he is at day 6. Tell: count the days; the 5-day window has closed, while the 7-day remdesivir window has not.
ruled out by a stated finding

A.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
A.q: A 70-year-old woman with interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension and a hematocrit of 52% has a resting room-air saturation of 89%. Which finding makes her qualify?
opts: A hematocrit of 52% is below the threshold of above 56% needed for polycythemia to count. It does not qualify her. Tell: the hematocrit must be above 56%.

Interstitial lung disease is not one of the qualifying comorbidities. The list is pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale and a hematocrit above 56%. Tell: it is the complications, not the lung diagnosis, that count.

At 89% alone she would not qualify, but she does not stand on 89% alone. Her pulmonary hypertension adds the comorbidity that makes the saturation qualify. Tell: 89% plus a listed comorbidity qualifies.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Her resting saturation of 89% is just above the Group I cutoff of 88%, so she needs a comorbidity. Pulmonary hypertension is one of the listed qualifying findings, so it makes her qualify as Group II.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
A.q: A 70-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a single sputum culture that grows Mycobacterium avium complex at a routine visit. His symptoms are at baseline and no chest imaging has been done. Which best describes his status?
opts: The isolate is Mycobacterium avium complex, but one culture with baseline symptoms and no imaging does not prove disease. Tell: every domain must be met, including a second culture of the same species or a qualifying lavage or biopsy.

Latent tuberculosis infection is shown by a skin test or interferon-gamma release assay with no disease. Tell: his finding is an environmental nontuberculous species in sputum, a different organism altogether.
Mycobacterium avium complex is a nontuberculous mycobacterium, not a member of the tuberculosis complex. Tell: species identification separates them, because transmission and treatment differ.

Correct. A respiratory isolate alone does not prove nontuberculous disease. Diagnosis requires all domains: compatible symptoms and imaging, exclusion of alternatives and usually 2 or more sputum cultures with the same species. He has one culture, no new symptoms and no imaging.
