B.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
B.q: A 63-year-old woman with confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 18 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 2. She has had no exacerbations in the past year. Under the current three-group scheme, which group is she in?
opts: Correct. A symptom score of 18 (10 or more) and a dyspnea grade of 2 (2 or more) mean more symptoms, and no exacerbations means low risk. More symptoms with low risk is group B, which starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic.
Group E needs high exacerbation risk, 2 or more moderate exacerbations or a hospitalization. She had none. Tell: symptoms alone, however heavy, cannot make a patient E.
Group A requires fewer symptoms, a symptom score under 10 and a dyspnea grade of 0 to 1. Her 18 and grade 2 exceed both. Tell: a score of 10 or more moves her out of A.
Group D belongs to the 2020 scheme and needs both more symptoms and high risk. Tell: with low risk she is B in either scheme. Her low risk keeps her out of D.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 34-year-old woman has had a cough for 10 days that began with a cold. Her sputum is green, and she asks for an antibiotic. Her temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate and oxygen saturation are normal, and her lungs have scattered rhonchi that clear with coughing and no focal findings. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Routine sputum culture and chest radiography are unnecessary in uncomplicated cases; imaging is for abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings or clinical risk that raise concern for pneumonia. She has none of these. Tell: order a test only when its result would change a decision.

Correct. Normal vital signs, no focal lung findings and rhonchi that clear with a cough describe uncomplicated acute bronchitis, usually a self-limited viral illness. Green or yellow sputum does not separate viral from bacterial infection, so no antibiotic is given; explain the expected course and agree on symptom goals.

Fluoroquinolones such as levofloxacin are not default bronchitis treatments, and antibiotic harms include adverse effects, Clostridioides difficile infection and resistance. Tell: a respiratory fluoroquinolone belongs to the community-acquired pneumonia pathway, not to a viral chest cold with normal vital signs.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate is named as not a default bronchitis treatment, and routine antibiotics are not prescribed for uncomplicated bronchitis regardless of cough duration or sputum color. Her normal vital signs keep her out of the pneumonia pathway. Tell: green sputum alone never earns an antibiotic.

B.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
B.q: A 21-year-old man with extrinsic asthma flares whenever he cleans his apartment, and allergy skin testing shows sensitivity to house dust mites. His controller and rescue inhalers are prescribed. Which non-drug measure should be added?
opts: Move from the city to a rural area
Moving is not a listed measure; trigger avoidance and environmental control are. Tell: his identified trigger is dust mites inside his home, so environmental control there is the measure.

Exercise is a listed trigger, but asthma treatment aims for no limitation on physical activity, so cutting activity is not the measure. Tell: his trigger, shown by skin testing and cleaning flares, is dust mites, so avoidance targets the home.
Reduce dust mite exposure at home

Correct. Non-pharmacological asthma treatment is trigger avoidance and environmental control. Dust mites are the most common inhaled allergen trigger, and his skin test and cleaning-related flares identify it, so reducing his exposure at home is the added measure.

Immunotherapy may be considered for allergic triggers, but it must be done in a controlled environment because it can induce bronchoconstriction. Tell: home use is unsafe, and the first non-drug step is avoiding the dust mite trigger.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 67-year-old woman with ventilator-associated pneumonia was started on cefepime plus vancomycin because methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is common in her unit. On day 3 her respiratory culture grows Pseudomonas susceptible to cefepime, and no Staphylococcus aureus grows. She is improving. What is the most appropriate change?
opts: Two antipseudomonal classes are for selected patients with resistance risk or high mortality risk at the start of therapy. Tell: her organism is susceptible to cefepime and she is improving, so the move is to narrow, not to broaden.

Moxifloxacin does not provide reliable Pseudomonas coverage, so it would not treat the organism that grew. Tell: narrow within an active antipseudomonal agent, here the cefepime her isolate is susceptible to.

Keeping both drugs ignores the culture, which grew no Staphylococcus aureus, and 14 days is longer than the usual 7-day course with an adequate response. Tell: once cultures clarify the cause, therapy is narrowed promptly, not continued unchanged.

Correct. Her culture shows cefepime-susceptible Pseudomonas and no Staphylococcus aureus, and she is improving, so therapy is de-escalated to the culture and susceptibility results: the vancomycin added for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is stopped and cefepime continues, usually for 7 days in total.

B.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
B.q: A 72-year-old man with chronic lung disease is drowsy and confused, with asterixis (a flapping tremor of the outstretched hands). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.22 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 75 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 30 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder best explains his findings?
opts: His bicarbonate is high, but his pH of 7.22 is low, and a primary metabolic alkalosis would raise the pH. The bicarbonate is renal compensation for the retained carbon dioxide. Tell: the pH direction names the primary disorder.
Respiratory alkalosis is a low carbon dioxide with a high pH. His carbon dioxide is 75 with a pH of 7.22, the reverse. Tell: asterixis and somnolence point to carbon dioxide retention.

Correct. The pH of 7.22 is acidemia, and the carbon dioxide of 75 is high and matches it, so it is respiratory acidosis. Bicarbonate of 30 is the renal response. Somnolence, confusion and asterixis are its listed clinical findings, and chronic lung disease fits.

Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate, and his is 30, which is high. The high carbon dioxide drives his acidemia and his neurologic findings. Tell: drowsiness, confusion and asterixis come from carbon dioxide retention.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 56-year-old man with newly confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 6, a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 1, and no exacerbations in the past year. Which initial medication is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. A score of 6 and a dyspnea grade of 1 mean few symptoms, and no exacerbations means low risk, so he is group A, which starts with 1 bronchodilator, short- or long-acting. He still needs smoking cessation if he smokes, and physical activity.

A long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic is the start for group B or E. His few symptoms and no exacerbations make him group A. Tell: the combination is for more symptoms or high risk.
Inhaled corticosteroids cannot be used alone in this disease; they must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist and they raise pneumonia risk. Tell: group A starts with a single bronchodilator.
Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, and he has had none. Tell: a low-symptom, low-risk patient starts on 1 bronchodilator, not systemic steroids.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 64-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is taught to breathe out slowly through pursed lips when she is short of breath. She asks why it helps. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Pursed lips act during expiration, slowing outflow and raising airway pressure; they do not speed inspiration. Tell: the problem being treated is airway collapse while breathing out.

Pursed-lip breathing works on airway pressure, not on the heart; heart rate is often above 100 in these patients for other reasons. Tell: the benefit is mechanical, holding airways open during expiration.
Mucus hypersecretion comes from gland hyperplasia in chronic bronchitis and is not changed by breathing technique. Tell: pursed-lip breathing raises airway pressure to prevent collapse.

Correct. Pursed-lip breathing increases intra-airway pressure, which keeps the airways open during expiration and allows more gas exchange. It counters the collapse of airways that loss of elastic recoil causes in emphysema.

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: A 67-year-old man has hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic, stable chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and osteoarthritis for which he takes aspirin. He feels weak. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 46 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.1 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is low. Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Correct. High pH with a high bicarbonate is metabolic alkalosis, and the low urine chloride marks the saline-responsive type. Diuretic therapy is a saline-responsive cause, and the low potassium and weakness fit; the carbon dioxide of 46 is the expected compensation.

Primary aldosteronism is a saline-unresponsive, hypertensive cause, and saline-unresponsive alkalosis has a high urine chloride, above 40 mEq/L. His urine chloride is low, which points to a saline-responsive cause such as his diuretic. Tell: low urine chloride means saline responsive.
ruled out by a stated finding

Salicylates (aspirin) are a listed toxic cause of respiratory alkalosis, a primary fall in carbon dioxide. His carbon dioxide is 46 and his bicarbonate 33, so the primary change is metabolic. Tell: a salicylate alkalosis has a low carbon dioxide, not a high bicarbonate.
ruled out by a stated finding

His lung disease would cause respiratory acidosis: a high carbon dioxide driving a low pH. His pH is 7.48, alkalemic, and the carbon dioxide of 46 is only the small rise that compensates a metabolic alkalosis. Tell: his pH is alkalemic, so the primary disorder is not an acidosis.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 34-year-old woman who works in a setting with ongoing tuberculosis transmission has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on targeted testing. She has no symptoms, her examination is normal and her chest radiograph is normal. Which best describes her tuberculosis status?
opts: Correct. A positive interferon-gamma release assay shows infection, and her clinical evaluation found no evidence of disease: no symptoms, a normal examination and a normal radiograph, which is usual in latent infection. Latent infection is asymptomatic and not infectious.

Progressive primary tuberculosis is disease that develops soon after initial infection when immune containment fails, so it brings clinical findings. Tell: a symptom-free woman with a normal examination and radiograph has contained infection, not progressive disease.

Reactivation is latent infection that has progressed to disease, often with impaired immunity, so it brings symptoms or imaging findings. Tell: nothing here has progressed; she is still at the latent stage.

Disease needs more than an immune response: symptoms such as persistent cough, fever, night sweats or weight loss, or suspicious imaging, then microbiologic testing. Tell: she has none of these, and the blood test cannot by itself distinguish latent infection from disease.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 71-year-old man is recovering in the hospital from an exacerbation. He has been clinically stable for 18 hours, walks across the room, eats and sleeps without waking from breathlessness, and his home oxygen is arranged, but he still needs albuterol every 2 hours. Which finding delays his discharge?
opts: Clinical stability for 12 to 24 hours is required, and 18 hours meets it. Tell: the criterion he fails is rescue use, needed every 2 hours rather than every 4 or less often.

Correct. A discharge criterion is needing inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonist no more often than every 4 hours. Every 2 hours means his airflow is not yet controlled enough for home, even though his other criteria are met.
Walking across the room, for a patient who was ambulatory, is a discharge criterion that he meets. Tell: his barrier is how often he still needs albuterol.
Completed follow-up and home-care arrangements, such as oxygen delivery, are discharge criteria, so this supports discharge. Tell: the albuterol frequency is what holds him.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
B.q: A 30-year-old man has had mild asthma since childhood, controlled with occasional albuterol. He asks whether his asthma is likely to become severe as he ages. Which reply is most accurate?
opts: Correct. Asthma severity rarely varies for a given patient: mild asthma rarely becomes severe, and severe asthma is usually severe at onset. His long history of mild disease predicts it will most likely stay mild.
Severity rises steadily with each decade
Asthma severity rarely varies over a patient's life. Tell: the course is stable severity, with severe asthma usually severe at onset rather than built up over decades.
Severe asthma is usually severe at onset, so it does not usually begin as mild disease. Tell: this reverses the course, in which a patient's severity stays largely the same from the start.
Most mild asthma turns severe within a decade
Severity rarely changes for a patient, so mild disease does not typically progress to severe. Tell: severe asthma is usually severe from the start, not a later stage of mild asthma.

B.topic: Reading the fraction from the flow
B.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
B.q: A 75-year-old man's family turned his home nasal cannula up to 9 L/min because he felt short of breath. About what fraction of inspired oxygen does he receive at that setting?
opts: Correct. A nasal cannula can be turned to any setting, but the fraction stops at 44% (reached at 6 L/min). At 9 L/min he gets no more than that, so the extra 3 liters add oxygen to his nose but not to his fraction.

56% would follow from continuing to add 4% per liter, but the cannula's fraction maxes out at 44%. The knob can turn over 6 L/min, yet the fraction does not rise. Tell: the cannula has a ceiling; the arithmetic stops at 6 L/min.
60% belongs to the low end of a non-rebreather mask's 60-100% range at 10-15 L/min. A cannula does not reach it. Tell: you need a reservoir bag device to get above 44%.
100% is the top of the non-rebreather's range, requiring a reservoir bag and 10-15 L/min. A cannula at 9 L/min cannot reach it. Tell: the cannula is a low flow device with a hard ceiling of 44%.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 68-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 45% predicted, a 6-minute walk distance of 200 meters, a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 3, and a body mass index of 20. What is his BODE (body mass index, obstruction, dyspnea, exercise) index score?
opts: Five undercounts by 2, as if the walk distance were scored 0 or the dyspnea grade missed. Tell: 200 meters scores 2 and a dyspnea grade of 3 scores 2.
Six misses 1 point, most often the body mass index: a value of 21 or less scores 1. Tell: his body mass index of 20 adds the final point to reach 7. A total of 7 predicts about 18% 4-year survival.

Correct. 1-second volume 45% (36 to 49) = 2 + walk 200 meters (150 to 249) = 2 + dyspnea grade 3 = 2 + body mass index 20 (21 or less) = 1, for a total of 7. A score of 7 to 10 predicts about 18% 4-year survival.
Eight overcounts by 1, as if the 1-second volume of 45% scored 3. Tell: 3 points is for 35% or less; 36% to 49% scores 2. His total stays at 7. Recount: 2 + 2 + 2 + 1.

B.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with heart disease has a severe metabolic alkalosis from vomiting. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.56 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 49 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 43 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). How does her alkalemia affect oxygen delivery to her tissues?
opts: Increased delivery is the effect of acidosis, which lowers hemoglobin's affinity and shifts the curve right. Her pH is 7.56. Tell: alkalosis holds oxygen on hemoglobin; acidosis releases it.
It shifts the curve to the right
A right shift is caused by acidosis. Alkalosis shifts the curve left, raising affinity and decreasing delivery. Tell: alkalosis left, acidosis right.
pH changes hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen in both directions; alkalosis raises affinity and decreases delivery. Tell: the dissociation curve shifts with pH.
ruled out by a stated finding
Correct. Alkalosis increases hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen and shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the left, so hemoglobin holds oxygen and delivery to the tissues decreases.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 10

B.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
B.q: In an eligible adult, what usually follows a dose of the 15-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine?
opts: Correct. The 15-valent conjugate vaccine usually requires the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine afterward, usually 1 year or more later. A 20- or 21-valent conjugate vaccine, by contrast, completes the series for an adult who has never had a conjugate vaccine.

The 15-valent conjugate vaccine is not repeated to finish the adult series; it is followed by the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine, usually 1 year or more later. Tell: the second product is a different vaccine type, the polysaccharide one.

A single dose completes the series only when it is the 20- or 21-valent conjugate vaccine. Tell: the 15-valent conjugate vaccine is the one that usually needs the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine afterward.

Pneumococcal vaccination is not given every year; yearly vaccination is the influenza rule. Tell: after the 15-valent conjugate vaccine, one 23-valent polysaccharide dose usually follows, about 1 year or more later.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: For suspected Pneumocystis pneumonia, which respiratory specimen is obtained first when it is feasible?
opts: Spontaneously expectorated sputum has poor sensitivity and should not be used to exclude infection. Tell: the sputum sample for Pneumocystis is induced, and a negative one leads on to bronchoalveolar lavage when suspicion stays high.
Lung biopsy is rarely needed and comes only when less invasive studies are nondiagnostic. Tell: start with induced sputum, then bronchoalveolar lavage; biopsy is not the first sample.

Correct. Induced sputum is obtained for microscopy and/or polymerase chain reaction when feasible; if it is negative or unavailable and suspicion remains high, bronchoalveolar lavage follows. A negative induced specimen does not exclude Pneumocystis pneumonia.

Bronchoalveolar lavage is the next specimen, considered when induced sputum is negative or unavailable and suspicion remains high, with its yield balanced against respiratory instability. Tell: when induced sputum is feasible it comes first, and lavage follows a negative result.

B.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
B.q: Which term names a pathologic condition with excessively alkaline body fluids or tissues?
opts: Hypocapnia, a low carbon dioxide, can produce an alkalosis but is a gas value, not the definition of the condition. The pathologic condition of excessively alkaline fluids is alkalosis. Tell: -capnia refers to carbon dioxide only.

Alkalemia is the blood finding, a pH above 7.45, not the underlying condition. The stem asks for the pathologic condition of excessively alkaline fluids or tissues, which is alkalosis. Tell: '-emia' is the number in blood, '-osis' is the process.

Acidosis is the condition of excessively acidic body fluids or tissues, the reverse of what the stem describes. The alkaline condition is alkalosis. Tell: the stem says alkaline, so look for the term built on alkal-.

Correct. Alkalosis is the pathologic condition of excessively alkaline body fluids or tissues. The resulting blood finding, a pH above 7.45, is called alkalemia, so the condition and the finding have different names.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 3

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: Smoking-related emphysema typically follows which pattern?
opts: Bronchial wall thickening is the imaging change of chronic bronchitis, an airway disease, not an emphysema pattern. Tell: smoking-related emphysema destroys centrilobular airspaces in the upper lobes.
Panlobular emphysema in the lower lobes is the alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency pattern. Tell: smoking damages the upper lobes in a centrilobular pattern.
Fibrosis is a restrictive change and, with silica or fiberglass, a different condition. Tell: smoking-related emphysema is an obstructive, upper-lobe, centrilobular destruction of airspaces.

Correct. Emphysema from smoking is centrilobular and predominantly in the upper lobes. The panlobular, lower-lobe pattern belongs to alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, which is why basilar emphysema prompts testing for it.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: How is psittacosis primarily acquired?
opts: Hot tubs, fountains and cruise ships spread Legionella in water droplets. Tell: psittacosis follows contact with sick birds.
Disturbed soil with bird or bat droppings is the source of histoplasmosis. Tell: psittacosis comes from the infected bird itself, by inhalation or mouth-to-beak contact.
Human-to-human transmission of psittacosis is rare, though possible. Tell: the main route is inhaling the organism while handling sick birds.

Correct. Psittacosis, caused by the obligate intracellular bacterium Chlamydia psittaci, is acquired mainly through the respiratory system when handling sick birds, or by mouth-to-beak resuscitation. Human-to-human transmission is rare.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 63-year-old woman develops ventilator-associated pneumonia on day 5 of mechanical ventilation. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus is common in her unit. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: This is a community-acquired pneumonia regimen. Ventilator-associated pneumonia is more likely Pseudomonas or multidrug-resistant organisms. Tell: the ventilator pathway uses an antipseudomonal beta-lactam, not ceftriaxone.

Correct. Local methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus prevalence adds vancomycin or linezolid to an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime. Cultures are obtained, and therapy is reassessed daily and de-escalated.

Linezolid covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, but moxifloxacin is not a reliable antipseudomonal agent, which leaves her most likely organisms uncovered. Tell: pair the staphylococcal agent with cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam.

Cefepime by itself fits hospital or ventilator pneumonia without methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus risk. The unit's prevalence of that organism calls for added vancomycin or linezolid. Tell: local resistance adds coverage.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: Which group uses a tuberculin skin test induration cut-off of 5 mm or more?
opts: Children under 5, or children exposed to high-risk adults, use the 10 mm cut-off. Tell: the young child is a 10, the recent close contact is a 5.
With no known tuberculosis risk factors, 15 mm or more is needed for a positive result. Tell: no risk factors means the highest cut-off.
Correct. The 5 mm cut-off applies to human immunodeficiency virus infection, recent close contacts, transplant recipients, major immunosuppression, and imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis.
High-risk congregate settings belong to the 10 mm group, with increased exposure risk, selected medical risks and children under 5. Tell: 5 mm is for contacts and the immunosuppressed.

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: A 45-year-old man with Guillain-Barré syndrome has worsening weakness and shallow breathing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 58 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What is the priority treatment for his acid-base disorder?
opts: Careful oxygen titration is the approach for chronic respiratory acidosis. His is acute (bicarbonate 26), and the priority is restoring ventilation. Tell: acute equals restore ventilation; chronic equals careful oxygen.

Correct. A high carbon dioxide with a low pH and a barely raised bicarbonate is acute respiratory acidosis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome is a listed neuromuscular cause. Acute respiratory acidosis is treated by restoring ventilation while the cause is treated.
Give sodium bicarbonate to raise the pH

His acidosis comes from retained carbon dioxide, so the fix is ventilation; therapy aimed at the pH itself is reserved for an unsustainable pH (below 6.7), alongside the cause. His pH is 7.26. Tell: respiratory acidosis is treated by breathing, not by bicarbonate.

Renal compensation begins only after 6 to 12 hours, takes days, and never returns the pH to normal. His breathing is failing now. Tell: compensation alone never restores the pH; the disorder must be corrected.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

B.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
B.q: On an arterial blood gas, which change shows a good response to oxygen therapy?
opts: Lower arterial oxygen with a lower pH
A lower arterial oxygen with a lower pH moves away from the goal. A good response is higher arterial oxygen, no rise in carbon dioxide, and correction of the pH. Tell: the key shows oxygen going up.
Unchanged oxygen with a higher pH

Unchanged oxygen with a higher pH does not show the key response, which is an increase in arterial oxygen without an increase in carbon dioxide, plus pH correction. Tell: an unchanged oxygen value is not a response to oxygen.
Higher arterial oxygen with a rise in carbon dioxide

A rise in arterial oxygen with a rise in carbon dioxide is not a good response; an increase in carbon dioxide is the listed hazard of carbon dioxide retention. The goal is higher oxygen without a carbon dioxide increase. Tell: carbon dioxide must not rise.
ruled out by a stated finding
Higher arterial oxygen with no rise in carbon dioxide

Correct. A good response on an arterial blood gas is an increase in the arterial oxygen pressure without an increase in the carbon dioxide pressure, together with correction of the pH. Oxygen should help without causing retention.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 61-year-old woman hospitalized with coronavirus disease 2019 and hypoxemia has an elevated D-dimer. She has no signs of venous thrombosis and no bleeding risk. Which anticoagulation plan is most appropriate?
opts: Therapeutic dosing requires an assessment of thrombosis and bleeding, not a D-dimer value alone. She has no signs of thrombosis. Tell: D-dimer elevation alone does not decide anticoagulant intensity.

Correct. Hospitalized patients receive venous thromboembolism prophylaxis unless contraindicated. Therapeutic dosing requires a thrombosis and bleeding assessment, and an elevated D-dimer alone neither diagnoses thrombosis nor sets the dose. She has no thrombosis, so the prophylactic dose fits.

An elevated D-dimer does not diagnose thrombosis, and hospital tests should answer a clinical question. She has no signs of thrombosis to image. Tell: give prophylaxis now rather than holding it for a test with no clinical question.

Venous thromboembolism prophylaxis is given to hospitalized patients unless contraindicated, and she has no bleeding risk. Tell: omitting prophylaxis leaves her unprotected; the D-dimer changes nothing about that.

B.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
B.q: A 20-year-old man has daily asthma symptoms and uses albuterol daily, but he wakes at night only once a month and has a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 85% predicted. He has some limitation playing pickup basketball. Which severity classification fits?
opts: Mild persistent asthma allows symptoms and rescue use on more than 2 days a week but not daily. His are daily. Tell: the word daily is the line between mild and moderate persistent asthma.

Correct. Daily symptoms, daily short-acting beta-2 agonist use and some limitation of activity are moderate persistent features. Even though his night waking and 85% function are milder, severity is assigned to the most severe category in which any feature occurs.

His night waking and lung function look intermittent, but daily symptoms and daily rescue use far exceed the intermittent limit of 2 or fewer days a week. Tell: severity follows the worst feature, not the best ones.

Severe persistent asthma requires symptoms throughout the day, rescue use several times a day, extreme limitation or function below 60%. He uses albuterol daily with some limitation and 85% function. Tell: daily rescue use is moderate; several times a day is severe.

B.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
B.q: A 31-year-old woman has spirometry for suspected asthma. Before a bronchodilator her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 61% predicted with a ratio of 55%; after albuterol it is 94% predicted, a 54% improvement. Which interpretation fits?
opts: Correct. A reduced 1-second volume and a reduced ratio before the bronchodilator show airflow limitation, and a 54% improvement after albuterol, far above the 12% threshold, shows reversibility. A positive bronchodilator response strongly supports asthma.

Fixed obstruction would barely change after a bronchodilator. Her 1-second volume rose by 54% of its starting value, from 61% to 94% predicted. Tell: a rise of 12% or more is the reversible pattern that supports asthma.

Spirometry does depend on effort, and coaching helps, but poor effort would not produce a clear 54% rise after a bronchodilator. Tell: a large, consistent response to albuterol reflects reversible obstruction, not inconsistent effort.

Before the bronchodilator her 1-second volume was 61% predicted with a 55% ratio, both reduced, so the test is not normal. Tell: the pre-bronchodilator values show obstruction, and the post-bronchodilator values show it reversing.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: A 47-year-old woman has a metabolic alkalosis with normal blood pressure; she denies vomiting, diuretics and antacids. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 46 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which test separates the saline-responsive from the saline-unresponsive type?
opts: The Winter formula predicts the carbon dioxide in metabolic acidosis; it does not type an alkalosis. Tell: Winter checks compensation in acidosis only.
Albumin matters for interpreting the anion gap, since low albumin lowers it. It does not split saline-responsive from unresponsive alkalosis. Tell: albumin goes with the gap.

Correct. Urine chloride differentiates the two types: it is low (below 25 mEq/L) in saline-responsive alkalosis and high (above 40 mEq/L) in saline-unresponsive alkalosis. Her history gives no obvious cause, so the test sorts the list.
The anion gap sorts metabolic acidosis into normal and elevated gap; it does not type an alkalosis. Tell: anion gap for acidosis, urine chloride for alkalosis.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 41

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
B.q: A 15-year-old soccer player has cough, chest tightness and wheezing that start within 3 minutes after hard running, peak about 10 to 15 minutes later, and clear within an hour. She has no symptoms at rest or at night. Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic, but the pattern of onset within 3 minutes, a 10-to-15-minute peak and resolution by an hour is the exercise-induced bronchospasm timeline. Tell: the precise post-exercise timing is the decisive clue.

Moderate persistent asthma brings daily symptoms and night awakenings more than once a week. She has none at rest or at night. Tell: symptoms tied only to exercise and gone within an hour fit exercise-induced bronchospasm.
ruled out by a stated finding
Catamenial asthma follows the menstrual cycle. Her symptoms follow exercise, appearing within minutes and clearing within the hour. Tell: the trigger is running, not a point in a monthly cycle.

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is common in children and adolescents, begins during or within 3 minutes after exercise, peaks in 10 to 15 minutes and resolves by 60 minutes, exactly this player's pattern, with no symptoms at rest or at night.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: When is the local or state tuberculosis program notified?
opts: Rifampin resistance calls for rapid susceptibility testing and expert management, but notification is required for any presumed or confirmed disease. Tell: drug resistance is not the trigger for reporting.
Notification is part of immediate management, at the start, so contacts and treatment can be coordinated. Tell: report at presumption or confirmation, not at the end of therapy.
Waiting for culture would delay reporting by weeks, because cultures grow slowly; presumed disease is reported too. Tell: the program hears about presumed cases, not just confirmed ones.

Correct. Immediate management of pulmonary tuberculosis starts with notifying the local or state tuberculosis program of presumed or confirmed disease, alongside airborne isolation when indicated and fit-tested N95 or higher respiratory protection for staff.
B.cite: 38. Mycobacterial Infections including Tuberculosis - Bobilin - 10-29-2025 SV.pptx, Slide 33

B.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
B.q: A 52-year-old woman reports severe breathlessness, stopping after about 100 meters on level ground, but her post-bronchodilator forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 82% predicted with a ratio of 0.68. Her heart evaluation is normal. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Her symptoms are real and unexplained by her spirometry, which calls for further evaluation, not reassurance. Tell: symptoms out of proportion to testing are a referral indication.
Triple therapy is considered for high exacerbation risk; she has no exacerbations described. Tell: when symptoms outrun the test results, the next step is a specialist's evaluation.

Correct. Her dyspnea grade of 3 is far worse than her near-normal airflow (grade 1, 82%) would explain. Symptoms out of proportion to pulmonary function tests, like diagnostic uncertainty, is a listed reason for pulmonology referral.
Long-term oxygen is for a baseline saturation below 88%; nothing shows that here. Tell: the mismatch between symptoms and spirometry calls for referral.

B.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
B.q: A 57-year-old smoker has chronic cough and mild breathlessness. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows a ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1 second to forced vital capacity of 0.76. How should this result be read?
opts: Grades 1 to 4 are given only to patients whose ratio is below 0.70. Tell: without confirmed obstruction there is no grade to assign. Grade 2 also needs a 1-second volume of 50% to 79% predicted.

A ratio of 0.76 is above the 0.70 cutoff, so obstruction is not confirmed. Tell: the diagnosis needs a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70. His cough may still be chronic bronchitis without obstruction.
It does not confirm the disease

Correct. The diagnosis requires a post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70, and his is 0.76. Chronic bronchitis without airflow obstruction is not chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, though smoking cessation remains essential for him.
Asthma is supported by reversibility, 12% or more after a bronchodilator, not by a ratio above 0.70. Tell: this result simply fails to confirm obstruction.

B.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
B.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
B.q: Sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145), chloride 104 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106) and bicarbonate 12 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26). What is the calculated anion gap?
opts: 12 is the bicarbonate value itself, not the gap. The gap is 140 - (104 + 12) = 24. Tell: the answer comes from the subtraction, not a single listed value.

Correct. Anion gap = sodium - (chloride + bicarbonate) = 140 - (104 + 12) = 140 - 116 = 24. That is above the normal 9 to 15, so this is an elevated anion gap, as expected with such a low bicarbonate.
36 comes from 140 - 104 without subtracting the bicarbonate. The gap subtracts chloride and bicarbonate: 140 - 116 = 24. Tell: both anions are subtracted.
48 adds the bicarbonate instead of subtracting it (140 - 104 + 12). The correct arithmetic is 140 - (104 + 12) = 24. Tell: chloride and bicarbonate are added together first and the sum is subtracted.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 47

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
B.q: A 32-year-old woman with long-standing asthma has had repeated exacerbations this year despite confirmed adherence and good inhaler technique. Her clinician suspects a hypersensitivity reaction to a mold. Which result supports that suspicion?
opts: Negative skin tests with a normal immunoglobulin E

Negative skin tests with a normal immunoglobulin E define intrinsic asthma, the non-allergic form. Tell: an Aspergillus hypersensitivity shows the opposite, a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response to the mold.
Normal antibody levels argue against a hypersensitivity to the mold. Tell: allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis produces a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response to Aspergillus fumigatus.
A raised exhaled nitric oxide by itself

Fractional nitric oxide identifies airway inflammation, which any active asthma can show, so on its own it does not point to a mold. Tell: the specific finding is a vigorous antibody response to Aspergillus.
Raised immunoglobulin E and G to Aspergillus

Correct. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus seen almost exclusively in asthma or cystic fibrosis. Exposure causes a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response that leads to acute symptoms and exacerbations, as in this woman.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has had a chronic cough with sputum for months. Her sputum acid-fast bacilli smear is positive. What does this smear result establish?
opts: Nontuberculous lung disease needs compatible symptoms and imaging, exclusion of alternatives and usually 2 or more sputum cultures of the same species. Tell: a smear names no species at all, so it cannot establish nontuberculous disease either.

Latent infection is identified by an immune-response test, a tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay, in a person with no evidence of disease after clinical evaluation. Tell: a sputum smear looks for acid-fast organisms, not for an immune response.
Acid-fast organisms, species not yet known

Correct. An acid-fast smear identifies a group of organisms, the acid-fast bacilli with lipid-rich, mycolic acid cell walls. It does not distinguish Mycobacterium tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria, and bronchiectasis raises the risk of nontuberculous disease, so the species still has to be identified.

A positive smear is not proof of tuberculosis: it identifies acid-fast organisms as a group and cannot separate Mycobacterium tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria. Tell: with bronchiectasis in her history, a nontuberculous species is just as possible until the species is known.
B.cite: 38. Mycobacterial Infections including Tuberculosis - Bobilin - 10-29-2025 SV.pptx, Slides 4, 5

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 66-year-old man admitted with nonsevere community-acquired pneumonia is improving on ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. On day 3 his blood cultures grow Streptococcus pneumoniae that is susceptible to narrower agents. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Duration follows clinical stability: stable nonsevere pneumonia may need fewer than 5 days, with a minimum of 3. A fixed 14 days of both drugs ignores the culture result and the shorter course. Tell: narrow and shorten when the patient improves.

Cefepime is an antipseudomonal beta-lactam for hospital-acquired pneumonia or Pseudomonas risk. He has neither, and his organism is a susceptible pneumococcus. Tell: switching to a broader antipseudomonal agent goes the wrong way.

Correct. Antibiotics are reassessed daily and narrowed when possible, and therapy is narrowed to culture and susceptibility results. He is improving and his organism and its susceptibilities are known, so broad empiric coverage is no longer needed; duration follows clinical stability.

Vancomycin covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and is added only for validated risk. His culture grew a susceptible pneumococcus and he is improving. Tell: a culture result is a reason to narrow, not to broaden.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
B.q: A 72-year-old woman with community-acquired pneumonia is alert and oriented. Her blood urea nitrogen is 26 mg/dL, respiratory rate 24/min and blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg. What is her CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) score?
opts: A total of 1 counts only one item, and she has two: urea above 20 mg/dL and age 65 or older. Tell: age scores a point by itself at 65 or older, so an older patient with any other item already has at least 2.

Correct. Confusion 0 (alert and oriented) + urea 1 (26 mg/dL is above 20) + respiratory rate 0 (24 is below 30) + blood pressure 0 (systolic not below 90, diastolic not 60 or lower) + age 1 (72) = 2. A total of 2 is moderate severity, with a risk of death of 9%, and the pathway sends her to the hospital.

A total of 3 adds a point she does not have: her respiratory rate of 24 is below 30, and her blood pressure of 128/76 is not low. Tell: only urea and age score here; 3 or more would be high severity, with a risk of death of 15 to 40%.

A total of 4 would need two more items, such as confusion and low blood pressure, and she is alert with a normal blood pressure. Tell: 4 or 5 is the band where transfer to critical care is especially considered, far above her two points.

B.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
B.q: A 72-year-old man with severe chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was intubated with a carbon dioxide of 78 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), and the ventilator brought it to 38 within a few hours. He has had no vomiting, nasogastric suction, diuretics or antacids. The next morning: pH 7.55 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 38 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). What best explains his alkalemia?
opts: Respiratory acidosis gives a low pH with a high carbon dioxide. His pH is 7.55 and his carbon dioxide 38, both pointing away from acidosis. Tell: acidosis lies below 7.35, and he is alkalemic.

Correct. His kidneys had retained bicarbonate for his chronic hypercapnia; when the carbon dioxide was lowered quickly, that bicarbonate of 32 was left unopposed, a post-hypercapnic metabolic alkalosis. This is why rapid, aggressive carbon dioxide reduction is avoided in chronic respiratory acidosis.

Respiratory alkalosis needs a low carbon dioxide, below 36. His is 38, within range; the high bicarbonate is what drives his pH up. Tell: in respiratory alkalosis the carbon dioxide, not the bicarbonate, is the abnormal value.
ruled out by a stated finding

Compensation never corrects the pH beyond normal, so an overshoot cannot explain a pH of 7.55. Here the compensating bicarbonate was stranded when the carbon dioxide it offset was removed. Tell: compensation alone stops short of 7.40.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

B.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
B.q: A 70-year-old woman with heart failure is started on oxygen. An hour later her arterial oxygen pressure has risen, but her arterial carbon dioxide has also risen and her pH has fallen. How should this response be read?
opts: A good response: pH is moving

The pH should correct toward normal for a good response, and hers fell. A falling pH alongside a rising carbon dioxide is moving the wrong way, not a sign of improvement. Tell: a good response needs the pH correcting, not just changing.
Not a good response: carbon dioxide is rising

Correct. A good response needs the arterial oxygen pressure to rise without a rise in arterial carbon dioxide, along with correction of the pH. Hers rose, but so did her carbon dioxide while the pH fell, so the oxygen is not working as it should and she needs close reassessment.
Cannot be judged without a chest film

Her blood gas already answers the question: arterial oxygen pressure, carbon dioxide and pH are the objective data for judging response. No chest film is needed to read this pattern. Tell: the gas values, not the imaging, decide whether the oxygen response is good.
A good response: oxygen pressure has risen

A rising arterial oxygen pressure alone is not enough. The response is judged as an increase in arterial oxygen pressure without an increase in arterial carbon dioxide, plus correction of the pH. Tell: look at all three values; one improved value does not make a good response.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 66-year-old man starts treatment for macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease and asks how long he will need it. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Correct. Treatment continues for at least 12 months after culture conversion, so the clock starts when cultures turn negative, not with the first dose. That makes the whole course longer than 12 months.
Symptom response does not set the duration; the regimen continues for at least 12 months after culture conversion. Tell: the anchor is the culture result, not how he feels.
Until his chest imaging is normal
Imaging does not set the duration of therapy; the regimen continues at least 12 months after cultures convert. Tell: the end point is anchored to culture conversion.
The 12 months are counted from culture conversion, not from the first antibiotic dose. Tell: the clock waits for negative cultures, so the whole course runs longer than a year.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
B.q: A 69-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with an exacerbation. She is alert and hemodynamically stable, but her blood gas shows rising carbon dioxide with respiratory acidosis despite bronchodilators, corticosteroids and antibiotics. Which support is most appropriate?
opts: Worsening hypercapnia on full treatment is far from the discharge criteria of clinical stability for 12 to 24 hours. Tell: she needs ventilatory support, not discharge.
High-flow nasal cannula is listed for hypoxia. Tell: rising carbon dioxide with acidosis is ventilatory failure, which needs noninvasive ventilation.

Correct. Noninvasive ventilation is used for hypercapnic respiratory failure in an exacerbation and reduces intubation rates and mortality. Her alertness and stable circulation make her a candidate, and it is one of the 3 therapies with a survival benefit.
Long-term azithromycin is a rare preventive option that raises resistance and side effects. Tell: acute hypercapnic failure is treated with noninvasive ventilation.

B.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
B.q: A 38-year-old man has attacks of severe one-sided headache around his eye, each lasting under an hour, several days in a row. His saturation is 99%. Which therapy is a listed special indication for him?
opts: A bag-valve mask is a resuscitator for a patient who is not breathing adequately, and he is breathing normally. It has nothing to do with a headache. Tell: the resuscitator is for failed ventilation; cluster headache is relieved by oxygen.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Severe one-sided headaches around the eye, brief and recurring daily for days, fit cluster headache, which is a listed special indication for oxygen. His saturation of 99% does not matter, because the indication here is the headache, not hypoxia.

Nebulized saline is not a listed therapy for cluster headache. A nebulizer delivers liquid medication directly to the airways, for medication choice or secretion clearance. Tell: nebulizers treat airway problems; cluster headache is one of the two special indications for oxygen.
No oxygen, since he is not hypoxic

A saturation of 99% would justify withholding oxygen only for hypoxia. Cluster headache and air hunger are the two special indications that apply even when the patient is not hypoxic. Tell: for these two special indications, oxygen is given despite a normal saturation.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. B.q: A 44-year-old man with untreated human immunodeficiency virus infection cleaned out a barn full of bird droppings 3 weeks ago. He is admitted to the intensive care unit with high fever, hypoxemia, hypotension and diffuse infiltrates, and his urine Histoplasma antigen is positive. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Histoplasmosis treatment follows severity and host risk. An intensive care admission with hypoxemia, hypotension and diffuse infiltrates in an immunocompromised host is severe disease, and severe pulmonary or disseminated histoplasmosis requires specialist-led amphotericin-based induction.
Observation is for mild acute disease in an immunocompetent adult. Tell: he is immunocompromised and critically ill, the opposite end of the severity range, so he needs amphotericin-based induction.

Itraconazole is considered for prolonged or progressive illness or higher-risk hosts who are not severely ill. Tell: an intensive care admission with hypoxemia and hypotension is severe disease, which starts with amphotericin-based induction under a specialist.

Fluconazole for 6 to 12 months treats mild, isolated pulmonary cryptococcosis. Tell: his exposure to bird droppings and positive urine Histoplasma antigen point to histoplasmosis, and his severity calls for amphotericin-based induction.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with a lung abscess has had two episodes of Clostridioides difficile colitis in the past year. Which part of a lung abscess plan should be avoided for her?
opts: Correct. Clindamycin is reserved for selected alternatives because of Clostridioides difficile risk, and she has had two episodes of that colitis. Her abscess is treated with a beta-lactam/beta-lactamase inhibitor instead, intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam followed by oral amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Intravenous ampicillin-sulbactam is the usual first choice for lung abscess. Tell: her colitis history is the reason clindamycin, the drug held back for its Clostridioides difficile risk, is the one to avoid; this beta-lactam combination stays.

Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate follows the intravenous phase in the usual lung abscess plan. Tell: the drug flagged for Clostridioides difficile risk is clindamycin, so this oral step remains part of her treatment.

Lung abscess treatment commonly lasts several weeks, guided by clinical and radiographic response, and her colitis history does not change that. Tell: the history changes which drug is avoided, not how long the abscess is treated.

B.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
B.q: A 71-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is admitted with a flare. His oxygen saturation is 86% on room air, and the team wants to give him an exact, adjustable fraction of inspired oxygen rather than a fraction that changes with his breathing. Which delivery device is the best choice?
opts: Correct. He has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and the team wants a precise, adjustable fraction of inspired oxygen that does not change with his breathing. The Venturi mask is an air-entrainment device: different ports set the fraction (24-50%), and it stays fixed whatever his demand.

A simple mask is also a low flow device, and its fraction varies with respiratory rate, inspiratory flow and tidal volume. It is used for mild to moderate respiratory distress and gives no fixed fraction. Tell: the simple mask has no ports that lock in a fraction, so it cannot be dialed to an exact number.
ruled out by a stated finding

A non-rebreather mask is a low flow device whose delivery varies with patient demand, so the fraction would drift as his breathing changes. It is meant for severe hypoxia with good ventilation, and his 86% is not that. Tell: a reservoir bag with a one-way valve means a variable fraction; ports mean a fixed one.

A nasal cannula gives a fraction that varies with respiratory rate, inspiratory flow and tidal volume, and it is used mostly for mild hypoxia. Each added liter raises the fraction only about 4%, so it cannot be dialed in. Tell: a cannula is set by liters per minute, a Venturi mask by choosing a port.
ruled out by a stated finding

B.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
B.q: A 29-year-old woman began hyperventilating at a high-altitude resort this afternoon. Before her kidneys respond, what is the initial compensation for her respiratory alkalosis?
opts: Cells release hydrogen ions for potassium

Correct. The initial response to respiratory alkalosis is cellular secretion of hydrogen ions in exchange for potassium. Later the kidneys excrete bicarbonate and retain chloride, lowering bicarbonate, potassium and raising chloride.
She hypoventilates to retain carbon dioxide

Hypoventilation is the compensation for a metabolic alkalosis. Her primary problem is the breathing itself, so the compensation must come from cells and kidneys. Tell: respiratory disorders are not compensated by the lungs.
Renal bicarbonate excretion is the later response, working over hours to days. The first response is cellular hydrogen ion secretion in exchange for potassium. Tell: cells act first, kidneys follow.
Retaining bicarbonate would raise her pH further; it is the compensation for respiratory acidosis. Tell: alkalosis is offset by losing bicarbonate, not keeping it.
B.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 43-year-old woman with suspected pulmonary tuberculosis has three sputum specimens collected. Which testing should be requested on the specimens?
opts: Acid-fast smear, then stop if negative

A smear is one part of the workup, and slow-growing cultures can take weeks to answer what a negative smear cannot. Tell: smear, culture and a rapid molecular test are requested together from the start.
Acid-fast smear, culture and a molecular test

Correct. The specimens go for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, a rapid molecular test is performed on at least one respiratory specimen, and molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing is obtained.
Gram stain and routine bacterial culture

Acid-fast organisms are looked for with an acid-fast smear and a mycobacterial culture, not routine bacterial testing. Tell: the request names the smear, the mycobacterial culture and a rapid molecular test.
Molecular test in place of culture

A rapid molecular test is performed on at least one specimen, but alongside, not instead of, mycobacterial culture; culture also supplies culture-based susceptibility testing. Tell: smear and culture stay in the request.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
B.q: A 38-year-old man has a positive interferon-gamma release assay on targeted testing. He has no symptoms. Which next step is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. A positive interferon-gamma release assay indicates infection, but neither it nor the skin test can distinguish latent infection from disease. A positive result requires clinical evaluation and chest imaging, so disease is excluded before any latent-infection treatment.

Tuberculosis disease must be excluded before latent-infection treatment begins. Tell: the positive blood test shows infection; clinical evaluation and chest imaging come before any preventive regimen.
Repeat the assay in 8 to 10 weeks
Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for an early negative result after recent exposure. Tell: his result is already positive, so the next move is evaluation for disease.

Isolation and reporting are for presumed or confirmed infectious tuberculosis disease. Tell: a symptom-free man with a positive blood test has evidence of infection, which first needs clinical evaluation and imaging.
