C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
C.q: A 61-year-old man who smokes has coughed up thick sputum most days for 4 months of each of the last 3 years. He has rhonchi, bluish lips and swelling of both ankles. His blood gas shows low oxygen and raised carbon dioxide, and his diffusing capacity is near normal. Post-bronchodilator spirometry shows a ratio of 0.64. Which subtype best describes his disease?
opts: Emphysema brings a thin, pursed-lip breather with preserved gas exchange until late and a reduced diffusing capacity. He has early hypoxemia and hypercapnia with a near-normal diffusing capacity. Tell: sputum, cyanosis and edema point to bronchitis.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Productive cough for at least 3 months a year over 2 years, rhonchi, cyanosis, edema, early hypoxemia and hypercapnia, and a near-normal diffusing capacity, with confirmed obstruction (ratio 0.64), are the chronic bronchitis picture (the blue bloater).

Chronic bronchitis without airflow obstruction is not this disease, but his ratio of 0.64 confirms obstruction. Tell: once the ratio is below 0.70, his chronic cough places him in the chronic bronchitis subtype.
ruled out by a stated finding

Asthma does not usually bring years of daily sputum, cyanosis, edema and chronic carbon dioxide retention in a smoker. Tell: his cough history meets the chronic bronchitis definition, with persistent obstruction.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 58-year-old man is admitted with coronavirus disease 2019. His oxygen saturation is 90% on room air, and he needs supplemental oxygen. Which medication is the core treatment?
opts: Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir belongs to the early outpatient pathway for high-risk patients with mild or moderate disease and no hypoxemia. He is hypoxemic and admitted. Tell: hypoxemia moves the patient to the hospital pathway, built on dexamethasone.

Antibacterial treatment is withheld in coronavirus disease 2019 without a bacterial complication, which he does not have. Tell: the indicated pathway is antiviral and supportive care plus dexamethasone for hypoxemia, not an antibiotic.

Correct. Hospitalized adults with hypoxemia receive dexamethasone, usually for up to 10 days or until discharge, with remdesivir considered by timing and respiratory support. Oxygenation and severity, not simply a positive test or elapsed time, decide the pathway, and his saturation of 90% puts him on it.

Molnupiravir is an outpatient adult alternative when the preferred early antivirals are unsuitable. It has no place in the hospital pathway for hypoxemia. Tell: hypoxemic inpatients get dexamethasone, with remdesivir considered.

D.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
D.q: A 67-year-old man on home oxygen for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease arrives with burns to his lips and nose after lighting a cigarette while wearing his cannula. Which hazard does this show?
opts: Hypercapnia, or carbon dioxide retention, is a listed hazard of oxygen, but it is retained gas, not a burn. His injury is burns after a lit cigarette. Tell: burns from a flame mean fire, not carbon dioxide.

Correct. A man on home oxygen lights a cigarette while wearing his cannula and burns his lips and nose. Oxygen is highly flammable, and fire is a listed hazard of oxygen therapy, which is why no smoking is taught for every home oxygen user.

Mucosal irritation is dryness or soreness of the nasal lining from oxygen, usually at higher flows without humidity. It does not involve burns from an ignition source. Tell: dry, irritated mucosa is mucosal irritation; burns after a lit cigarette are fire.

Vasoconstriction is the effect of oxygen in a myocardial infarction, not a burn mechanism. His injury came from an open flame. Tell: a burn from an ignition source is fire; vasoconstriction is a cardiac concern when oxygen is not needed.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 74-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an exacerbation with marked breathlessness. Before attributing it to the exacerbation, his clinician wants to exclude acute heart failure. Which test is most useful for that purpose?
opts: Spirometry confirms the diagnosis and grades airflow in stable disease. Tell: to exclude acute heart failure during an exacerbation, B-type natriuretic peptide is used.

Correct. Exacerbation evaluation includes oxygen saturation, a blood gas, a chest x-ray, an electrocardiogram, and B-type natriuretic peptide or troponin. B-type natriuretic peptide is the test for suspected associated heart failure, one of the diagnoses to exclude.
The 6-minute walk feeds the survival index in stable disease and is not an exacerbation test. Tell: heart failure is screened with B-type natriuretic peptide.
An alpha-1 antitrypsin level diagnoses the deficiency in young, unexposed or basal-emphysema patients. Tell: it plays no role in excluding heart failure during an exacerbation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 62-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease who smokes is asked about his smoking and is clearly advised to quit, with a link to his diabetes and heart risk. Using the Five A's approach, which step should come next?
opts: Arrange is the fifth and last step, setting up follow-up to monitor progress. Tell: before arranging follow-up, the clinician assesses readiness and then assists with a plan.

Correct. After Ask and Advise, the Five A's continue with Assess, evaluating the person's readiness and willingness to change, then Assist with actionable steps, and Arrange follow-up. Readiness shapes how the clinician helps.
Ask has already been done; it opens a nonjudgmental conversation about the behavior. Tell: the sequence is Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange, so Assess comes next.
Assist, helping set realistic steps and strategies, is the fourth step and depends on knowing his readiness. Tell: Assess comes between Advise and Assist.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: Which presentation separates pneumonia from acute bronchitis?
opts: Correct. Apart from walking pneumonia, pneumonia presents more severely than bronchitis: higher fevers and chills, pleuritic or atypical chest pain, a productive cough and shortness of breath with tachypnea. Bronchitis tends to bring a low-grade fever.
A central, substernal wheeze over the bronchial airways is a feature of acute bronchitis. Tell: pneumonia shows focal findings such as crackles, dullness or consolidation, with tachypnea.
A low-grade fever with chills, body aches and fatigue is the cold-like start of acute bronchitis. Tell: pneumonia brings higher fevers and a faster breathing rate.
Colored sputum occurs in both and does not separate viral from bacterial illness. Tell: severity (higher fever, tachypnea, focal findings) is what points to pneumonia.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
D.q: A 17-year-old runner with exercise-induced bronchospasm uses albuterol before every practice, yet still has frequent symptoms during training. Which change is most likely to prevent his episodes?
opts: Asthma treatment aims for no limitation on physical activity, so giving up running is not the goal. Tell: regular inhaled corticosteroid use best prevents exercise-induced bronchospasm and keeps him training.
Saving albuterol for after symptoms start

Albuterol helps most when used before exercise, and moving it to after symptoms begin gives up that protection. Tell: when pre-exercise albuterol is not enough, prevention comes from a regular inhaled corticosteroid.

Cromolyn prevents symptoms but does not relieve them once present, so taking it during an episode does not help. Tell: the agent that best prevents exercise-induced bronchospasm is a regular inhaled corticosteroid.

Correct. Exercise-induced bronchospasm is treated with a short-acting beta-2 agonist before exercise but is best prevented with regular inhaled corticosteroid use. His frequent symptoms despite pre-exercise albuterol call for the regular controller.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 65-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is starting pulmonary rehabilitation and asks what it will involve. Which description is accurate?
opts: Rehabilitation is described as something that cannot be done alone; it needs a healthcare professional or interdisciplinary team. Tell: it is supervised training, not a solo home routine.
A surgical procedure on the lungs
Possible surgical need is a reason for pulmonology referral, not rehabilitation. Tell: rehabilitation trains breathing, strength, secretion clearance and energy conservation.
Antibiotics treat exacerbations with purulent sputum, and long-term use is rare because of resistance. Tell: rehabilitation is exercise, breathing technique and education.

Correct. Pulmonary rehabilitation covers clearing secretions, breathing techniques, strengthening exercises, energy conservation and avoiding fatigue, and patient education. It cannot be done alone; it needs a healthcare professional or interdisciplinary team.

D.io: Select the appropriate equipment and supplies necessary for initiating oxygen therapy.
D.q: Which two airways are listed as artificial airways, as opposed to tracheal airways?
opts: The nasal cannula and simple mask are oxygen delivery devices, not artificial airways. The artificial airways are the oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways. Tell: the artificial airways are named for the pharynx.

The endotracheal tube and tracheostomy are listed as tracheal airways, a separate group from the artificial airways. The artificial airways are oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal. Tell: tracheal means placed in the trachea.

The Venturi mask and trach collar are oxygen delivery interfaces, not artificial airways. The artificial airways are the oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal airways. Tell: the key airways are named for the pharynx.
Correct. The oropharyngeal airway and the nasopharyngeal airway are the two listed as artificial airways. The tracheal airways, the endotracheal tube and tracheostomy, are listed separately.

D.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
D.q: A 44-year-old woman who moved to a high-altitude town months ago has a chronic respiratory alkalosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 27 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 19 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which serum electrolyte pattern accompanies her renal compensation?
opts: Low chloride with a high bicarbonate is the compensation of chronic respiratory acidosis. Her bicarbonate is 19 and her carbon dioxide low. Tell: alkalosis compensation lowers bicarbonate and keeps chloride.
Normal chloride with a high anion gap
A high gap with a normal chloride is the pattern of elevated-gap metabolic acidosis, a low pH disorder. Her pH is 7.47. Tell: the anion gap sorts metabolic acidosis, not respiratory alkalosis.
High potassium accompanies acidosis, and low chloride belongs to chronic respiratory acidosis. Her alkalosis lowers potassium and raises chloride. Tell: flip both values for a respiratory alkalosis.

Correct. In respiratory alkalosis the kidneys excrete bicarbonate and retain chloride, giving a reduced bicarbonate, hyperchloremia and hypokalemia (cells also secrete hydrogen ions in exchange for potassium). Her bicarbonate of 19 shows that compensation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 78-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has an exacerbation. After treatment in the office his breathing is somewhat better, but he has new swelling of both legs, he lives alone, and he has no one to help at home. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Admission criteria include new physical signs such as edema, significant comorbidities with an exacerbation, age, and lack of home or outpatient resources. His new edema, advanced age and lack of support at home meet several of them.
Rehabilitation is considered at discharge after an exacerbation, not as acute treatment. Tell: his new edema and lack of support at home call for admission first.

Intensive care is for hemodynamic instability, major infection, need for invasive ventilation, sepsis, altered mental status or respiratory acidosis. Nothing in his history suggests these. Tell: a ward admission fits his criteria.

More than 80% of exacerbations can be managed outpatient, but his new edema and lack of home resources are listed admission criteria. Tell: who can care for the patient at home is part of the decision.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
D.q: A 34-year-old woman who works in a furniture-finishing plant has had cough and wheezing for 6 months. She notes the symptoms ease on weekends and nearly vanish during a 2-week vacation, then return within days of going back to work. She has no history of allergies. Which diagnosis best explains her pattern?
opts: Catamenial asthma follows the menstrual cycle, a monthly rhythm. Her symptoms follow her work schedule, easing on weekends and vacations. Tell: a weekly on-off pattern tied to the job points to the workplace, not to hormones.

Extrinsic asthma is atopic and allergen-triggered, and she has no allergy history. Tell: the weekly work-linked rhythm, with improvement away from the plant, is the occupational pattern, and occupational sensitization does not require atopy.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Symptoms that improve on weekends and vacations and return at work point to occupational asthma from a workplace sensitizer, here chemicals in furniture finishing. Occupational sensitization is independent of atopy, so her lack of allergies does not argue against it.
Exercise-induced bronchospasm is triggered by exertion and clears soon after. Her symptoms persist through the work week and clear only away from work. Tell: the trigger is a place, not an activity.

D.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: What is the treatment of metabolic acidosis, whether the anion gap is normal or elevated?
opts: Give isotonic saline for every case

Isotonic saline treats saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and saline infusion is itself a cause of normal-gap acidosis. The treatment is to treat the underlying disorder. Tell: saline fits the alkalosis, not the acidosis.
Correct. For both increased and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis, the treatment is to treat the underlying disorder. The compensatory response is also assessed, using the Winter formula.
Stopping diuretics is part of treating saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis. Metabolic acidosis is treated by treating its underlying disorder. Tell: diuretics are a cause of the alkalosis.

A paper bag is not necessary even in hyperventilation, where it fails to correct carbon dioxide and has only a placebo effect. Metabolic acidosis is treated by treating the underlying disorder. Tell: the gap type does not change the treatment, which targets the cause.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: What is the preferred treatment for psittacosis in adults?
opts: Amoxicillin is a beta-lactam for healthy outpatients with typical community-acquired pneumonia. Tell: Chlamydia psittaci is an obligate intracellular bacterium, treated with doxycycline.
A macrolide is the alternative discussed with infectious disease when tetracyclines are unsuitable, and macrolide failures have occurred. Tell: the preferred adult drug is doxycycline.

Correct. Doxycycline is preferred in adults, started promptly when psittacosis is strongly suspected; improvement often begins within 48 to 72 hours. If tetracyclines are unsuitable, a macrolide is discussed with infectious disease, though macrolide failures have occurred.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Tell: psittacosis is treated with doxycycline.

D.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
D.q: A 69-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease says that, walking on level ground, he has to stop for breath after about 100 meters or after a few minutes. Which modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade fits?
opts: Grade 1 is shortness of breath when hurrying on the level or walking up a slight hill. Tell: he stops on level ground after about 100 meters, a heavier limitation.
Grade 2 is walking slower than people of the same age on the level, or stopping for breath at one's own pace. Tell: a defined stop at about 100 meters or a few minutes is grade 3.

Correct. Grade 3 is stopping for breath after walking about 100 meters or after a few minutes on the level. A grade of 2 or more counts as more symptoms, which places him in group B or E depending on exacerbation risk.
Grade 4 is being too breathless to leave the house, or breathless when dressing or undressing. Tell: he still walks outside, stopping after 100 meters, which is grade 3.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 58-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is newly disoriented to place and time. His blood urea nitrogen is 31 mg/dL, respiratory rate 32/min and blood pressure 86/52 mm Hg. What is his CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) score?
opts: A total of 2 would be moderate severity, but he has four positive items: new confusion, urea above 20 mg/dL, respiratory rate of 30 or more and systolic pressure below 90. Tell: each of those adds 1, so he is well into the high-severity band.

A total of 3 misses one item. He scores all four clinical items, confusion, urea, respiratory rate and blood pressure; only age fails, at 58. Tell: count each item separately; a low systolic pressure and new disorientation both score.

Correct. Confusion 1 (new disorientation) + urea 1 (31 is above 20) + respiratory rate 1 (32 is 30 or more) + blood pressure 1 (systolic below 90) + age 0 (58) = 4. That is high severity, with a risk of death of 15 to 40%: hospital, urgent senior review and a decision about critical care, especially at 4 or 5.
A total of 5 needs every item, including age 65 or older, and he is 58, so age adds nothing. Tell: the 65 in the name is an age threshold, and he is below it, so his maximum is 4.

D.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
D.q: A 45-year-old woman with severe persistent asthma has needed 4 courses of oral corticosteroids this year despite confirmed adherence and good technique with her inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting beta-2 agonist. Which step is most appropriate?
opts: Theophylline gives mild bronchodilation but has a narrow toxic-therapeutic range and is rarely used because of toxicity concerns. Tell: refractory disease needing repeated steroids is a specialist referral, where steroid-sparing antibody therapy is available.
Refer to a lung or allergy specialist

Correct. With adherence and technique confirmed, her repeated steroid-requiring exacerbations make her asthma refractory. Monoclonal antibody agents are used by pulmonology and allergy specialists and reduced the need for corticosteroids in trials, so referral to a specialist fits.

Immunotherapy must be done in a controlled environment because it can induce bronchoconstriction, and it targets allergic triggers. Tell: her problem is refractory severe asthma, which calls for specialist care.

Removing part of a regimen she uses correctly would not explain or fix her exacerbations. Tell: refractory, steroid-dependent asthma despite adherence calls for a specialist, who can offer agents that reduce the need for steroids.

D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 34-year-old woman has glaucoma treated with an oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitor, type 2 diabetes treated with metformin, and daily aspirin use for headaches. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.32 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 30 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 15 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 140 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 115 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which of her medicines best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Metformin causes an elevated-gap acidosis, above 15. Her gap is 140 - (115 + 15) = 10, normal, and her chloride is high, the pattern of the normal-gap list. Tell: metformin sits in the mnemonic for an increased gap.

Salicylates are on the elevated-gap list, and an elevated-gap acidosis is normochloremic with a gap above 15. Her gap is 10 with a high chloride. Tell: a normal gap with a high chloride points to the normal-gap list, not aspirin.
A respiratory cause, not a medicine

A respiratory acidosis needs a high carbon dioxide; hers is 30, low, and her bicarbonate of 15 is what matches the pH. The low carbon dioxide is compensation, as the Winter formula (1.5 x 15 + 8 = 30.5) predicts.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Low pH and low bicarbonate make a metabolic acidosis; the gap is 140 - (115 + 15) = 10, within 9 to 15, with a high chloride: a normal-gap, hyperchloremic acidosis. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are on the normal-gap list (loss of bicarbonate).
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 47, 52, 55, 56, 58

D.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
D.q: A 26-year-old woman has asthma symptoms only 1 day a week and uses albuterol 1 day a week, but she wakes at night with cough twice a week. She has no activity limitation, and her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 86% predicted. Which severity classification fits?
opts: Her daytime symptoms, rescue use and 86% function would fit intermittent, but severity follows the worst feature, and waking twice a week exceeds the intermittent limit of 2 or fewer times a month. Tell: one moderate feature outranks several mild ones.

Mild persistent asthma allows night waking 3 to 4 times a month. She wakes twice a week, which is more than once a week, the moderate persistent level. Tell: twice weekly is roughly 8 times a month, past the mild limit.

Correct. Severity is assigned to the most severe category in which any feature occurs. Her daytime symptoms and lung function are intermittent-level, but night awakenings more than once a week (twice weekly) are a moderate persistent feature, so she is moderate persistent.

Severe persistent asthma brings waking often 7 times a week with symptoms throughout the day and function under 60%. She wakes twice a week with 86% function. Tell: her worst feature reaches moderate, not severe.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 60-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and few symptoms asks to be started on an inhaled corticosteroid by itself because a friend with asthma uses one. Which regimen should be avoided in him?
opts: Every patient should get the yearly influenza vaccine, which reduces hospitalizations and death. Tell: vaccination fits him; an inhaled corticosteroid alone is the regimen to avoid.

Correct. In this disease, inhaled corticosteroids must be combined with a long-acting beta agonist, and then with a long-acting antimuscarinic as triple therapy, and cannot be used on their own. They also raise pneumonia risk. Alone, they are an asthma treatment.
Smoking cessation is essential for every group and carries a survival benefit. Tell: it belongs in his plan; the steroid alone does not.
A single bronchodilator is the appropriate start for group A, few symptoms and low risk. Tell: it suits him; the regimen to avoid is a steroid inhaler used by itself.

D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A 37-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis has worsening weakness and shallow, labored breathing over a day. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.27 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 57 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Correct. The pH of 7.27 is acidemia, and the carbon dioxide of 57 is high and matches it (respiratory). Bicarbonate rose only about 1 per 10 mm Hg (17 above 40 gives about 26), so it is acute. Myasthenia gravis is a listed neuromuscular cause of acute respiratory acidosis.
Her pH of 7.27 is low, so this cannot be an alkalosis. Her bicarbonate of 26 is inside the normal range, not high. Tell: metabolic alkalosis would need a high pH and a high bicarbonate.

Chronic compensation would raise bicarbonate about 3.5 per 10 mm Hg, to about 30 here (57 is 17 above 40). Her 26 is the acute response to a one-day crisis. Tell: the kidneys have not had time, and a sudden onset signals acute.

Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate, and hers is 26, which is normal. The high carbon dioxide from weak, shallow breathing matches the acidemia. Tell: a normal bicarbonate with a high carbon dioxide means respiratory.
ruled out by a stated finding
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slides 22, 26, 59

D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A 58-year-old man with chronic kidney failure who has missed several dialysis sessions is nauseated and fatigued. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 29 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 13 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); sodium 138 mEq/L (normal 135 to 145 mEq/L), chloride 100 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: His carbon dioxide is low, but his pH of 7.26 is acidemia. A low carbon dioxide with a low pH is compensation for the metabolic acidosis, not a primary alkalosis. Tell: alkalosis requires a high pH.

Correct. The pH of 7.26 is acidemia, and the bicarbonate of 13 is low and matches it: metabolic. Gap = 138 - (100 + 13) = 25, above 9 to 15, so it is elevated; uremia is an elevated-gap cause. The carbon dioxide of 29 is compensation (Winter 1.5 x 13 + 8 = 27.5, plus or minus 2).
Respiratory acidosis needs a high carbon dioxide, and his is 29. The low bicarbonate of 13 matches the acidemia. Tell: a low carbon dioxide with a low bicarbonate means the lungs are compensating.
ruled out by a stated finding

The gap is 138 - (100 + 13) = 25, above 15, so it is elevated, not normal. A normal-gap acidosis would have a gap within 9 to 15 and a high chloride, and his chloride of 100 is normal. Tell: do the subtraction before choosing the gap type.
ruled out by a stated finding
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 55

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
D.q: A 67-year-old woman meets the criteria for macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex lung disease, without cavitation or severe disease. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Inhaled liposomal amikacin as first therapy
Inhaled liposomal amikacin is for persistent positive cultures after at least 6 months of treatment, not for initial therapy. Tell: start with azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin.

That four-drug combination is the initial phase for drug-susceptible tuberculosis. Tell: her organism is a nontuberculous species, and macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex gets azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin.

Correct. Macrolide-susceptible Mycobacterium avium complex pulmonary disease is treated with azithromycin, ethambutol and a rifamycin, under specialist direction, continued for at least 12 months after culture conversion.
Azithromycin is the macrolide in the regimen, but it is combined with ethambutol and a rifamycin. Tell: three drugs, continued for at least 12 months after culture conversion.
D.cite: 38. Mycobacterial Infections including Tuberculosis - Bobilin - 10-29-2025 SV.pptx, Slide 40

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for patients with asthma in the following patient populations. 1. adolescent 2. adult 3. elderly
D.q: A 72-year-old woman with asthma, already on an inhaled corticosteroid and a long-acting beta-2 agonist, has heart disease and worries about side effects. Her clinician is considering adding tiotropium. Which property of tiotropium is reassuring for her?
opts: Fast onset that suits rescue use
Tiotropium has a slow onset of action, so it is not a rescue medicine. Tell: her rescue medicine stays the short-acting beta-2 agonist; tiotropium's appeal for her is its low side-effect burden.

Correct. Tiotropium, an anticholinergic, has little or no systemic absorption and therefore few side effects. It inhibits only the cholinergic reflex part of bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion, and it is less effective than beta-2 agonists with a slow onset.

Tiotropium inhibits the cholinergic reflex component of bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion; it is not an anti-inflammatory controller. Tell: anti-inflammatory control comes from her inhaled corticosteroid.

Anticholinergics are less effective than beta-2 agonists because they block only the cholinergic component of bronchoconstriction. Tell: its advantage is safety, from little systemic absorption, not strength.

D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension treated with a thiazide diuretic is light-headed on standing. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.49 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 46 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 34 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.2 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is low. Along with isotonic saline, which medication change is indicated?
opts: Mineralocorticoids cause a hypertensive, saline-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis, so adding one would worsen his. Tell: mineralocorticoids are on the cause list, not the treatment list.
Antacids are a cause of saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, so starting one adds alkali to an alkalemia. Tell: antacid, diuretic and vomiting sit together on the cause list.

Correct. Low urine chloride and orthostatic symptoms mark a saline-responsive metabolic alkalosis, and diuretic therapy is a listed cause. Treatment is isotonic saline for the volume deficit and discontinuing the diuretic.
A second diuretic would deepen the volume contraction and the alkalosis; diuretics are discontinued in saline-responsive alkalosis. Tell: the drug causing the alkalosis is stopped, not doubled.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 44

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
D.q: A 66-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease had 3 moderate exacerbations in the past year. Her blood eosinophil count is 110. She is starting maintenance therapy. Which regimen is most appropriate?
opts: Adding an inhaled corticosteroid is considered in group E when eosinophils are 300 or more. Hers are 110. Tell: without that eosinophil count, the steroid's pneumonia risk is not justified.
Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, not daily maintenance. Tell: exacerbation prevention comes from long-acting inhaled bronchodilators.
A single bronchodilator is the group A start, for low risk and few symptoms. Three exacerbations make her group E. Tell: high risk calls for both long-acting bronchodilators.

Correct. Three moderate exacerbations make her high risk, group E, which starts on a long-acting beta agonist plus a long-acting antimuscarinic. Her eosinophil count of 110 is below 300, so an inhaled corticosteroid, with its pneumonia risk, is not added.

D.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
D.q: A 28-year-old woman with a severe asthma attack is tiring, and her carbon dioxide has risen over an hour to 60 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). Using an acute bicarbonate rise of about 1 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg rise in carbon dioxide, from midpoints of 40 and 24, what bicarbonate is expected?
opts: 24 assumes no change at all; even acutely the bicarbonate rises about 1 per 10 mm Hg, to 26. Tell: some bicarbonate rise appears even acutely.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Carbon dioxide rose 20 (40 to 60); acutely bicarbonate rises about 1 per 10, so 24 + 2 = 26 mEq/L. Asthma is a listed cause of acute respiratory acidosis, and a near-normal bicarbonate marks an acute process.
31 uses the chronic ratio of 3.5 per 10 (24 + 7). Her carbon dioxide rose over an hour, so the acute ratio applies: 26. Tell: an hour is acute.
34 uses 5 per 10, the chronic ratio for respiratory alkalosis, and adds it. Acute respiratory acidosis gives 24 + 2 = 26. Tell: match the ratio to the disorder and its stage.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 59

D.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
D.q: A 78-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has mild hypoxia, saturation 87%, during a cold. A student suggests a non-rebreather mask at 15 L/min "to be safe." Why should that be avoided?
opts: It is meant for severe hypoxia

Correct. His hypoxia is mild at 87%, and a non-rebreather mask is used in severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well, delivering 60-100% at 10-15 L/min. For mild hypoxia the nasal cannula is the most commonly used device, so the non-rebreather overshoots his need.

A non-rebreather can raise his saturation; at 10-15 L/min it delivers 60-100%. The problem is that its high fraction is meant for severe hypoxia, and his is mild at 87%. Tell: this mask is powerful, which is why it is kept for severe hypoxia.
It is a fire hazard in hospitals

Fire is a listed hazard of any oxygen therapy, whichever device is used, so it is not a reason to avoid this mask in particular. The reason here is that the non-rebreather is for severe hypoxia and his is mild. Tell: a hazard shared by every device cannot single out one of them.
It causes vasoconstriction in the lungs

Vasoconstriction is a risk of oxygen therapy in general, flagged for myocardial infarction, not a reason tied to this mask. He has no cardiac event, and his issue is a device too strong for mild hypoxia. Tell: vasoconstriction goes with a myocardial infarction; severity decides the device.

D.io: Identify mechanisms for maintaining acid-base homeostasis.
D.q: A 57-year-old man with severe obesity and a high fever from pneumonia has a carbon dioxide of 62 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). What usually causes a raised carbon dioxide like his?
opts: Correct. Hypercapnia is usually the result of under-excretion (hypoventilation), not excess production. At steady state carbon dioxide production matches excretion, so a high level means ventilation is not keeping up.
Hyperventilation increases excretion and lowers carbon dioxide (hypocapnia). His is raised. Tell: hypercapnia is under-breathing, hypocapnia over-breathing.
Fever increases carbon dioxide production, but hypercapnia is usually from under-excretion, not excess production; normal breathing clears the extra. Tell: blame the breathing first.
Excess bicarbonate retained by the kidneys
Retained bicarbonate is compensation for a raised carbon dioxide; it does not raise the carbon dioxide itself. Tell: carbon dioxide is set by ventilation, bicarbonate by the kidneys.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
D.q: A 44-year-old man is about to start a tumor necrosis factor inhibitor. He has no symptoms of tuberculosis and has never been tested for it. Which step regarding tuberculosis is most appropriate before he starts?
opts: Correct. Tumor necrosis factor inhibitors raise the risk of progression after tuberculosis infection, and testing is targeted at people at increased risk. A skin test or interferon-gamma release assay detects the immune response to infection; a positive result then needs clinical evaluation and chest imaging.
Latent-infection treatment follows a positive test and exclusion of disease. Tell: the first step is a test for infection; treatment decisions follow its result and a clinical evaluation.

Sputum specimens are collected when pulmonary tuberculosis disease is suspected from symptoms or suspicious imaging. Tell: he is symptom-free, so the question is infection, answered by a skin test or interferon-gamma release assay.
No testing because he has no symptoms

Symptoms may be mild or absent, and testing targets people at increased risk, whether or not they have symptoms. Tell: his planned tumor necrosis factor inhibitor is a progression risk, which is the reason to test.
D.cite: 38. Mycobacterial Infections including Tuberculosis - Bobilin - 10-29-2025 SV.pptx, Slides 15, 19

D.io: Evaluate the patient’s response to oxygen therapy.
D.q: A 60-year-old man with heart failure is on oxygen while his fluid overload is treated. Over two days his breathing eases, his saturation stays at target, and his vital signs settle. Which ongoing step is part of evaluating his oxygen therapy?
opts: Stopping saturation checks would drop the objective data used to judge response. The target varies, but the measurement continues. Tell: stable results are a reason to keep monitoring, not to stop.

Correct. Evaluating response ends with vital signs and further monitoring for complications. His breathing has eased and his saturation holds, but he remains on oxygen, so the hazards of oxygen therapy still need watching.

Home oxygen qualification is performed at the time of need, with documentation of hypoxia at rest, exertion or sleep, when a patient is going home. He is still in treatment for fluid overload. Tell: qualification is about home coverage, not about evaluating his current response.
Raise his flow to secure the gains
Raising the flow when he is already at target would add oxygen he does not need and risk its hazards. His saturation stays at target. Tell: at target, the plan is to monitor, not to increase.

D.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
D.q: Which toxic or pharmacologic agent causes respiratory alkalosis?
opts: Licorice causes a saline-unresponsive metabolic alkalosis with hypertension, a metabolic cause. Salicylates cause respiratory alkalosis. Tell: the stem asks for a respiratory cause, and licorice is metabolic.
Recreational drugs that depress the central nervous system cause respiratory acidosis. Salicylates cause respiratory alkalosis. Tell: the direction of the effect on breathing sets the type.
Intravenous sedation depresses breathing and causes respiratory acidosis. Salicylates drive hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. Tell: sedatives slow breathing, salicylates speed it up.
Correct. The toxic and pharmacologic causes of respiratory alkalosis are salicylates, caffeine, nicotine, catecholamines and thyroxine. Each drives hyperventilation, which lowers carbon dioxide.
D.cite: PAJ5500 CMSI Acid Base MBF 2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
D.q: Between exacerbations, the physical examination of a patient with asthma is often what?
opts: A barrel chest from chronic hyperinflation is the chronic obstructive pulmonary disease picture. The asthma exam is often normal between attacks. Tell: a persistent barrel chest implies fixed air trapping, which asthma usually does not have.

Clubbing is not an asthma finding; it suggests another chronic lung or heart disease. Between exacerbations the asthma examination may be entirely normal. Tell: asthma's reversible airway disease leaves no permanent marks such as clubbing.

Wheezing usually appears during exacerbations; between attacks the exam is often normal because the obstruction is reversible. Tell: fixed, constant findings suggest irreversible disease such as chronic obstructive pulmonary disease rather than asthma between attacks.

Correct. The examination may be normal between exacerbations, which is why an objective lung function measurement is needed for the diagnosis. Extrinsic asthma may still show nasal mucosal swelling, increased secretions, eczema or nasal polyps.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
D.q: A 20-year-old man with spirometry-confirmed asthma notices flares in spring and whenever he visits a friend with dogs. He wants to know exactly what he is reacting to. Which test identifies his triggers?
opts: Spirometry measures airflow and its reversibility, which already confirmed his asthma; it cannot name an allergen. Tell: identifying triggers needs skin or blood allergy testing.

Correct. Allergy testing, by skin or blood test, is useful to identify allergen triggers. His seasonal and dog-related flares suggest pollen and pet dander, the inhaled allergens that activate mast cells, and testing guides which ones to avoid.

Methacholine challenge shows airway hyper-responsiveness when spirometry is not diagnostic; his asthma is already confirmed, and the test names no allergen. Tell: to learn what he reacts to, allergy testing is the tool.
Fractional nitric oxide testing identifies airway inflammation, not which allergen causes it. Tell: the test that names a specific trigger, such as dog dander or pollen, is allergy testing.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 64-year-old woman with severe community-acquired pneumonia in the intensive care unit had methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus isolated from her sputum last year. She has been started on ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. Which agent should be added?
opts: Clindamycin is held back even in lung abscess because of Clostridioides difficile risk, and it is not an agent listed for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia. Tell: the listed agents are vancomycin or linezolid.

Moxifloxacin is a respiratory fluoroquinolone that can partner a beta-lactam in severe pneumonia, but it is not a methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus agent and is not reliable for Pseudomonas. Tell: the agents named for resistant staphylococcus are vancomycin or linezolid.

Correct. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus coverage is added only for validated risks, and a prior respiratory isolate is one. The agents named for it are vancomycin or linezolid, added to the beta-lactam combination; cultures are obtained and therapy de-escalated as results return.

Ertapenem is named as not a reliable antipseudomonal option and is not one of the agents listed for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Tell: her validated risk is the resistant staphylococcus, so the add-on is vancomycin or linezolid.

D.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
D.q: A 70-year-old woman with cirrhosis and an albumin of 1.9 g/dL (normal 3.5 to 5.0 g/dL) has a metabolic acidosis, a chloride of 110 mEq/L (normal 98 to 106 mEq/L) and an anion gap of 11 (normal 9 to 15). Which finding most limits how much the normal gap can reassure you?
opts: Correct. Albumin accounts for most of the normal anion gap, so hypoalbuminemia lowers the gap and can hide added unmeasured anions. A normal gap does not exclude a high-gap acidosis and should not override clinical concern.

The acidosis is what the gap is meant to sort; it does not distort the number. Hypoalbuminemia does, by removing the anion that makes up most of the normal gap. Tell: look for the listed errors: low albumin, sodium extremes, antibiotics.

Losing unmeasured cations (calcium, magnesium, potassium) raises the gap, so it would make a normal value less likely, not falsely reassuring. Her low albumin lowers it. Tell: fewer cations raise the gap; less albumin lowers it.

A high chloride marks a true normal-gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis; it is a finding, not an error in the gap. Her low albumin is the listed source of error. Tell: hypoalbuminemia sits on the error list; chloride does not.

D.q: A 48-year-old man has had a cough for 6 days with yellow sputum. His temperature is 101.8°F and his respiratory rate 24/min, and there are crackles with dullness to percussion over the left lower lobe. He asks for an antibiotic because his sputum is yellow. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Supportive care fits uncomplicated acute bronchitis, where consolidation should not be detected. Tell: focal crackles and dullness with fever are the cue to think pneumonia and image, not to treat as bronchitis.
An antibiotic for the yellow sputum

Purulent or colored sputum does not establish a bacterial infection and does not justify antibiotics. Tell: his fever and focal findings should prompt evaluation for pneumonia rather than empiric bronchitis antibiotics, and that evaluation starts with a chest radiograph, not with an antibiotic chosen for sputum color.

Routine sputum culture is unnecessary in uncomplicated cases, and in pneumonia cultures are obtained selectively for severe disease, resistant-pathogen risk or treatment failure. Tell: the test that answers his question, is this pneumonia, is the chest radiograph.
A chest radiograph to confirm pneumonia

Correct. Fever, a raised respiratory rate and focal crackles with dullness are the findings that raise concern for pneumonia rather than uncomplicated bronchitis, and suspected pneumonia is confirmed with a chest radiograph. The yellow sputum is not what changes the plan: the fever and focal findings are.

D.q: Alongside clinical judgment, which tool is preferred to support the admission decision in community-acquired pneumonia?
opts: Correct. The Pneumonia Severity Index plus clinical judgment is preferred for admission decisions; the five-item confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure and age score complements it but does not replace clinical judgment.
The chest radiograph confirms that pneumonia is present but is not the preferred admission tool. Tell: the place of care is chosen with the Pneumonia Severity Index plus judgment.

A white blood cell count alone does not set the place of care, and routine blood counts do not help every stable outpatient. Tell: the admission decision uses the Pneumonia Severity Index with judgment.
Sputum cultures are selective, for severe disease or resistant-pathogen risk, and their results come too late to decide admission. Tell: the Pneumonia Severity Index plus judgment guides disposition.

D.q: A 57-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia is intubated for respiratory failure and admitted to the intensive care unit. He has no validated risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas. Which empiric regimen is most appropriate?
opts: A beta-lactam by itself leaves out the partner drug: severe pneumonia is treated with a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: severe means a combination regimen.

Vancomycin covers methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and cefepime covers Pseudomonas, but severity alone does not mandate that coverage. Tell: severity changes the site of care and regimen, not automatic broad-spectrum coverage, and he has no validated risk.

Correct. Mechanical ventilation makes this severe community-acquired pneumonia, treated with a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas coverage is added only for validated risks, which he lacks; cultures are obtained and therapy de-escalated later.

Respiratory fluoroquinolone monotherapy is an option for nonsevere inpatient pneumonia. Severe pneumonia uses a beta-lactam combination regimen. Tell: once a patient is ventilated, a beta-lactam must be part of the regimen.

D.q: When should palliative care be integrated for older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?
opts: In the final weeks of life

Waiting until the final weeks loses the chance to plan with caregivers and advance directives. Tell: for older adults palliative care starts early. Late referral leaves little time for advance directives.

Palliative care is not a last resort after drug failure; for older adults it is integrated early alongside treatment. Tell: early integration with caregivers and advance directives is the listed approach.
Correct. For older adults palliative care is integrated early, with caregiver involvement and advance directives. For working-age adults it is introduced as the disease advances.
When the patient asks for it
Waiting for the patient to ask delays the planning that early integration provides. Tell: for older adults clinicians bring palliative care in early, with caregivers and advance directives.

D.q: Which tests are requested on the sputum specimens in suspected pulmonary tuberculosis?
opts: Antigen and antibody testing are not part of the tuberculosis sputum workup; sputum is sent for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture plus molecular testing. Tell: the organism is sought directly in the specimen.
The tuberculin skin test is an intradermal injection read on the forearm at 48 to 72 hours, unrelated to sputum. Tell: sputum looks for the organism, the skin test for an immune response.

Correct. Each specimen is sent for an acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a rapid molecular test on at least one respiratory specimen and molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing.
The interferon-gamma release assay is a blood test of the immune response to infection, not a sputum test. Tell: sputum goes for smear, culture, molecular and susceptibility testing.

D.q: A 47-year-old man who aspirated gastric contents during a witnessed seizure was managed with oxygen and airway support and no antibiotic. Three days later he is worse, with a new fever, purulent sputum and a persistent infiltrate. Which complication should be suspected?
opts: A resolving chemical injury improves with support; worsening 3 days later is the opposite pattern. Tell: persistence or worsening after aspiration pneumonitis is a reason to reassess for infection, not to keep waiting.

Asthma exacerbations are on the cough differential, but he has no asthma history and has a persistent infiltrate with purulent sputum after aspiration. Tell: the infiltrate and the aspiration history point to infection.

Acute bronchitis is a self-limited viral infection of the large airways without consolidation. His persistent infiltrate after an aspiration does not fit. Tell: a persistent infiltrate is a parenchymal process, not a large-airway one.

Correct. Pneumonitis is managed with support, and persistence or worsening raises concern for secondary infection, a complication or another diagnosis. New fever, purulent sputum and a persistent infiltrate after 3 days point to a secondary bacterial infection, which now needs the applicable pneumonia regimen.

D.q: A 29-year-old woman's roommate was diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis 10 weeks ago, and they have lived apart since. She has no symptoms. Her tuberculin skin test, read at 72 hours, shows 7 mm of induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: The result is positive, but not because any induration counts: the skin test is read against the patient's risk-based cut-off of 5, 10 or 15 mm. Tell: her positive result comes from the 5 mm threshold for recent close contacts.
Positive; recent close contacts use 5 mm

Correct. A recent close contact of infectious tuberculosis is in the 5 mm group, with human immunodeficiency virus infection, transplant, major immunosuppression and imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. 7 mm is at least 5 mm, so the test is positive and she needs evaluation for active disease.

10 mm applies to increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings and children under 5. Tell: living with a person who has infectious pulmonary tuberculosis makes her a recent close contact, whose cut-off is 5 mm.

15 mm is the cut-off for a person with no known tuberculosis risk factors, which does not describe her. Tell: a recent close contact has a major risk, so her cut-off is 5 mm and her 7 mm of induration is positive.

D.q: A 55-year-old man with no medical conditions has never received a pneumococcal vaccine. Which pneumococcal vaccination is appropriate for him?
opts: Correct. All adults aged 50 or older who have never had a pneumococcal conjugate vaccine, or whose history is unknown, are vaccinated. One dose of the 20-valent or 21-valent conjugate vaccine completes the series; a 15-valent conjugate vaccine is usually followed by the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine.

Pneumococcal vaccination is a series completed by one 20-valent or 21-valent conjugate dose, not an annual vaccine. Tell: the yearly vaccine is influenza; the pneumococcal series is done once completed.
Pneumococcal vaccination is recommended for all adults aged 50 or older who have not had a conjugate vaccine. At 55 he already qualifies. Tell: the age threshold is 50, not 65.

A 15-valent conjugate vaccine usually needs the 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine afterward, so by itself it leaves the series incomplete. Tell: a single dose completes the series only with the 20-valent or 21-valent conjugate vaccine.

D.q: Which statement about sputum production in this disease is accurate?
opts: Its absence rules out the disease
Patients do not always have sputum, so its absence cannot exclude the disease, especially emphysema. Tell: spirometry, not sputum, confirms the diagnosis.
It is present in every patient
Sputum is not universal; emphysema-only patients typically do not produce much. Tell: sputum reflects mucus hypersecretion from the chronic bronchitis component.
It is typical of pure emphysema
Emphysema-only cases typically lack prominent sputum; mucus hypersecretion is the chronic bronchitis pattern. Tell: the thin, pursed-lip breather has dyspnea more than sputum.

Correct. Patients do not always produce sputum: it is seen with chronic bronchitis or a combined presentation and is typically not prevalent in emphysema-only cases. Its absence does not exclude the disease.

D.q: Why is an interferon-gamma release assay preferred over the tuberculin skin test for most BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin)-vaccinated patients?
opts: The vaccine makes skin tests falsely negative

The vaccine works the other way: it can cause a false-positive tuberculin skin test, as some nontuberculous mycobacterial exposures can. Tell: vaccination pushes the skin test toward positive, which is why the blood assay is preferred.
It separates latent from active disease

Neither the blood assay nor the skin test distinguishes latent infection from tuberculosis disease; a positive result requires clinical evaluation and imaging. Tell: the assay's advantage is about vaccination, not staging.
Its cut-offs are adjusted for vaccine history

The blood assay is not read against induration cut-offs, and the skin test itself is interpreted with standard risk-based thresholds regardless of vaccination history. Tell: nothing is adjusted for the vaccine; the blood assay is simply not made positive by it.
It is not made positive by the vaccine

Correct. BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin) vaccination does not cause a positive interferon-gamma release assay, which measures immune responses to tuberculosis-specific antigens, whereas the vaccine can cause a false-positive skin test. The assay is therefore preferred for most vaccinated patients.

D.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
D.q: A 22-year-old man with mild persistent asthma well controlled on an inhaled corticosteroid dislikes inhalers and asks to switch to montelukast tablets alone. Which statement should guide the counseling?
opts: It works as well as his inhaled steroid

Leukotriene modifiers are less effective than inhaled corticosteroids when used alone, so the switch would trade a better controller for a weaker one. Tell: the tablet's role is add-on therapy or exercise-induced bronchospasm, not replacing the inhaled steroid.
It is less effective than his inhaled steroid

Correct. Montelukast is a leukotriene modifier with modest clinical benefit, useful as add-on therapy, and less effective than inhaled corticosteroids as monotherapy. His inhaled steroid is the preferred first-line treatment for persistent asthma.
It is a rescue medicine for attacks

Montelukast is a long-term control medicine; quick relief comes from a short-acting beta-2 agonist, which every patient needs. Tell: rescue medicines act within minutes on smooth muscle, while leukotriene modifiers are controllers.
It is a long-acting beta-2 agonist

Montelukast is a leukotriene modifier, not a beta-2 agonist. Long-acting beta-2 agonists such as salmeterol bronchodilate for up to 12 hours and must be paired with an inhaled corticosteroid. Tell: montelukast is a tablet; long-acting beta-2 agonists are inhaled.

D.q: A 33-year-old man who moved 6 months ago from an area with high tuberculosis incidence has 2 months of pleuritic chest pain, dyspnea, fever and weight loss. Imaging shows a unilateral pleural effusion with no lung infiltrate, and his interferon-gamma release assay is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Bacterial pneumonia is on the differential of fever and respiratory symptoms. Tell: 2 months of illness with weight loss, recent arrival from a high-incidence area, a positive tuberculosis-antigen blood test and an effusion without infiltrate point to pleural tuberculosis.

Latent infection has no evidence of disease after clinical evaluation. Tell: a pleural effusion with pain, dyspnea, fever and weight loss is disease, so his positive assay means more than latent infection.

Spinal tuberculosis presents with back pain, vertebral destruction or neurologic deficits. Tell: his symptoms are pleuritic pain and dyspnea with an effusion, the pleural form of extrapulmonary tuberculosis.

Correct. Tuberculosis can involve almost any organ; pleural disease presents with effusion, pleuritic pain or dyspnea, and fever and weight loss fit tuberculosis. His residence in a high-incidence area is an exposure risk and the positive assay shows infection; organ-specific specimens may be needed.

D.q: A 67-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a resting oxygen saturation of 91% on room air, and she stays at 91% during a walking test. She asks for home oxygen. Which statement is accurate?
opts: She needs oxygen over 15 hours a day
Long-term oxygen for more than 15 hours a day requires severe resting desaturation, 88% or less. Tell: her 91% is moderate desaturation, which does not qualify.
Exertional oxygen is for desaturation to 88% or less with exertion. She stays at 91% while walking. Tell: moderate exertional desaturation, 89% to 93%, gives no indication.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. A resting saturation of 89% to 93% is moderate resting desaturation, with no indication for long-term oxygen, and her saturation stays at 91% with exertion. Oxygen is indicated with severe hypoxemia, an arterial oxygen pressure under 55 mmHg or saturation of 88% or less.
She needs a sleep study first
A sleep apnea evaluation is for desaturation at night only. Tell: her daytime readings are moderate, and nothing suggests nocturnal-only desaturation.

D.q: A 22-year-old woman had asthma as a young child, then had no symptoms throughout adolescence. Over the past 2 months her episodic wheezing and night cough have returned. Which statement best explains her course?
opts: Correct. Asthma presents at any age, with a peak at 3 years; it may become asymptomatic during adolescence and may return in adulthood. Her childhood asthma, quiet teenage years and returning symptoms follow that pattern.
Her first diagnosis must have been wrong

A symptom-free adolescence does not disprove childhood asthma; asthma can become asymptomatic in adolescence and return later. Tell: her course, early onset then a quiet gap then return, is a known pattern.
Asthma that remits in adolescence stays gone
Remission in adolescence is not permanent for every patient; asthma may return in adulthood. Tell: her returning wheeze and night cough after a quiet adolescence fit that described course.
Wheeze returning at 22 means cardiac asthma

Cardiac asthma is wheezing from decompensated heart failure, and nothing in her history suggests heart failure. Tell: in a young adult with childhood asthma, returning symptoms fit asthma coming back after a quiet adolescence.

D.q: A 70-year-old woman with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and an echocardiogram showing pulmonary hypertension has a resting room-air saturation of 89%. Which statement about home oxygen applies to her?
opts: Correct. Her resting saturation of 89% is above the Group I cutoff of 88% or less, so on its own it would not qualify. The echocardiogram showing pulmonary hypertension adds the comorbidity that makes a saturation of 89% qualify, which is Group II (recertified at 3 months).

She does qualify: a saturation of 89% plus pulmonary hypertension meets Group II criteria. The 89% alone would not, but the comorbidity changes the answer. Tell: 89% by itself fails, but 89% plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56% qualifies.
ruled out by a stated finding

Group I requires a saturation of 88% or less (or arterial oxygen pressure of 55 mm Hg or less) at rest. At 89% she is just above that, so she falls into the conditional group. Tell: 88% or less is Group I; 89% needs a comorbidity and is Group II.
She qualifies for sleep oxygen alone

Her qualifying finding is at rest, not during sleep. The sleep criterion is a saturation of 88% or less with a drop of 5% or more from baseline, and nothing here describes sleep. Tell: sleep oxygen requires a documented overnight drop; her stem gives a resting value.

D.q: What percentage of patients with asthma become worse with aspirin?
opts: Correct. About 1 to 5% of asthmatics become worse with aspirin, through a genetic predisposition that increases inflammatory mediators. Aspirin is among the medication triggers to avoid.
This overstates the share. Aspirin sensitivity affects about 1 to 5% of people with asthma. Tell: aspirin sensitivity is 1% to 5%, not 10% to 15%.
This is far too high; about 1 to 5% of asthmatics worsen with aspirin. Tell: aspirin sensitivity is a small subgroup, not a quarter of patients.

Half of patients is a large overstatement; aspirin-sensitive asthma is 1 to 5% of asthmatics. Tell: if half of patients reacted, aspirin sensitivity would be a defining feature of asthma rather than a subtype.

D.io: Identify the indications, benefits, and hazards of oxygen therapy.
D.q: A 68-year-old woman with diabetes and an acute myocardial infarction has an oxygen saturation of 87% on room air. Which is the right approach to oxygen?
opts: Wait for an arterial blood gas first

An arterial blood gas is not required before treating. A pulse oximeter reading of 87% already shows she is below 91%, and delaying oxygen leaves hypoxia uncorrected. Tell: the threshold rests on the saturation she already has; no extra test is needed to start.

Vasoconstriction is the reason oxygen is withheld in a myocardial infarction, but that applies unless the saturation is below 91%. At 87% she is below it, so the exception applies. Tell: withhold when the saturation is 91% or higher, give when it is below 91%.
Give oxygen, since saturation is below 91%

Correct. Her saturation of 87% is below the 91% cutoff. Oxygen is held back in a myocardial infarction because of vasoconstriction, but only while the saturation is 91% or higher. She is hypoxic, so the benefit of correcting hypoxia wins and she should receive oxygen.
Withhold oxygen because of her diabetes

Diabetes is not a listed reason to withhold oxygen. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction, and the myocardial infarction rule turns on a saturation under 91%. Tell: the saturation decides, not her comorbidity.

D.q: A 68-year-old woman is admitted for repair of a hip fracture. On hospital day 4 she develops fever, purulent sputum and a new infiltrate that was not on her admission chest radiograph. She has not been intubated. How should this pneumonia be classified?
opts: Correct. Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops 48 hours or more after admission and was not incubating on admission. Her new infiltrate appeared on day 4 after a clear admission film, and she was never intubated, so the ventilator label does not apply.

Aspiration pneumonitis is a sterile chemical injury with abrupt decline after a witnessed aspiration, and fever can occur without infection. No aspiration event is described, and she has purulent sputum with a new infiltrate. Tell: pneumonitis follows a witnessed event within hours.

Ventilator-associated pneumonia develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation, and she has never been intubated. Tell: without a breathing tube there is no ventilator-associated label, however long the stay.
ruled out by a stated finding

Community-acquired pneumonia is acquired outside the hospital or present early in admission. Hers began on day 4 after a clear admission film. Tell: an infiltrate that appears 48 hours or more into the stay is hospital acquired.
ruled out by a stated finding

D.q: A 48-year-old man is admitted with cough, night sweats and weight loss, and his sputum smear shows acid-fast bacilli. Infectious pulmonary tuberculosis is presumed. Where should he be placed?
opts: Correct. Presumed infectious pulmonary tuberculosis calls for an airborne infection isolation room when indicated, with fit-tested N95 or higher-level respiratory protection for staff, because pulmonary disease releases infectious aerosols during coughing, speaking or singing.
Contact precautions with gown and gloves

Tuberculosis is airborne, spread by aerosols from the lungs or larynx, so gowns and gloves do not address it. Tell: airborne isolation and fit-tested N95 respiratory protection are what the setting calls for.
Cultures can take weeks, and waiting in a shared space exposes others to infectious aerosols. Tell: isolation starts on presumption of infectious disease, not after culture confirmation.

Pulmonary tuberculosis spreads through infectious aerosols, and risk rises with shared indoor air, so a shared ward exposes others. Tell: presumed infectious disease goes to an airborne infection isolation room.

D.q: A 52-year-old woman has had a sudden fever, myalgias, a frontal headache and a dry cough for one day, at the peak of a busy influenza season. A rapid influenza antigen test is negative. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: It points to a bacterial cause

A negative influenza antigen test says nothing about bacteria; antibiotics treat a bacterial syndrome, not a negative viral test. Tell: the negative result reflects the test's low sensitivity, not another organism.

Correct. Rapid antigen tests have limited sensitivity, and a negative result does not exclude influenza, especially during high community activity. Her sudden typical illness at the peak of the season keeps influenza likely; molecular testing confirms it when the result affects management.

Rapid antigen tests have limited sensitivity, so a negative result does not rule out influenza, especially during high community activity. Tell: in peak season with a classic illness, a negative antigen test is an unreliable reassurance.

The test is a diagnostic screen with limited sensitivity, not a measure of contagiousness, and a negative result does not exclude influenza. Tell: she should be treated as possibly infectious while the diagnosis is confirmed.

Five weeks later she is no better: her cough and fatigue are worsening, but she is not hypoxemic and is managing at home. Which treatment is most appropriate?
opts: Observation is the usual plan for mild acute disease in an immunocompetent adult. Tell: her illness is prolonged and worsening rather than mild, which is the case for considering itraconazole.

Amphotericin-based induction is for severe pulmonary or disseminated disease. Tell: she is not hypoxemic and is managing at home, so her disease is prolonged and progressive but not severe, and an oral azole is considered first.

Fluconazole for 6 to 12 months treats mild, isolated pulmonary cryptococcosis, a different fungal infection. Tell: her bird-roost soil exposure and positive urine Histoplasma antigen make this histoplasmosis, for which the azole named is itraconazole.

Correct. Histoplasmosis is treated by severity and host risk. Her illness is prolonged and progressive but not severe, so itraconazole is considered, with monitoring of interactions and drug levels; observation fits mild acute disease in an immunocompetent adult, and amphotericin is for severe disease.

D.q: A 23-year-old woman with asthma has a personal best peak flow of 450 L/min. This morning she has cough and chest tightness, and her peak flow is 300 L/min (67% of her best). According to her written asthma action plan, which zone is she in?
opts: Action plans are built on peak flow against personal best, not office spirometry, so her zone can be set now: 67% is yellow. Tell: home peak flow monitoring exists precisely so patients can act on their own readings.
The red zone is below 50% of personal best, under 225 for her, with symptoms such as being very short of breath. At 300 (67%) she is above it. Tell: the red line is half of personal best.

The green zone, doing well, requires 80% or more of personal best, which for her is 360 or higher. At 300 she is below it and symptomatic. Tell: cough and chest tightness alone rule out the doing-well zone.

Correct. Her reading of 300 of a best 450 is 67%, inside the yellow zone of 50% to 79% of personal best, where asthma is getting worse. The plan adds quick-relief medicine (a short-acting beta-2 agonist) while she keeps taking her green-zone controller.

D.q: A 55-year-old woman with a bicarbonate of 9 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L) from ethylene glycol ingestion has a carbon dioxide of 28 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). By the Winter formula, what does her carbon dioxide show?
opts: Appropriate compensation would leave carbon dioxide at about 19.5 to 23.5 for a bicarbonate of 9. Her 28 is above that range, so compensation alone does not explain it. Tell: compare the measured carbon dioxide with the calculated range.
ruled out by a stated finding

Metabolic acidosis is compensated by the lungs lowering carbon dioxide; renal compensation answers respiratory disorders. Her carbon dioxide of 28 is above the Winter range of 19.5 to 23.5. Tell: the Winter formula checks the breathing response, not the kidneys.

Correct. Winter formula: 1.5 x 9 + 8 = 21.5, plus or minus 2, so about 19.5 to 23.5. Her 28 is higher than expected, so she has a metabolic acidosis together with a respiratory acidosis, which can be a sign of impending respiratory failure.

A respiratory alkalosis is a primary fall in carbon dioxide, and her 28 is higher than the Winter prediction, not lower. A carbon dioxide above the expected range means an added respiratory acidosis. Tell: higher than expected is the acidosis warning.
