Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
D.q: A 36-year-old woman with human immunodeficiency virus infection starts trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for Pneumocystis pneumonia. Her arterial oxygen pressure on room air is 61 mm Hg. Which therapy should be added?
opts: Pentamidine is an alternative to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, not an add-on for low oxygen. Deterioration is reassessed for toxicity, coinfection or failure rather than met with an automatic switch. Tell: her oxygen value triggers a steroid, not a second antimicrobial.

Correct. Adjunctive corticosteroids are indicated in Pneumocystis pneumonia linked to human immunodeficiency virus when the room-air arterial oxygen pressure is below 70 mm Hg, and hers is 61. Prednisone is started as early as possible, ideally within 72 hours of starting treatment.

Her room-air arterial oxygen pressure of 61 mm Hg is below the threshold of 70, which is exactly when adjunctive steroids are indicated. Tell: compare the stated value with 70 mm Hg; below it, a steroid is added as early as possible.

The adjunct is a systemic corticosteroid, prednisone, given over 21 days; an inhaled steroid does not provide it. Tell: the room-air oxygen below 70 mm Hg calls for systemic prednisone started early, not an inhaler.

D.io: Describe airflow obstruction in COLD and methods for assessing the severity of the obstruction
D.q: A 59-year-old woman has a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.66 and a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 83% predicted. Which airflow grade fits?
opts: Correct. Her ratio of 0.66 confirms obstruction, and a post-bronchodilator 1-second volume of 83% predicted meets the grade 1 (mild) threshold of 80% or more. Her airflow is near normal even though the ratio is abnormal.
Grade 2, moderate, covers 50% up to 80% predicted. At 83% she is above it. Tell: 80% or more is grade 1. Her ratio confirms the disease, but her airflow is near normal, so the mildest grade applies.
Grade 3, severe, covers 30% to 49% predicted, far below her 83%. Tell: a near-normal 1-second volume cannot be severe, whatever the ratio. The ratio confirms obstruction; it does not set the grade.
Grade 4, very severe, is below 30% predicted; she has 83%. Tell: very severe means less than a third of predicted airflow. Her low ratio alone does not raise the grade; only the 1-second volume does.

E.q: A 51-year-old man has 5 weeks of cough, night sweats and weight loss, and pulmonary tuberculosis is suspected. Which sputum collection plan is appropriate?
opts: Three samples, 1 each week for 3 weeks
Three is the right number, but specimens are collected 8 to 24 hours apart, not a week apart. Tell: the whole set is collected within a few days, with at least one early-morning specimen.
Three samples 8 to 24 hours apart, 1 early morning

Correct. Suspected pulmonary tuberculosis calls for 3 sputum specimens collected 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen, sent for acid-fast smear and mycobacterial culture, with a rapid molecular test on at least one.
One sample, collected at any time of day
A single specimen falls short of the 3 specimens required, and timing matters. Tell: collect 3 specimens 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one taken early in the morning.
Two samples, collected 1 hour apart in clinic
Two specimens an hour apart are too few and too close together. Tell: the plan is 3 specimens 8 to 24 hours apart, with at least one early-morning specimen.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
E.q: A 19-year-old college student has had episodes of wheezing, chest tightness and cough for 2 years, worse at night and after cleaning his dusty dorm room. He has allergic rhinitis and atopic dermatitis (eczema). Between episodes his lung exam is normal. Spirometry shows a reduced forced expiratory volume in 1 second that improves 18% after albuterol. Which diagnosis is most likely?
opts: Correct. Episodic wheeze, chest tightness and cough worse at night, a dust trigger, allergic rhinitis and eczema (the atopic triad), a normal exam between episodes, and an 18% rise in the 1-second volume after albuterol (12% or more is a positive response) make allergic, extrinsic asthma the diagnosis.

Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a lower airway mimic, but its obstruction is largely irreversible and it follows years of smoke exposure. This student's obstruction reversed by 18% after albuterol. Tell: a large bronchodilator response in a young atopic patient supports asthma.
ruled out by a stated finding

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic in the differential, but it would not produce reversible lower airway obstruction on spirometry or travel with eczema and rhinitis. Tell: reversible obstruction plus atopy places the problem in the lower airways, not the larynx.

Intrinsic asthma is non-atopic and of later, adult onset, often with nasal polyps and aspirin sensitivity. This 19-year-old has rhinitis, eczema and a dust trigger, an atopic picture. Tell: the atopic triad and an allergen trigger point to extrinsic, not intrinsic, asthma.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
E.q: A 28-year-old woman with moderate persistent asthma is given a peak flow meter to assess her control at home. When should she take her readings?
opts: Readings taken only during symptoms cannot establish her baseline or show the morning-to-afternoon variation that marks poor control. Tell: the schedule is morning before and afternoon after the bronchodilator, every day.
Once a month at the clinic
Peak flow is a personal, at-home measurement; monthly office readings cannot show daily variation. Tell: the 20% day-to-day or morning-to-afternoon change can only be seen with regular home readings.

Exercise adds a separate trigger and bedtime is not the reference point. Tell: the comparison that shows control is morning before the bronchodilator against afternoon after it, with a 20% change meaning poor control.

Correct. Peak flow is measured in the morning before the bronchodilator and in the afternoon after it. A 20% change between those readings, or from day to day, indicates poor control, so this schedule lets her and her clinician see variation.

E.q: Which factors select the empiric antibiotic regimen for hospital-acquired pneumonia?
opts: Whether onset was early or late in the stay

Onset timing matters for naming the pneumonia (hospital-acquired begins 48 hours or more after admission), but early versus late timing alone does not select the regimen. Tell: the regimen comes from local resistance data, prior cultures and recent antibiotics, not from the day count.

The health care-associated pneumonia category is retired, and therapy is not based on it: nursing-home residence or health care exposure alone does not mandate broad-spectrum therapy. Tell: hospital-acquired pneumonia is treated by the local antibiogram and the patient's resistance risk, not by where the patient lived.
Local antibiogram and patient resistance risk

Correct. For hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia, empiric therapy follows the local antibiogram and the patient's own resistance risks, with prior cultures and recent antibiotics. A common backbone is an antipseudomonal beta-lactam such as cefepime or piperacillin-tazobactam, chosen by that local data.
The color of the patient's sputum

Sputum color does not establish a bacterial cause or choose an antibiotic; antibiotics treat a bacterial syndrome, not sputum color. Tell: for hospital-acquired pneumonia the empiric choice rests on the local antibiogram and the patient's resistance risks.

E.q: A 54-year-old woman who had a kidney transplant takes long-term prednisone and anti-rejection drugs. She has 10 days of progressive shortness of breath and a dry cough, and her chest radiograph shows diffuse bilateral perihilar infiltrates. Induced sputum microscopy and Pneumocystis molecular testing are negative, but suspicion remains high. Which test should be done next?
opts: Correct. A negative induced specimen does not exclude Pneumocystis, and bronchoalveolar lavage is considered when induced sputum is negative and suspicion remains high. Her transplant, steroid use and perihilar infiltrates keep suspicion high, and the lavage sample goes for microscopy or molecular testing and other infections.

Spontaneously expectorated sputum has poor sensitivity for Pneumocystis and should not be used to exclude the infection. After a negative induced sample, a weaker specimen adds nothing. Tell: the step after a negative induced sputum goes deeper, to lavage, not back to plain sputum.

Lactate dehydrogenase is nonspecific and cannot confirm Pneumocystis or establish treatment failure. Her problem is a negative specimen with high suspicion, which only a better respiratory sample can answer. Tell: a nonspecific blood marker cannot replace microbiologic confirmation.

Pulmonary function testing is not a routine acute diagnostic test for Pneumocystis, and a normal diffusing capacity cannot reliably exclude it. Tell: she needs organism confirmation from the lower airway, which lavage provides and a breathing test cannot.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for respiratory infections in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
E.q: A 77-year-old man with community-acquired pneumonia has a PSI (Pneumonia Severity Index) total of 104 points. Which risk class does that total fall in?
opts: Class II covers 51 to 70 points, with a mortality of 0.6%. His 104 points are far above it. Tell: Class II is the low end of the scored classes, and a total over 100 cannot sit there.
Class III covers 71 to 90 points, with a mortality of 0.9%. His 104 points are above that band. Tell: once a total passes 90 it moves to Class IV, where mortality jumps about tenfold, to 9.3%.

Correct. On the interpretation table, 91 to 130 points is Class IV, with a mortality of 9.3%. The index plus clinical judgment is the preferred support for the admission decision, and a total just over 100 already carries roughly a 1 in 10 risk of death.
Class V starts at 131 points, with a mortality of 27.0%. His 104 points fall short of it. Tell: Class IV runs from 91 to 130, so 104 is a Class IV total.

E.io: Describe the major buffer systems of the body.
E.q: A 60-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis is hypoventilating, and her carbon dioxide is rising. Following water + carbon dioxide <-> carbonic acid <-> hydrogen ion + bicarbonate, what happens to her hydrogen ion concentration?
opts: Falling hydrogen ion follows a fall in carbon dioxide, as in hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. Her carbon dioxide is rising. Tell: more carbon dioxide means more acid.

Correct. Added carbon dioxide drives the carbonic acid reaction to the right, forming more carbonic acid and then more hydrogen ion and bicarbonate, so pH falls: hypoventilation, raised carbon dioxide, acidemia.
It is unchanged; bicarbonate absorbs it

Bicarbonate is formed alongside the hydrogen ion in this reaction; it does not cancel it, and the pH falls. Compensation never fully corrects the pH. Tell: both products of the reaction rise together.
It rises once the kidneys respond
The hydrogen ion rises as soon as carbon dioxide rises; the kidneys respond later (6 to 12 hours) by retaining bicarbonate to blunt it. Tell: the chemistry is immediate; the renal response is slow.

E.io: Identify and discuss vaccines which prevent respiratory infections.
E.q: A 45-year-old man gets hives whenever he eats eggs and asks whether he can receive this season's influenza vaccine. He has never reacted to an influenza vaccine. What is the most appropriate plan?
opts: Correct. Egg allergy does not require an egg-free product or precautions beyond routine vaccine safety measures. He has never reacted to an influenza vaccine, so he receives an age- and health-appropriate vaccine this season like any other adult.
An egg-free product is not required for egg allergy; any age- and health-appropriate vaccine may be used with routine safety measures. Tell: egg allergy changes nothing about product choice.

Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for everyone aged 6 months or older without a contraindication, and egg allergy is not a contraindication. Tell: skipping leaves him unprotected for no reason.

Specialist supervision applies to a severe reaction to a prior influenza vaccine, where an alternate vaccine may be possible. He has never reacted to one. Tell: his allergy is to eggs, which needs only routine safety steps.

E.q: Which physical findings may accompany extrinsic (allergic) asthma?
opts: These belong to a systemic autoimmune disease, not to allergic asthma. The allergic asthma findings are nasal swelling and secretions, eczema and nasal polyps. Tell: atopic skin disease is eczema, not a facial butterfly rash.
Swollen nasal mucosa, eczema, and nasal polyps

Correct. Extrinsic, allergic asthma may bring swelling of the nasal mucosa, increased secretions, atopic dermatitis or eczema, and nasal polyps, even when the chest exam is clear between attacks. These reflect the atopic triad of rhinitis, asthma and dermatitis.
Cyanosis, edema, and distended neck veins

Cyanosis, edema and distended neck veins describe right heart strain in chronic lung disease, not the allergic findings of extrinsic asthma. Tell: allergic asthma shows its atopy in the nose and skin, not in signs of heart failure.

These suggest chronic infection, fibrosis or malignancy, not allergy. Extrinsic asthma may show nasal mucosal swelling, increased secretions, eczema and nasal polyps. Tell: the allergic findings match the atopic triad, nose and skin.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following pulmonary conditions: 1. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease / chronic obstructive lung disease a. Chronic bronchitis subtype b. Emphysema subtype
E.q: Long-term supplemental oxygen is indicated when the resting arterial oxygen pressure falls below which value?
opts: Correct. Supplemental oxygen is indicated when the arterial oxygen pressure is below 55 mmHg or the saturation below 88%, and it is proven to decrease the risk of death, prolong life and improve quality of life.
A threshold of 65 mmHg is too high; the indication is a pressure below 55 mmHg or saturation below 88%. Tell: oxygen treats severe resting hypoxemia, not mild lowering.
A threshold of 75 mmHg would treat many patients without severe resting hypoxemia. Tell: the line is below 55 mmHg. That value is well above the severe hypoxemia that oxygen treats.
A threshold of 85 mmHg is near normal and far above the indication. Tell: long-term oxygen starts below 55 mmHg or a saturation below 88%. Such a patient has no resting hypoxemia.

E.io: Identify compensatory mechanisms for simple acid-base disorders.
E.q: A 30-year-old woman with a normal-gap metabolic acidosis from a ureteral diversion has a bicarbonate of 14 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). By the Winter formula, what carbon dioxide range is expected if she is compensating appropriately?
opts: 19 to 23 is 1.5 x 14 = 21, plus or minus 2, without adding the 8. The formula adds 8, giving 29 and a range of 27 to 31. Tell: the midpoint of the range is 29.
20 to 24 uses 1.0 instead of 1.5 times the bicarbonate (14 + 8 = 22). The formula is 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 29, giving a range of 27 to 31. Tell: the multiplier is 1.5.
Correct. Winter formula: expected carbon dioxide = 1.5 x 14 + 8 = 21 + 8 = 29, plus or minus 2, so 27 to 31 mm Hg. The formula needs only the bicarbonate, whatever the anion gap is or its cause.
36 to 44 is the normal range, and in metabolic acidosis the lungs lower the carbon dioxide below it. Winter gives 27 to 31. Tell: expected carbon dioxide falls as bicarbonate falls.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A 47-year-old man who races pigeons has 6 days of fever, severe headache and a dry cough, with a lower-lobe infiltrate. A respiratory nucleic acid test detects Chlamydia psittaci. He has no drug allergies. Which treatment is preferred?
opts: A macrolide is the alternative only when tetracyclines are unsuitable, discussed with infectious disease, and macrolide treatment failures have occurred. Tell: he has no allergy, so the preferred adult drug, doxycycline, is used.

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is the preferred treatment for Pneumocystis pneumonia, an opportunistic infection of immunocompromised hosts. Tell: bird exposure and Chlamydia psittaci point to psittacosis, treated with doxycycline.

Amoxicillin is the outpatient choice for community-acquired pneumonia without comorbidities, aimed at the usual pneumonia pathogens such as pneumococcus. Tell: a bird keeper with Chlamydia psittaci on testing has psittacosis, for which doxycycline is preferred.

Correct. Bird exposure, severe headache, a dry cough and a lower-lobe infiltrate with Chlamydia psittaci on a respiratory nucleic acid test is psittacosis. Doxycycline is preferred in adults, started promptly and continued about 10 to 14 days after the fever resolves to prevent relapse.

E.io: Define, describe, and discuss aspergillosis as it relates to asthma.
E.q: A 29-year-old man with long-standing asthma has had several exacerbations this year despite good inhaler technique and compliance. Testing shows a strong hypersensitivity to Aspergillus fumigatus with markedly raised immunoglobulin E and immunoglobulin G antibodies to the mold. Which diagnosis explains his worsening?
opts: Correct. Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis is a hypersensitivity reaction to Aspergillus fumigatus that occurs almost exclusively in asthma or cystic fibrosis; exposure causes a vigorous immunoglobulin E and G response that produces acute asthma symptoms and exacerbations, as in this patient.

Occupational asthma comes from workplace chemicals and improves away from work. His trigger is an identified mold with a vigorous antibody response. Tell: the stem names Aspergillus and the antibodies, the hallmark of allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis.

Non-compliance is the most common reason for poor control, but the stem states good technique and compliance. Tell: once compliance is confirmed, the antibody response to Aspergillus is the stated explanation for his exacerbations.
ruled out by a stated finding

Steroid-resistant asthma is very uncommon, and nothing here shows a failed steroid response. His specific antibody response to Aspergillus explains the exacerbations. Tell: a named mold with raised immunoglobulin E and G points to aspergillosis, not to drug resistance.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), patient education, and prognosis of asthma.
E.q: A 26-year-old woman in a severe asthma exacerbation sits leaning forward with hunched shoulders and uses her accessory muscles. Loud wheezing earlier has faded, and now she has only decreased breath sounds with a prolonged expiration. What does the loss of wheezing most likely indicate?
opts: A good response would ease her work of breathing as the wheeze faded. Her accessory muscle use and posture persist. Tell: a quiet chest plus hard work of breathing means severe obstruction.

Vocal fold dysfunction is an upper airway mimic in the differential, not an explanation for wheeze fading in a known severe exacerbation. Tell: decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration describe severe lower airway obstruction.

Her increased work of breathing, with accessory muscle use, leaning forward and hunched shoulders, argues against recovery. Tell: in a severe exacerbation, wheeze can vanish because too little air moves to make it.

Correct. Wheezing may not be present in severe exacerbations, which may show only decreased breath sounds with prolonged expiration. With her accessory muscle use and posture, a quiet chest signals worse obstruction, not improvement.

E.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
E.q: Which test result separates emphysema from chronic bronchitis and asthma?
opts: Correct. The diffusing capacity is reduced in emphysema, because destroyed alveoli and bullae limit gas transfer, separating it from chronic bronchitis (normal or near normal) and asthma. Spirometry alone cannot tell emphysema from chronic bronchitis.
A small bronchodilator response marks irreversible obstruction, shared by both subtypes. Tell: the measurement that singles out alveolar destruction is diffusing capacity.
A post-bronchodilator ratio below 0.70 confirms obstruction in both subtypes. Tell: it shows that the disease is present, not which subtype dominates.
A raised bicarbonate reflects compensation for chronic carbon dioxide retention, which comes earlier in chronic bronchitis. Tell: emphysema is singled out by a reduced diffusing capacity.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
E.q: A 79-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease cannot generate a strong inhalation, and his rheumatoid arthritis makes it hard to load and handle his current dry powder inhaler. Which device is most appropriate for him?
opts: Stopping maintenance would remove the drugs that prevent exacerbations. Tell: a device problem is solved by changing the device, not by stopping treatment.

Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease and are not a substitute for inhaled maintenance. Tell: the fix is a device he can use, such as a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer.

Correct. Arthritis and low peak inspiratory flow limit dry powder inhalers in older adults, so a pressurized metered-dose inhaler with a spacer, a soft mist inhaler or a nebulizer is considered. The spacer reduces the need for a forceful, well-timed breath.
Dry powder inhalers depend on a strong inspiratory flow and hand dexterity, the 2 things he lacks. Tell: switching brands within the same device type does not solve the problem.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.io: Explain how acid-base disorders affect electrolytes and oxygenation.
E.q: Which electrolyte change may accompany chronic respiratory acidosis?
opts: Correct. In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride, so serum chloride may fall (hypochloremia) while bicarbonate rises. Chloride leaves with the acid the kidney excretes.

A high chloride goes with the compensation for respiratory alkalosis (kidneys retain chloride) and with normal-gap metabolic acidosis. Chronic respiratory acidosis lowers chloride. Tell: chloride is lost with ammonium chloride in this disorder.

Low calcium with tetany belongs to respiratory alkalosis, where a high pH increases calcium binding with albumin. Chronic respiratory acidosis may cause hypochloremia. Tell: tetany points to alkalosis, hypochloremia to chronic respiratory acidosis.

Sodium is not the electrolyte change listed for chronic respiratory acidosis. The renal excretion of acid as ammonium chloride may cause hypochloremia. Tell: the electrolyte that moves is chloride, which leaves in the urine with ammonium.

E.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
E.q: What change between morning and afternoon peak flow readings indicates poor asthma control?
opts: Five percent is ordinary variation and does not signal poor control. A 20% change, morning to afternoon or day to day, does. Tell: the poor-control line is a fifth of the reading, not a few percent.

Ten percent is not the cutoff; poor control is a 20% change in morning-to-afternoon or day-to-day readings. Tell: 10% resembles the bronchodilator-response figures in spirometry, a different test and a different threshold.
Correct. A 20% change between morning and afternoon peak flow measurements, or a 20% change from day to day, indicates poor asthma control and should prompt a review of the treatment plan.
Fifty percent is not the variability threshold; a 20% swing already indicates poor control. Tell: 20% is the swing between readings that matters.

E.topic: Flow rates and fraction of inspired oxygen
E.io: Compare and contrast the different oxygen delivery systems.
E.q: What fraction of inspired oxygen does room air provide?
opts: A fraction of 16% is below the 21% of room air, so it cannot be room air; delivery devices only raise the fraction above 21%. Tell: the number to anchor is 21%.
Correct. Room air provides a fraction of inspired oxygen of .21, or 21%. That is the baseline from which every oxygen device adds, as in the nasal cannula's 24% at 1 L/min and 28% at 2 L/min.
A fraction of 24% is what a nasal cannula delivers at 1 L/min, so it is already oxygen-enriched, not room air. Room air is 21%. Tell: 24% is the first step above room air.
A fraction of 28% is what a nasal cannula delivers at 2 L/min, so it is enriched with oxygen rather than room air. Room air is 21%. Tell: this value is the second step above room air.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: A 68-year-old woman with bronchiectasis has a year of chronic cough with sputum, fatigue and weight loss. Computed tomography shows nodular bronchiectasis, alternative diagnoses have been excluded, and two sputum cultures grow Mycobacterium avium complex. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Correct. Mycobacterium avium complex is a common cause of nontuberculous lung disease, and bronchiectasis raises the risk. She meets every diagnostic domain: compatible symptoms and imaging (nodular bronchiectasis), exclusion of alternatives, and 2 or more sputum cultures with the same species.

A respiratory isolate alone does not prove disease, which is why diagnosis needs every domain. Tell: she has compatible symptoms, nodular bronchiectasis, alternatives excluded and two cultures of the same species, so the criteria are met.

Chronic pulmonary aspergillosis is on the differential of chronic cough and cavitary or bronchiectatic disease. Tell: her cultures identify Mycobacterium avium complex twice, the microbiologic evidence for nontuberculous disease.

Tuberculosis is caused by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex, and her cultures grew a different, environmental species. Tell: Mycobacterium avium complex is a nontuberculous mycobacterium, so the species identification decides it.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. E.q: A 27-year-old woman with no known tuberculosis risk factors has a tuberculin skin test for a school requirement. At 48 hours a trained reader measures 12 mm of transverse induration. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Correct. With no known tuberculosis risk factors, her cut-off is 15 mm, the highest of the three thresholds. 12 mm of induration is below 15 mm, so the result is negative for her, even though it would be positive for someone in the 5 mm or 10 mm groups.

5 mm is reserved for human immunodeficiency virus infection, recent close contact, transplant, major immunosuppression or imaging suggesting prior tuberculosis. Tell: none of these applies to her, so the 15 mm cut-off is used.
10 mm is for increased exposure risk, selected medical risks, high-risk congregate settings or age under 5. Tell: she has no known risk factors, which puts her at 15 mm, and 12 mm falls short.

Repeat testing 8 to 10 weeks after the last exposure is for an early negative result after a recent exposure, and she has had none. Tell: a skin test reading in millimeters is compared with her risk group's cut-off, which gives a clear answer.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: What does a positive acid-fast smear of sputum establish?
opts: The smear cannot confirm Mycobacterium tuberculosis, because nontuberculous mycobacteria are acid-fast too. Species identification comes from culture and molecular tests. Tell: a smear names a group of organisms, not the species.

Immune responses to tuberculosis infection are what the tuberculin skin test and the interferon-gamma release assay detect. A smear looks for the organism itself in the specimen. Tell: smear = organism; skin and blood tests = immune response.
A group of organisms, not the species

Correct. An acid-fast smear identifies a group of organisms, the acid-fast bacilli with lipid-rich, mycolic acid cell walls. It does not distinguish Mycobacterium tuberculosis from nontuberculous mycobacteria, so culture and molecular testing must name the species.

Susceptibility comes from separate molecular and culture-based drug-susceptibility testing ordered on the specimens. The smear only shows that acid-fast bacilli are present. Tell: susceptibility is its own test, not a smear reading.

E.q: A 52-year-old woman with acute bronchitis was managed with supportive care 10 days ago and at first improved. She now returns with a new temperature of 102.2°F, shortness of breath and crackles at the left base. What is the most appropriate next step?

A worsening cough means reconsidering the diagnosis, and suspected pneumonia is confirmed with chest radiography.

Fever or focal findings should prompt evaluation for pneumonia rather than empiric bronchitis antibiotics; an antibiotic without a diagnosis skips the step that decides the regimen. Tell: new crackles with fever call for imaging first.

The 2 to 3 week cough applies to an uncomplicated course; improvement followed by worsening, new fever and dyspnea are return precautions that mean the course is no longer uncomplicated. Tell: reassurance fits a steady cough, not a relapse with fever.

E.q: A 40-year-old man has a pH of 7.30 (normal 7.35 to 7.45) and a carbon dioxide of 52 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg). To decide whether this respiratory problem is acute or chronic, which value is compared with its expected level?
opts: The anion gap sorts metabolic acidosis and says nothing about respiratory chronicity. The rise in bicarbonate does. Tell: the gap uses sodium, chloride and bicarbonate to type a metabolic disorder.
Correct. For a respiratory disorder, compensation is renal, so the expected bicarbonate is checked. A small rise (about 1 per 10 mm Hg) means acute, and a large rise (about 3.5 per 10) means chronic.

The expected carbon dioxide is calculated for a metabolic disorder, as with the Winter formula. A respiratory disorder is checked by its bicarbonate. Tell: his carbon dioxide is the primary problem, so it is not the compensation check.

opts: Doxycycline covers the usual organisms of an uncomplicated exacerbation, Haemophilus influenzae and streptococci, but not Pseudomonas. Tell: her prior Pseudomonas culture moves the choice to levofloxacin.

Correct. Her increased, purulent sputum meets the indication for antibiotics, and a previous Pseudomonas culture creates pseudomonal concern. Levofloxacin is the oral choice for pseudomonal concern, a respiratory fluoroquinolone that also covers atypical, gram-positive and gram-negative organisms.
Azithromycin, a macrolide, is very active against atypical organisms and is an uncomplicated-exacerbation option. Tell: it is not the pseudomonal choice; levofloxacin is.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a first-line option for uncomplicated exacerbations without Pseudomonas coverage. Tell: a history of Pseudomonas calls for levofloxacin.

Piperacillin-tazobactam is an antipseudomonal backbone for hospital-acquired and ventilator-associated pneumonia. Her pneumonia is community acquired with no Pseudomonas risk. Tell: the hospital pathway's drugs do not move to the community pathway without a validated risk.

Amoxicillin by itself is an outpatient regimen for patients without comorbidities. She needs a ward bed and an inpatient regimen. Tell: inpatients start with a beta-lactam plus a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.

E.q: A 66-year-old woman is being discharged after a hospitalization for an exacerbation. Her blood eosinophil count is elevated. Which action belongs in her discharge bundle?
opts: Holding maintenance therapy raises the risk of another exacerbation. Tell: the bundle starts long-acting bronchodilators promptly, before she leaves. Prompt start is part of the bundle.
Pulmonary rehabilitation is considered as part of the discharge bundle, and it reduces readmissions. Tell: rehabilitation is planned at discharge, not put off for months.

Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only, not long-term use after discharge. Tell: maintenance after an admission is long-acting inhaled therapy, plus an inhaled steroid with high eosinophils.

Correct. The discharge bundle begins long-acting bronchodilators promptly, considers an inhaled corticosteroid if eosinophils are elevated (as hers are), checks inhaler technique, considers pulmonary rehabilitation, arranges follow-up and explains the recovery timeline.

Tell: onset 48 hours or more after admission moves her off the community pathway.

Vancomycin or linezolid is added only when methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus risk or local prevalence supports it, and she has no such risk. Tell: without that risk, one antipseudomonal agent with methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus coverage is enough.
ruled out by a stated finding

Piperacillin-tazobactam is one of the usual single agents for hospital-acquired pneumonia without major risks, but the choice between it and cefepime is made with the local antibiogram. Tell: her hospital's Pseudomonas isolates are mostly resistant to it and susceptible to cefepime.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Pneumonia that begins 48 hours or more after admission is hospital-acquired. With no major resistance or high mortality risk, one antipseudomonal agent with methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus coverage is chosen using the local antibiogram, and hers favors cefepime over piperacillin-tazobactam.

opts: Vaccines prevent exacerbations and pneumonia and are given routinely, not after an exacerbation. Tell: yearly influenza and age-65 pneumococcal vaccination are both due now.

Correct. Every patient should get a yearly influenza shot, proven to reduce hospitalizations and death, and every patient should receive the pneumococcal vaccine at age 65 to reduce community-acquired pneumonia. At 66 and unvaccinated, she needs both.
The pneumococcal vaccine is due at 65, but the yearly influenza shot is the vaccine proven to reduce hospitalizations and death. Tell: it is October, and she needs both.
The yearly influenza vaccine is due, but at 66 she has also passed the age-65 point for the pneumococcal vaccine. Tell: both vaccines are due in a 66-year-old who has had neither.

E.q: A 57-year-old man with confirmed chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a symptom assessment test score of 7 and a modified Medical Research Council dyspnea grade of 1. He has had no exacerbations in the past year. Under the current three-group scheme, which group is he in?
opts: Group E is high risk: 2 or more moderate exacerbations or 1 hospitalization in the past year. He had none. Tell: without exacerbations, his group is set by symptoms alone.
Group B is low risk with more symptoms: a symptom score of 10 or more or a dyspnea grade of 2 or more. His 7 and grade 1 are below both. Tell: fewer symptoms keep him in A.
Group C belongs to the 2020 four-group scheme (few symptoms, high risk), and he is low risk anyway. Tell: the current scheme has only A, B and E. Without high risk, he cannot be C in either scheme.

Correct. A symptom score of 7 (under 10) and a dyspnea grade of 1 (0 to 1) mean fewer symptoms, and no exacerbations means low risk. Low symptoms with low risk is group A, which starts with a single bronchodilator.

E.q: A 55-year-old woman develops severe hypoxia, saturation 79%, from pneumonia. She is alert, breathing at a steady rate with good chest rise, and her arterial carbon dioxide is normal. Which device delivers the high fraction she needs?
opts: A simple mask is meant for mild to moderate respiratory distress and delivers about 35-50% at 5-10 L/min. Her saturation of 79% calls for a higher fraction than that. Tell: the simple mask has no reservoir bag, while the non-rebreather has a bag that holds oxygen for the high fraction she needs.

A bag-valve mask is a resuscitator used to assist breathing for a patient who is not ventilating. She is alert, breathing at a steady rate with good chest rise, so she is breathing on her own. Tell: a bag-valve mask is for the patient who is not breathing adequately; this patient is ventilating well.
ruled out by a stated finding

A nasal cannula is a low flow device for mild hypoxia, and its fraction tops out at 44% even if the knob is turned higher. At 79% she needs a high fraction, which a cannula cannot supply. Tell: mild hypoxia and a ceiling of 44% point to the cannula; severe hypoxia with a reservoir bag points to the non-rebreather.

Correct. Her saturation of 79% is severe hypoxia, yet she is alert, breathing steadily with good chest rise, so she is still ventilating well. The non-rebreather mask is the device for severely hypoxic patients who are still ventilating well, giving 60-100% at 10-15 L/min through its reservoir bag.

E.q: A 52-year-old man has hypertension that is hard to control and muscle weakness. He takes no diuretics, has not vomited, and eats a bag of black licorice every day. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.47 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 47 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L); potassium 3.0 mEq/L (normal 3.5 to 5.0 mEq/L); urine chloride is high. Which part of his history best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Correct. High pH with a high bicarbonate is metabolic alkalosis; the high urine chloride makes it saline unresponsive, and his high blood pressure puts it in the hypertensive group, which lists licorice. Low potassium with weakness fits.

Vomiting (loss of hydrochloric acid) causes a saline-responsive alkalosis with a low urine chloride, below 25 mEq/L, and volume contraction. His urine chloride is high and he is hypertensive. Tell: vomiting-type alkalosis has a low urine chloride.
ruled out by a stated finding

Hyperventilation causes respiratory alkalosis, with a carbon dioxide below 36. His is 47 and his bicarbonate 33, so the primary change is metabolic. Tell: respiratory alkalosis lowers the carbon dioxide; his is raised as compensation.
ruled out by a stated finding

Antacids cause a saline-responsive alkalosis, with a low urine chloride. His is high, and he is hypertensive rather than volume contracted. Tell: a high urine chloride steers you to the saline-unresponsive list.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.q: A 19-year-old college student has just been prescribed albuterol for newly diagnosed asthma. Which side effects should she be told to expect?
opts: Thrush and hoarseness are local side effects of inhaled corticosteroids, reduced with a spacer and rinsing. Tell: albuterol is a bronchodilator, and its side effects are tremor and palpitations.

Bruising and truncal obesity are side effects of systemic corticosteroids, which also cause osteoporosis and hypertension. Tell: a short-acting bronchodilator causes tremor and palpitations, not steroid effects.
Insomnia, dyspepsia and acid reflux are side effects of theophylline, the methylxanthine. Tell: albuterol's side effects come from beta-2 stimulation, tremor and palpitations.

Correct. Short-acting beta-2 agonists such as albuterol relax airway smooth muscle for about 3 to 6 hours, and their side effects include muscle tremors and palpitations. Knowing this keeps a new user from stopping her rescue inhaler out of alarm.

E.q: A 71-year-old man with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has a stable chronic respiratory acidosis. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 60 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 33 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which serum electrolyte finding is expected?
opts: Hyperchloremia is the pattern of respiratory alkalosis compensation (kidneys retain chloride) and of normal-gap metabolic acidosis. His kidneys are excreting chloride. Tell: chronic respiratory acidosis is the low-chloride state.

His kidneys retain bicarbonate to offset the carbon dioxide; his is 33, high. A low bicarbonate marks metabolic acidosis or respiratory alkalosis compensation. Tell: the compensation for retained carbon dioxide is retained bicarbonate.
An elevated gap marks a metabolic acidosis with added unmeasured anions; his disorder is respiratory, with a high bicarbonate. Tell: the gap is a tool for metabolic acidosis.

Correct. In chronic respiratory acidosis the kidneys excrete acid as ammonium chloride and retain bicarbonate, so hypochloremia accompanies the raised bicarbonate of 33. This is the renal compensation.

E.q: A 71-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease was started on daily oral prednisone by another clinic 6 months ago as maintenance therapy. He has had no recent exacerbation. Which part of his regimen should be stopped or avoided?
opts: Correct. Oral corticosteroids are for acute exacerbations only in this disease, which is why they are missing from the list of common chronic therapies. Maintenance is built from albuterol as needed and long-acting inhaled bronchodilators, with an inhaled corticosteroid only when indicated.
Every patient should have an albuterol inhaler to prevent or reduce symptoms, as needed. Tell: the rescue inhaler stays; daily oral steroids, meant for exacerbations, are what does not belong.
The yearly influenza vaccine is proven to reduce hospitalizations and death and is given to every patient. Tell: it stays in his plan; the drug to stop is the maintenance oral steroid.

Long-acting antimuscarinics such as tiotropium limit bronchoconstriction, help prevent exacerbations, and are poorly absorbed with mainly dry mouth. Tell: they are standard maintenance; the oral steroid is not.

E.q: A 58-year-old woman with asthma and nasal polyps developed wheezing, facial flushing and a runny nose within an hour of taking aspirin last year. She now has painful knee osteoarthritis and asks for an anti-inflammatory pain reliever. Which drug is the most appropriate choice?
opts: Indomethacin is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug, the group that worsens aspirin-sensitive asthma, so her aspirin reaction rules it out. Tell: only the selective agents (celecoxib, meloxicam) are allowed in aspirin-sensitive asthma.

Naproxen is a non-selective anti-inflammatory drug, and patients with aspirin-sensitive asthma cross-react with that group. Her past aspirin reaction rules it out. Tell: the safe choices for her are the selective agents, celecoxib and meloxicam.

Diclofenac is on the list of non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs to avoid in aspirin-sensitive asthma, and her flushing and wheeze after aspirin show that sensitivity. Tell: selective agents such as celecoxib are the ones she may use.

Correct. Her wheeze, flushing and rhinorrhea after aspirin mark aspirin-sensitive asthma, so non-selective anti-inflammatory drugs must be avoided. Selective agents such as celecoxib or meloxicam may be used, which treats her knee pain without the cross-reaction.

E.q: A 26-year-old man is found unresponsive at a party with pinpoint pupils and a respiratory rate of 6. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.24 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 62 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 26 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which acid-base disorder is present?
opts: Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate driving the low pH, and his bicarbonate is 26, within normal. The raised carbon dioxide of 62 is the value that matches the acidemia. Tell: when bicarbonate is normal and carbon dioxide is high, the problem is respiratory.
ruled out by a stated finding

Chronic respiratory acidosis would show a much larger bicarbonate rise, about 3.5 mEq/L per 10 mm Hg, or near 32 here (22 mm Hg above 40). His 26 is the small acute rise. Tell: a bicarbonate near 26 means the kidneys have not had their 6 to 12 hours or more.

Correct. The pH of 7.24 is acidemia, and the carbon dioxide of 62 is high, which matches it, so the problem is respiratory. Bicarbonate rose only about 1 per 10 mm Hg (22 above 40 gives about 26), the acute response. A slow rate of 6 fits central nervous system depression.

Respiratory alkalosis is a high pH from a low carbon dioxide. He has a pH of 7.24 and a carbon dioxide of 62, and both point the other way. Tell: check the pH first; 7.24 is acidemia, so no alkalosis is possible.

Arterial blood gas: pH 7.48 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 31 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 23 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which of his conditions best accounts for this blood gas?
opts: Metformin causes an elevated-gap metabolic acidosis, a low pH with a low bicarbonate. His pH is 7.48. Tell: metformin drives the pH down.
Antacids cause a metabolic alkalosis with a high bicarbonate above 26. His bicarbonate is 23, and his primary change is the low carbon dioxide. Tell: antacid alkalosis raises bicarbonate.
ruled out by a stated finding
Diabetic ketoacidosis is an elevated-gap metabolic acidosis with a low pH. His pH is 7.48, alkalemic. Tell: ketoacidosis lowers bicarbonate and pH.

E.q: A 54-year-old man with severe pneumonia is on an aerosol mask from an air-entrainment nebulizer. The team wants to raise its fraction to 0.80. Why is that setting a concern?
opts: This device is not capped at 0.28. It can deliver higher fractions, and the concern is the specific recommendation not to go above 0.50. Tell: the limit is a recommended ceiling of 0.50, not 0.28.
The recommendation is the opposite: use above 0.50 is not recommended. Reading it as recommended would invert the ceiling. Tell: 0.50 is a ceiling, not a floor.
It changes with his breathing rate

An air-entrainment system gives a fixed fraction that does not fluctuate with patient demand. A fraction that follows breathing rate describes the cannula, simple mask or non-rebreather. Tell: air entrainment is steady; the concern with 0.80 is the recommended ceiling.

Correct. A fixed-fraction air-entrainment nebulizer can deliver higher fractions, but setting above 0.50 is not recommended. His team wants 0.80, which is beyond that ceiling, so it is a concern even though his pneumonia is severe.

E.q: A 69-year-old woman with long-standing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease comes for a routine visit, at her baseline. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.34 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 58 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 32 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). opts: Acute compensation raises bicarbonate only about 1 per 10 mm Hg, to about 26 here (58 is 18 above 40). Her 32 shows the fuller renal response of chronic disease. Tell: she is at her baseline with long-standing lung disease, so the kidneys have had days.

Correct. Her carbon dioxide of 58 is high and her pH of 7.34 is just below normal, so the process is respiratory acidosis. Bicarbonate is 32, a rise of about 6 (1.8 x 3.5), the size of chronic compensation. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is a classic chronic cause.

Metabolic acidosis needs a low bicarbonate, below 22, driving the pH down; hers is 32, high. The raised carbon dioxide of 58 is what matches her low pH, and the high bicarbonate is the kidneys' compensation. Tell: in metabolic acidosis the bicarbonate and carbon dioxide both fall.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.q: A 41-year-old woman who rehearses with a church choir indoors for hours each week is diagnosed with infectious pulmonary tuberculosis. She asks how she could have spread it to other choir members. Which describes how tuberculosis spreads in this setting?
opts: Tuberculosis spreads through the air, as infectious aerosols from pulmonary or laryngeal disease. Tell: the exposure that matters for her choir is shared indoor air, especially when prolonged and poorly ventilated, not shared objects.

Correct. Pulmonary and laryngeal tuberculosis release infectious aerosols during coughing, speaking or singing, and risk rises with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation. A choir rehearsing indoors for hours fits that pattern.
Risk increases with prolonged shared indoor air and poor ventilation, the opposite of a brief outdoor meeting. Tell: the choir risk comes from hours of singing together indoors.

Transmission is airborne, from aerosols released while coughing, speaking or singing. Tell: the exposure risks are close contact with an infectious person and prolonged time in enclosed, poorly ventilated spaces, not touch.

E.q: A 72-year-old man has a post-bronchodilator ratio of 0.48 and a forced expiratory volume in 1 second of 26% predicted. Which airflow grade fits?
opts: Grade 1, mild, needs 80% predicted or more. At 26% he is far below. Tell: his airflow is about a quarter of predicted. His very low ratio and 26% airflow both show advanced obstruction.
Grade 2, moderate, covers 50% up to 80% predicted. At 26% he is well under it. Tell: under 30% is the very severe band. Moderate means at least half of predicted airflow.
Grade 3, severe, is 30% to 49% predicted. At 26% he has dropped below its lower limit. Tell: below 30% is grade 4. Severe stops at 30%; anything lower is very severe.
Correct. With the ratio below 0.70, a post-bronchodilator 1-second volume of 26% predicted is below 30%, grade 4, very severe. Grade 3 covers 30% to 49%.

In older adults the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose. Tell: her age and borderline value call for clinical context, not an automatic label.

Correct. In adults 65 and older, the fixed 0.70 ratio may overdiagnose, so clinical context is weighed. A borderline ratio with near-normal airflow and mild symptoms in an 84-year-old calls for that judgment.

Alpha-1 antitrypsin testing is aimed at young patients or those with few exposures, and mild breathlessness at 84 with a borderline ratio does not point to it. Tell: in an elderly patient the stated caution is overdiagnosis from the fixed ratio.

Oseltamivir is the preferred influenza antiviral for high-risk patients, including in pregnancy, and pregnancy in any trimester makes her high risk. Tell: pregnancy is a reason to give oseltamivir, not to avoid it.

Nirmatrelvir/ritonavir is a preferred early treatment for high-risk patients within 5 days of onset, after a review of drug interactions and kidney and liver issues. The pregnancy warning on the list belongs to molnupiravir. Tell: the avoid-in-pregnancy statement names molnupiravir.

E.q: A 78-year-old man with dysphagia after a stroke is admitted to a general ward with nonsevere aspiration pneumonia and started on ceftriaxone plus azithromycin. He has never had methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas isolated. On day 2, imaging newly shows a pleural empyema. Which change to his antibiotics is appropriate?
opts: Correct. Aspiration pneumonia is treated with the community or hospital regimen for its setting and severity, and anaerobic coverage is added only when abscess or empyema is suspected, not routinely. The new empyema is that trigger; drainage is also considered when indicated.

Aspiration pneumonitis is a sterile chemical injury managed with support and no prophylactic antibiotics. He has an infectious syndrome with an infiltrate and now an empyema, which is established infection that needs antibiotics. Tell: chemical injury needs support; infection needs antibiotics.

Vancomycin is the methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus agent, given only when that coverage is indicated, and he has never had the organism isolated. Tell: an empyema after aspiration calls for anaerobic coverage, not resistant-organism coverage.
ruled out by a stated finding
Leaving the regimen unchanged would be right for uncomplicated aspiration pneumonia, but an empyema changes it. Tell: anaerobic coverage is reserved for abscess or empyema, and he now has one.

Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: Four adults have community-acquired pneumonia, are stable for outpatient treatment and have no risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas. Which one fits amoxicillin as a single drug?
opts: The one with no chronic conditions

Correct. Amoxicillin, or doxycycline, is the outpatient choice when there are no comorbidities and no methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas risk. Each of the others has a listed comorbidity, which calls for a beta-lactam plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone.

Diabetes is on the comorbidity list, so this patient needs amoxicillin-clavulanate, cefpodoxime or cefuroxime plus azithromycin or doxycycline, or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: amoxicillin alone is reserved for the outpatient with no comorbidities.
ruled out by a stated finding

Asplenia is a listed comorbidity, alongside chronic heart, lung, liver or renal disease, diabetes, alcoholism and malignancy, so this patient takes the comorbidity regimen. Tell: amoxicillin alone fits only the patient without comorbidities.
ruled out by a stated finding
The one with chronic liver disease

Chronic liver disease is a listed comorbidity, which moves this patient to the combination regimen (a beta-lactam such as amoxicillin-clavulanate plus azithromycin or doxycycline) or a respiratory fluoroquinolone. Tell: any listed comorbidity rules out amoxicillin alone.
ruled out by a stated finding

E.q: An 80-year-old woman who lives in a nursing home is brought in with 2 days of fever and productive cough, and her admission chest radiograph shows a new infiltrate. She has never had methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus or Pseudomonas isolated from her airway and has not recently been hospitalized for intravenous antibiotics. How should this pneumonia be classified?
opts: Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops 48 hours or more after admission and was not incubating on admission. Her infiltrate was present on the admission film. Tell: the clock for hospital-acquired pneumonia starts at admission, and her illness began before she arrived.
ruled out by a stated finding

Ventilator-associated pneumonia develops more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation, and she is not intubated. Tell: this label needs a breathing tube in place for more than 48 hours before the pneumonia starts.
ruled out by a stated finding

Correct. Community-acquired pneumonia is acquired outside the hospital or present early in admission, and prior health care contact does not exclude it. The health care-associated category is retired, and nursing-home residence alone does not mandate broad-spectrum therapy; her lack of resistant-organism risks keeps her on the community pathway.

The health care-associated pneumonia category is retired, so nursing-home residence or health care exposure alone no longer defines a separate class or mandates broad-spectrum therapy. Tell: assess specific resistant-organism risks instead of applying the old label.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following respiratory infections: 1. Acute bronchitis 2. Pneumonia: 3. Bacterial 4. Viral 5. Atypical (including but not limited to chlamydia psittacosis and mycoplasma) 6. Fungal (including but not limited to cryptococcosis, histoplasmosis, pneumocystis jiroveccii) 7. Aspiration pneumonia 8. Lung abscess 9. Influenza 10. Coronavirus (COVID-19)
E.q: A healthy 29-year-old woman has acute histoplasmosis confirmed by urine antigen after clearing out a bat-infested attic. Ten days after onset her fever is resolving and her cough is improving, and she is not short of breath. Which management is most appropriate?
opts: Amphotericin-based induction led by a specialist is for severe pulmonary or disseminated disease. She has a mild, improving illness. Tell: amphotericin is the top of the severity ladder, and she is at the bottom.

Correct. Severity and host risk guide treatment, and mild acute disease in an immunocompetent adult often needs observation rather than antifungals. She is healthy and already improving, so neither itraconazole nor amphotericin is needed.

Prolonged azole therapy, usually at least 12 months, is for chronic cavitary disease, and itraconazole is otherwise considered for prolonged or progressive illness or higher-risk hosts. Tell: she is healthy and improving, which is the observation pathway.

Fluconazole for 6 to 12 months is the regimen for mild isolated pulmonary cryptococcosis, a different fungus. Her antigen confirmed histoplasmosis. Tell: the 6 to 12 month fluconazole course belongs to Cryptococcus, not to mild histoplasmosis.

E.io: List the components of patient education in treating asthma, including use of peak flow meters, metered-dose inhalers, nebulizers.
E.q: A 30-year-old man with asthma follows a written action plan. His personal best peak flow is 600 L/min. Today he is very short of breath, his quick-relief medicine has not helped, and his peak flow is 260 L/min. Which action-plan zone is he in?
opts: Green requires 80% or more of personal best (480 or higher) and no symptoms. He is far below that and very short of breath. Tell: he has none of the doing-well features.

Correct. A peak flow of 260 out of a personal best of 600 is about 43%, below 50% of personal best, and he is very short of breath despite quick-relief medicine. Those are red-zone, medical-alert findings: take the rescue medicine and call the doctor or get help now.

The yellow zone is 50% to 79% of personal best, 300 to 474 for him. At 260 he is below it, and quick-relief medicine has failed. Tell: failure of the quick-relief medicine is itself a red-zone criterion.

Waiting is unsafe: under 50% of personal best with failed quick-relief medicine is the red, medical-alert zone, which calls for action now. Tell: action plans are built so that a red reading leads to immediate action, not a delay.

E.io: Identify medical care strategies for chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD)/ chronic obstructive lung disease (COLD) for the following populations. 1. adult 2. elderly
E.q: A 76-year-old woman with group E chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is recovering from a hospitalization. She is breathless walking around her home and has never been referred for rehabilitation. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: No referral because of her age
Age is not a reason to withhold rehabilitation; older adults are under-referred and should be referred actively. Tell: her group E disease makes rehabilitation essential.

Possible surgical need is a pulmonology referral reason, but nothing in her story suggests a surgical lesion. Tell: her breathlessness and recent admission call for rehabilitation, essential in group E.

Correct. Pulmonary rehabilitation is essential for groups B and E and, next to smoking cessation, tends to be the most effective therapy, reducing dyspnea and readmissions. Older adults are less often referred, so she should be referred actively.
Behavioral health is among the other resources, but it does not treat her exertional breathlessness. Tell: rehabilitation trains breathing, strength and energy conservation.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following mycobacterial infections: a. Tuberculosis b. Atypical mycobacterial disease
E.q: What must be done before starting treatment for latent tuberculosis infection?
opts: A positive result is not repeated; it requires clinical evaluation and chest imaging to look for disease. Tell: the step before latent treatment is excluding disease.
Symptoms would point to disease, which needs evaluation now and a different regimen. Tell: latent treatment starts only after disease has been excluded.
A negative assay would argue against infection, not prepare for latent treatment; the skin test and blood assay may stay positive after treatment anyway. Tell: the requirement is excluding disease.

Correct. Tuberculosis disease is excluded before latent treatment begins, because a positive skin test or blood assay shows infection but cannot separate latent infection from disease. Interactions, pregnancy and source-case resistance are also checked.

E.q: In the CURB-65 (confusion, urea, respiratory rate, blood pressure, age 65 or older) score, which respiratory rate earns a point?
opts: A rate of 20 is far below the threshold. Tell: the respiratory rate point needs 30 or more breaths per minute, the same rate that earns points in the Pneumonia Severity Index.
A rate of 24 does not reach the scoring threshold. Tell: the point is given at 30 or more breaths per minute.
Correct. A respiratory rate of 30 or more breaths per minute scores 1 point, as do confusion, urea above 20 mg/dL (7 mmol/L), systolic pressure below 90 or diastolic 60 or less, and age 65 or older.
Thirty-five overstates the threshold, so patients breathing 30 to 34 times a minute would be missed. Tell: the point starts at 30 breaths per minute.

E.q: A 62-year-old man's chest radiograph and sputum smear lead his clinician to presume pulmonary tuberculosis; culture results are weeks away. Which reporting step is appropriate now?
opts: Report if drug resistance is found

Notification is for every presumed or confirmed case, not just resistant ones; rifampin resistance additionally needs rapid susceptibility testing and expert management. Tell: resistance changes the regimen, not whether to report.

Correct. The local or state tuberculosis program is notified of presumed or confirmed tuberculosis, so reporting does not wait for culture. Public-health coordination also guides the criteria for ending isolation.
No report; the clinician manages it
Tuberculosis care is coordinated with the local or state tuberculosis program, and isolation ends by public-health criteria among others. Tell: a presumed case is reported now, not managed privately.
Reporting covers presumed as well as confirmed tuberculosis, and cultures can take weeks. Tell: a presumed case is reported to the local or state tuberculosis program now.

E.io: Develop a treatment plan for patients with asthma based on symptoms and physical examination.
E.q: A 47-year-old woman has asthma symptoms 3 days a week, wakes at night 3 times a month, and uses albuterol 3 days a week but not daily. She has minor limitation of activity. Her forced expiratory volume in 1 second is 72% predicted with a ratio reduced by 4%. Which severity classification fits?
opts: Most of her features are mild persistent, but mild persistent requires a 1-second volume above 80%; hers is 72%. Severity follows the worst feature. Tell: lung function between 60% and 80% sets her one class higher.

Correct. Her symptoms, night waking, rescue use and minor limitation fit mild persistent, but a 1-second volume between 60% and 80% predicted (72%) is a moderate persistent feature, and severity follows the most severe category in which any feature occurs.

Intermittent asthma allows symptoms on 2 or fewer days a week and a 1-second volume above 80%. She has 3 days a week and 72% function. Tell: both her symptoms and her spirometry exceed the intermittent column.

Severe persistent asthma needs a 1-second volume below 60% or features such as symptoms throughout the day. Her worst feature, 72%, sits in the moderate band. Tell: 72% is above the 60% line that marks severe disease.

E.io: Identify the etiologies, clinical manifestations, and management of simple acid-base disorders, including: a. Respiratory acidosis b. Respiratory alkalosis c. Metabolic acidosis d. Metabolic alkalosis
E.q: A 23-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes has diabetic ketoacidosis with Kussmaul respirations (deep, rapid breathing). Arterial blood gas: pH 7.19 (normal 7.35 to 7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 21 mm Hg (normal 36 to 44 mm Hg), bicarbonate 8 mEq/L (normal 22 to 26 mEq/L). Which approach corrects her acid-base disorder?
opts: Rebreathing would blunt her compensation, and a paper bag is not necessary even in hyperventilation, with only a placebo effect. Her acidosis is metabolic, and the cause is treated. Tell: a bag does not treat a metabolic acidosis.

Correct. Elevated-gap metabolic acidosis is treated by treating the underlying disorder; her pH of 7.19 is acidemic but not in the unsustainable range below 6.7. Her deep breathing is compensation and is left alone.
Bicarbonate until her pH is normal

Therapy to normalize the pH may be warranted at unsustainable values (below 6.7), along with treatment of the cause. At 7.19 she needs the ketoacidosis treated. Tell: treat the cause; pH-directed therapy belongs to unsustainable values.
Slow her breathing to retain carbon dioxide
Her deep, rapid breathing is the compensation lowering carbon dioxide; slowing it would drop her pH further. Tell: compensatory hyperventilation is protective in metabolic acidosis.

E.topic: Metabolic acidosis and the anion gap
E.io: Identify simple acid-base disorders by interpreting diagnostic test results and patient presentations
E.q: An elevated anion gap is usually due to which change?
opts: Fewer unmeasured anions would lower the gap. An elevated gap usually means more unmeasured anions. Tell: the gap moves with the anions in the same direction.
Correct. An elevated anion gap is usually due to an increase in unmeasured anions. Less often it is due to a decrease in unmeasured cations (calcium, magnesium, potassium, gamma-globulins).
More unmeasured cations would lower the gap; a decrease in unmeasured cations is the less common cause of an elevated gap. Tell: cations move the gap the opposite way.

A high chloride goes with normal-gap (hyperchloremic) acidosis, where chloride replaces the lost bicarbonate. An elevated gap usually means more unmeasured anions. Tell: the chloride is part of the formula, not the gap.

E.q: A 71-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and heart failure is hospitalized on day 5 of influenza, confirmed by molecular testing, with hypoxemia. Which antiviral is most appropriate?
opts: Correct. Hospitalized patients generally receive oral or enteric oseltamivir, which is preferred for hospitalized, severe and high-risk patients and is started even after 48 hours. His age, lung and heart disease and admission all point to it, with renal dose adjustment.

Inhaled zanamivir is avoided in chronic obstructive lung disease because of bronchospasm risk, and hospitalized patients generally receive oseltamivir instead. Tell: his lung disease and admission both rule out the inhaled drug.
ruled out by a stated finding
Baloxavir is not recommended for hospitalized influenza and is limited to uncomplicated illness within 48 hours. He is hospitalized on day 5. Tell: admission and timing both rule it out.
ruled out by a stated finding
Amantadine and rimantadine are not recommended because of resistance. Tell: the hospital antiviral is oseltamivir, given orally or by enteric tube.

E.io: Describe how PFTs are utilized to aid in the diagnosis of pulmonary diseases and monitoring of patients with those diseases
E.q: A 35-year-old man has had stable, well-controlled asthma for 2 years. How often should his spirometry be repeated to monitor progression?
opts: Monthly spirometry is far more often than needed for stable disease; home peak flow readings handle frequent monitoring. Tell: office spirometry for monitoring is repeated once a year.

Repeating spirometry every 3 months is more often than recommended for monitoring stable asthma. Tell: the interval for monitoring progression with spirometry is annual, while peak flow covers day-to-day control.

Correct. Spirometry is best done before and after a short-acting bronchodilator and is repeated annually to monitor progression. For this man with stable, controlled disease, a yearly test tracks his lung function between routine follow-up visits.
A 5-year gap is too long; spirometry is repeated annually to monitor progression. Tell: once a year is the monitoring interval, so 5 years would miss changes in his lung function.

E.io: Discuss patient education for oxygen delivery
E.q: A 71-year-old man starting home oxygen asks why he must be so careful at home if oxygen is "just air." Which property of oxygen underlies the safety teaching?
opts: It is toxic to breathe for visitors
Oxygen is not described as toxic to visitors. The hazards listed are carbon dioxide retention, fire, mucosal irritation and vasoconstriction. Tell: the home safety teaching rests on flammability.
Oxygen being heavier than water is not a property stated and has no bearing on the teaching. The reason for the care is that oxygen is highly flammable. Tell: the key property is flammability.

Correct. Oxygen is highly flammable, which is why home oxygen teaching includes no smoking in the home, staying away from heat sources, avoiding petroleum products and posting signs. Oxygen is not just air, and fire is a listed hazard.

Oxygen does not turn into carbon monoxide. Carbon monoxide appears in the teaching only as a reason for working carbon monoxide alarms. Tell: alarms detect carbon monoxide; flammability is the property of oxygen.

E.io: Discuss the selection and application of oxygen delivery
E.q: A 73-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is ready for discharge after his treatment is optimized. His resting saturation on room air is 87%, and he has no pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale (right-sided heart failure from lung disease) or high hematocrit. How often will his home oxygen be recertified?
opts: An interval of every 1 month is not one of the stated intervals. The two are 12 months for Group I and 3 months for Group II. Tell: only 12 months and 3 months appear as recertification intervals, and his criteria give 12.

Every 3 months applies to Group II, the conditional group with a saturation of 89% plus pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%. He has none of those and a saturation of 87% qualifies him as Group I. Tell: earlier recertification goes with a chronic complication.

Correct. His resting room-air saturation is 87%, at or below 88%, which is the Group I qualification (conditional Group II needs a comorbidity such as pulmonary hypertension, cor pulmonale or a hematocrit above 56%). Group I patients are recertified every 12 months.

An interval of every 24 months is not stated either; Group I is recertified at 12 months and Group II at 3 months. Tell: with an uncomplicated resting saturation of 87%, the answer is the longer listed interval, 12 months.
